generated_by: Claude (Cowork), five drafting agents plus a merge review. Model-drafted framing: read the protocol notes.
sources_note: Built from the four review packets, seeds, deterioration timelines and review matrices, the current case JSON (ground truth), CHANGELOG v0.18a to v0.18c, and the v0.18a audit doc.
protocol_notes: Independence: each physician answers every question before seeing any other reviewer's answer or the recommendation. The tool should also hide the other reviewers' answers until all have submitted.

Anchoring beyond the recommendation: the context, the option wording and the order of options were written by the same model that drafted much of the content under review. Tell reviewers this, give every question a free-text "none of these" answer, and ask them to flag any question they think is framed to favor an option.

Play before reading: each case reviewer should play their case cold, at least once in the default mode and once doing nothing, before opening its question bank. The bank then cannot shape their first impression, and the 14.3 checklist's final item is met by a physician rather than by tests.

Conflicts of interest: a physician who wrote a case's seed should not be the only signer of questions about departures from that seed, and the product owner should not be the only signer of platform choices they made as owner. Reviewers should declare any relationship to the product (equity, pay, co-authorship) and to vendors of drugs or devices named in a case. Claude must never record a sign-off, only apply decisions a named physician made.

Who signs: name one accountable physician per case (an EM attending) and one for the platform set. Where a question is outside EM (DIPH toxicology, AFRVR and CHFE cardiology, MGCA infectious disease or critical care), add a relevant specialist reviewer for that case's high-priority items. Record name, date, the case pack SHA-256 reviewed and the question id with every answer.

Disagreements: agree the rule before review starts. A suggested rule is that disagreement on a high-priority item goes to a short synchronous discussion between the reviewers. If they still disagree, the more conservative option (the one less likely to teach harm) is applied, the item is marked contested, and the debrief note says that practice varies. Record dissent with the decision rather than overwriting it.

Measure agreement: before the full review, have all reviewers answer the same five platform questions and compare. Low agreement on those means the questions or options need rewriting before anyone answers the rest.

Verification evidence: for "verify" items, the reviewer should attach what they looked at (a screenshot, the source passage, the clip), so a later reader can see what was checked, not only that it was.
Scope and fatigue: the full set is long. Order sessions by priority, cap each session at about 45 minutes, and allow "defer" as an answer rather than forcing a guess.

Re-review triggers: any change Claude makes after sign-off (including applying these answers) changes the pack hash. Define in advance which changes need a fresh sign-off (any tag, deadline, vital, halt reason, result or note text) and which do not (layout, spelling).

Separate decision from release: signing a question means the decision is made, not that the case is released. Release still needs the 14.3 checklist completed against the updated pack, played end to end in the interface.
merge_log: AFRVR-14 (untreated respiratory failure plateau) removed and merged into ALL-03, whose recommendation contradicted it.
ALL-03 option C replaced (non-terminal peri-arrest phase would exceed AFRVR's six-phase ceiling) with an escalation option; recommendation changed B to C to respect the AFRVR seed instruction.
CHFE-22 recommendation changed A to B so it no longer contradicts ALL-22 and ALL-23.
Relabelled 72 verify-task options so 'confirmed' reads as the outcome of the reviewer's own check, not as a claim that the content is correct.

An independent verifier re-checked all 58 high-priority questions against the case files. It found 5 errors and 13 minor issues, and all were corrected. The worst: CHFE-06 option B softened the beta-blocker tag in the one phase where he is at 74/46, and DIPH-11 argued fairness from Easy-mode prompt times.
Prompt times quoted in questions are Easy-mode figures unless a question says otherwise. Normal mode, the default, triples prompt deadlines but not deterioration deadlines (see ALL-02).

cases.title: Atrial fibrillation with RVR and acute decompensated HFrEF, 68M
cases.summary: A 68-year-old man arrives by EMS with a day of palpitations and breathlessness: AF at 160, BP 132/78, RR 30, SpO2 88 percent on room air, and a newly found EF of 30 to 35 percent with diffuse B-lines on bedside ultrasound. The case crosses two axes, breathing supported or not and rate controlled or not, into six phases: arrival, breathing supported, rate controlled but congested, stabilized, respiratory failure (reached at four minutes without a mask) and intubated, plus a halt and a handoff. The seed supplied the diagnosis, vitals, exam, ECG, labs, ultrasound findings, the six critical actions, the diltiazem nuance, the accepted drugs, the three wrong paths, the endpoint and the disposition. A model supplied the phases, every deadline and effect size, the two-dose rate-control rule, the halting crystalloid bolus, the interview beyond your history, the consultants, every note and reference, and the v0.18a audit corrections, none of which a physician has signed. AFRVR is generated from case_1_shell.py and case_2_actions.py (plus content and interview generator parts not in this upload), so edits go in the .py sources and a rebuild overwrites hand edits to the JSON.

cases.title: Acute decompensated HFrEF with hypertensive acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema (SCAPE), 65M
cases.summary: A 65-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 25 to 30 percent) arrives by EMS after five days off furosemide and a salt load: HR 118, BP 188/104, RR 32, SpO2 85 on 6 L, warm and wet. The live phases are a two-by-two of positive pressure against a nitrate (presentation, niv_supported, nitrate_responding, stabilizing), then diuresis (improving), a timed slide into impending_respiratory_failure when a treatment is missing, and a post_intubation_hypotension branch whenever he is intubated. There is no physician seed: a language model wrote every number, tag, deadline, halt and note, so you are authoring ground truth in review. The v0.18a audit on 28 Sep 2026, also model-drafted, then changed many tags and notes (beta blockers, sedation, airway, softened halts, nitrate routes, discouraged traps, gases), and those changes need your sign-off as well.

cases.title: Diphenhydramine overdose with QRS widening and seizure, 18F
cases.summary: An eighteen-year-old woman arrives by EMS delirious, dry and 40.1 C, about five hours after swallowing a bottle of diphenhydramine, with her mother as the only historian. On arrival the QRS is already 132 ms on a tracing nobody has ordered. At 240 seconds she seizes unless bicarbonate and a benzodiazepine or propofol are already in, then passes through a post-ictal phase, and untreated blockade leads to a stable wide-complex tachycardia and pulseless VT, while bicarbonate narrows the QRS and cooling plus a toxicology call reach the stabilized phase. Dr Kelly Medwid supplied the patient, the presenting vitals, the exam, the laboratory values, the four-minute seizure, the physostigmine trap and the debriefing guide. Everything else (phases, later vitals, deadlines, ECG numbers, reference ranges, the magnesium, most tags and all wording) is model output, and DIPH-SEED.md is itself a conversion document in which only the quoted passages are her words. The v0.18a audit of 28 September 2026 changed physostigmine, flumazenil, procainamide and the seizure rules, so the review packet is stale on those points.

cases.title: Meningococcemia with septic shock, DIC and adrenal crisis (Waterhouse-Friderichsen), 21F
cases.summary: A previously well 21-year-old college student arrives by EMS with fever, severe limb pain and a non-blanching rash on her ankles, in compensated septic shock with hyponatremia, hyperkalemia and hypoglycemia from bilateral adrenal hemorrhage. The case has two deficits treated by two drugs: an antibiotic for the organism and hydrocortisone for the adrenal failure, plus volume, and it branches into adrenal crisis or progressive meningococcemia depending on which is missing, then frank shock, then (on the clock) arrest. The intended path is arrival to improving to ICU handoff, with a vasopressor-dependent resolution when the meningococcal branch was entered. The seed supplied the diagnosis, six states with vitals and labs, the triggers, five critical actions, the LP constraint and age and sex. The model wrote every tag, halt, note, consultant and interview answer, and the v0.18a audit changed several of them on 28 Sep.

questions.title: Is four minutes without positive pressure the right time for him to start tiring?
questions.question: If no positive pressure has been applied 240 seconds after arrival, the case moves him to respiratory failure. Is that a deadline you will defend, and is the nurse's warning early enough in the default difficulty mode?
questions.context:
He arrives at a saturation of 88 percent on room air, a respiratory rate of 30 and a ventricular rate of 160. If the mask is not on 240 seconds after arrival, he moves to respiratory failure: HR 166, BP 118/70, RR 38, SpO2 82, drowsy at GCS 13. Supplemental oxygen raises the displayed saturation but does not stop this clock. Only the mask (flag on_niv) or a tube does.

The seed says respiratory support is an immediate priority and that he may end up intubated, but it gives no time. Four minutes is the model's compression so that wrong path three can be shown inside a ten-minute case. It is not a claim about real disease tempo.

**Warning timing.** The nurse offers CPAP or BiPAP at 80 seconds and repeats it at 200 seconds, 40 seconds before he tires. Those are the authored (Easy mode) times. The simulator starts in Normal mode, which multiplies every prompt deadline by three and does not slow the deterioration. In Normal mode the first mask prompt is due at 240 seconds, the same second he tires, and the repeat at 600 seconds. The default-difficulty decision belongs to the platform set, but it decides whether this particular deadline is fair.
questions.current: presentation.transitions[3]: when "NOT flag on_niv set", after_seconds 240, measured_from phase_entry, to respiratory_failure (case_1_shell.py, PHASES, phase "presentation"). The mask prompt is case_actions non_invasive_positive_pressure_ventilation.prompt, 80 s with escalation at 200 s (case_2_actions.py).

quotes.text: The claim is that a man at a saturation of 88 percent, a respiratory rate of 30 and a ventricular rate of 160 begins to fail inside four minutes if nothing is done for his breathing.

Teaching point: in acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema with respiratory failure, respiratory support is an immediate treatment priority, not something to defer until the arrhythmia is completely controlled.
Normal multiplies every prompt deadline, escalation and follow-up deadline by three.

options.label: Keep 240 seconds
options.detail: He tires four minutes after arrival without a mask. The nurse warns at 80 and 200 seconds in Easy mode.
options.tradeoff: Keeps the case short and the lesson sharp. In Normal mode the learner can tire before hearing any mask prompt.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off.

options.label: Lengthen to 360 seconds
options.detail: He tires six minutes after arrival. In Normal mode the first mask prompt (240 s) now lands two minutes before the deterioration.
options.tradeoff: Fair in both modes without a platform change. Weakens the urgency the seed asks for and lengthens the do-nothing path.
options.implementation: case_1_shell.py, phase presentation, the NOT flag on_niv set transition: after_seconds 240 to 360. Update its author_rationale, packet §2.1, and the Clock scenarios in AFRVR-scenarios.json. Regenerate the case JSON and the deterioration timeline.

options.label: Keep 240, fix the warning at platform level
options.detail: The clinical claim stays at four minutes. The unfair Normal-mode timing is handled by the platform default-difficulty decision (for example Easy as default, or unscaled prompts for deterioration warnings).
options.tradeoff: Separates the clinical claim from the interface question. Depends on a platform change that may not happen, and until it does the case stays unfair in Normal mode.
options.implementation: No case change. Record sign-off of 240 s and attach this case to the audit open item "Default difficulty".

questions.reasoning: Four minutes is a compression either way, and the seed's intent (support the breathing now) is served better by a short clock than a long one. The real defect is that the default mode delivers the warning at or after the deterioration, which is a platform scaling problem rather than a clinical one. The strongest argument against C is that it leaves the case unfair until the platform acts, and B fixes that inside the case today.
questions.evidence: No trial measures time to fatigue in untreated cardiogenic pulmonary edema. This is a teaching compression, stated as such in the case.
sources: audit v0.18a Open items: Default difficulty

brief: Arrives at SpO2 88 percent, RR 30, rate 160. Without mask or tube by 240 seconds, he tires.
Oxygen does not stop the clock. Four minutes is a teaching compression.
Normal mode triples prompt deadlines, so the first mask prompt lands at 240 seconds.
short.now: Respiratory failure at 240 s without mask. Nurse offers mask at 80 s and 200 s in Easy mode.

opts.A: No change. In Normal mode he can tire before hearing any mask prompt.
opts.B: He tires at six minutes. Normal-mode prompt comes two minutes earlier. Less urgency.
opts.C: Clock stays. Unfair in Normal mode until the platform changes difficulty defaults, which may not happen.

short.why: A short clock serves the seed's intent to support breathing now, and the late warning is a platform scaling problem. Against this, the case stays unfair in Normal mode until the platform acts.

resolved.decision: Keep 240 s. No change.

questions.title: Should controlling the rate restart the four-minute clock before he tires?
questions.question: When the rate is controlled without a mask, a new 240-second clock starts in the rate-controlled phase, so rate control buys up to four more minutes. Is that what you want the case to teach?
questions.context:
The second rate-control dose moves him from arrival to rate_controlled_congested (HR 108, RR 32, SpO2 86). That phase has its own 240-second exit to respiratory failure, measured from phase entry. The engine can measure only from phase entry or from when a guard became true, so the clock restarts.

The packet says the deadline was set equal "so the case does not teach that treating the rate buys time". The mechanics do the opposite. A resident who controls the rate at about 200 seconds and never applies the mask tires at about 440 seconds instead of 240. The later the rate is controlled before the first deadline, the closer the total gets to eight minutes.

The packet also offers the opposite view: a patient at 108 has better diastolic filling and might tire more slowly. When he does tire, a heart-rate workaround makes him read about 131 rather than 166, and the nurse says his rate has crept up.
questions.current: rate_controlled_congested.transitions[2]: when "NOT flag on_niv set", after_seconds 240, measured_from phase_entry, to respiratory_failure (case_1_shell.py, phase "rate_controlled_congested").

quotes.text: It is set to the same four minutes deliberately, so the case does not teach that treating the rate buys time that has not been shown to exist. If you disagree, lengthen it.
Evolution: the heart rate improves, the respiratory rate stays around 32, SpO2 stays around 86 to 89 percent, the patient remains markedly dyspnoeic, and the B-lines persist.

options.label: Keep 240 s from phase entry
options.detail: Rate control without a mask resets the clock to a full four minutes.
options.tradeoff: Simple, already tested. Contradicts the stated rationale: rate control does buy time in the simulator.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off, and correct packet §2.1 and the transition author_rationale so they describe the reset.

options.label: Shorten to 120 s
options.detail: Total time without a mask stays close to four minutes in a typical run (rate controlled at 100 to 200 s, then 120 s more).
options.tradeoff: Matches the stated intent in typical runs. No single number reproduces a cumulative clock, so a very early rate-control run tires sooner than an untreated one and a very late one still gets extra time. The 200 s mask escalation would no longer fire in that phase.
options.implementation: case_1_shell.py, phase rate_controlled_congested, the NOT flag on_niv set transition: after_seconds 240 to 120. Update author_rationale, packet §2.1, the "Wrong path 1 continued" scenario, and check the validator's stranded-prompt note for the 200 s escalation.

options.label: Lengthen to 360 s
options.detail: Accept the packet's alternative: a rate-controlled patient tires more slowly, and the case shows it.
options.tradeoff: Physiologically arguable. Teaches that treating the rate buys a lot of time, which is the reading wrong path one warns against.
options.implementation: case_1_shell.py, phase rate_controlled_congested, the NOT flag on_niv set transition: after_seconds 240 to 360. Update author_rationale, packet §2.1 and the matching scenario.

questions.reasoning: The seed's wrong path one says a lower rate does not rescue him, and the current clock rewards rate control with up to four extra minutes, which works against that lesson. A shorter second deadline keeps total unsupported time near four minutes for most runs. The strongest argument against it is physiological: a slower ventricle may genuinely tire more slowly, and B makes an early rate-control run tire sooner than an untreated one would.
questions.evidence: No data address how fast a rate-controlled but unsupported patient tires. Both directions are teaching choices.

brief: Controlling the rate without a mask starts a fresh 240-second clock in the rate-controlled phase.
The packet says equal deadlines avoid teaching that rate control buys time. The mechanics do the opposite.
The packet also notes better diastolic filling at HR 108 might slow his tiring.
short.now: Rate control without mask resets to 240 s. Rate controlled at about 200 s means tiring at about 440 s.

opts.A: Rate control buys up to four more minutes. Packet and rationale corrected to describe the reset.
opts.B: Total unmasked time near four minutes in typical runs. Very early rate control tires sooner.
opts.C: A rate-controlled patient visibly tires more slowly. Teaches that rate control buys a lot of time.

short.why: Wrong path one says a lower rate does not rescue him, yet the clock rewards rate control. Against this, a slower ventricle may truly tire more slowly, and early rate-control runs tire sooner.

resolved.decision: Second clock shortened from 240 s to 120 s.

questions.title: When drowsy and hypercapnic, should the mask stay critical and the tube only recommended?
questions.question: In respiratory failure (GCS 13, venous pH 7.22, pCO2 64) the mask is tagged critical and intubation recommended. Should both be acceptable, or should the tube be preferred?
questions.context:
The respiratory failure phase is where an untreated patient lands at four minutes. He is drowsy and confused but obeys commands, has stopped talking, and has a respiratory acidosis. The case's rescue design is that the mask still works here: applying it moves him to breathing_supported, or to stabilized if the rate is already controlled.

Tags in this phase: positive pressure critical, intubation recommended, induction agents and paralytics recommended, synchronized cardioversion neutral. Outside this phase intubation is discouraged, including in rate_controlled_congested (SpO2 86, RR 32, severe distress).

In CHFE, the v0.18a audit treated "intubating a man who can no longer protect his airway was taught as an avoidable error" as a critical finding and changed that case so mask and tube are both recommended once he is tiring. AFRVR was not changed the same way. Altered mental status is commonly listed as a relative contraindication to non-invasive ventilation, although a monitored trial in hypercapnic pulmonary edema is also common practice.
questions.current: case_actions[non_invasive_positive_pressure_ventilation].tag: critical when "phase is presentation OR phase is respiratory_failure OR phase is rate_controlled_congested". case_actions[intubate_rapid_sequence].tag: recommended when "phase is respiratory_failure", otherwise discouraged (case_2_actions.py).

quotes.text: The rescue. Positive pressure applied late still works

quotes.source: audit v0.18a Physician critical findings, CHFE
quotes.text: Intubating a man who can no longer protect his airway was taught as an avoidable error
GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6). Drowsy, confused, obeys commands. No focal deficit.

options.label: Keep: mask critical, tube recommended
options.detail: A learner who intubates in respiratory failure without trying the mask is told they missed a critical action.
options.tradeoff: Keeps the case's message that late positive pressure still rescues. Penalizes a defensible airway decision in a drowsy hypercapnic patient.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off.

options.label: Both recommended in respiratory failure
options.detail: Mask and tube are both credited as reasonable once he is tiring, as CHFE now does. The mask stays critical on arrival and in the rate-controlled phase.
options.tradeoff: Consistent across cases and fair to either airway choice. A learner who never used the mask is still reported as missing it from the arrival phase they passed through.
options.implementation: case_2_actions.py, non_invasive_positive_pressure_ventilation tag: remove respiratory_failure from the critical rule and add {"when": "phase is respiratory_failure", "value": "recommended"} above the default. Rerun the Wrong path 3 scenarios and regenerate the matrix.

options.label: Tube preferred in respiratory failure
options.detail: Intubation becomes critical in respiratory failure and the mask becomes neutral there.
options.tradeoff: Matches practice for a patient who cannot protect his airway. Removes the late-rescue lesson, and GCS 13 with obeyed commands is not clearly an airway-protection failure.
options.implementation: case_2_actions.py: intubate_rapid_sequence tag critical in respiratory_failure. Positive pressure tag neutral in respiratory_failure. Consider whether the mask should still move him to breathing_supported from that phase (case_1_shell.py).

questions.reasoning: A drowsy, hypercapnic patient who has stopped talking is a situation where both a monitored mask trial and intubation are defensible, and scoring one of them as a missed critical action overstates the certainty. B also matches the CHFE decision the audit already made. The strongest argument against it is that AFRVR's central sequencing lesson is that positive pressure works even late, and B softens the score for a learner who skips it at that point.
questions.evidence: Guidance on non-invasive ventilation in altered mental status is mostly expert consensus. Many trials excluded patients with a reduced conscious level (from memory, verify). No strong evidence favors either choice at GCS 13.
sources: audit v0.18a Fixes made: CHFE "Mask or tube both recommended once he is tiring"

brief: In respiratory failure he has GCS 13, venous pH 7.22, pCO2 64, obeys commands, stopped talking.
CHFE now credits mask and tube equally once tiring. AFRVR was not changed.
Altered mentation is a relative contraindication to the mask, though monitored trials are common.
short.now: In respiratory failure, mask critical, intubation recommended. Late mask still rescues him. Intubation discouraged elsewhere.

opts.A: Intubating without a mask trial is reported as a missed critical action.
opts.B: Either airway choice credited once tiring. Mask stays critical in earlier phases.
opts.C: Intubation critical, mask neutral in respiratory failure. The late-rescue lesson is lost.

short.why: Both a monitored mask trial and intubation are defensible here, and B matches the CHFE audit decision. Against this, the case's central lesson is that late positive pressure works, and B softens that.

resolved.decision: Mask stays critical, tube recommended. No change.

questions.title: Should metoprolol earn the critical rate-control credit before the mask is on?
questions.question: Metoprolol satisfies the critical rate-control act in every phase, while esmolol is discouraged until the mask is on and propranolol and labetalol are always discouraged. Should beta-blocker credit depend on positive pressure being in place?
questions.context:
Rate control is scored as one act. digoxin_bolus is the covering action and covers amiodarone and metoprolol, so any of the three satisfies the critical expectation at any time, including at a saturation of 88 percent with diffuse B-lines before any positive pressure. The shared note says a low-dose beta blocker is defensible "once oxygenation is supported" and is "the least forgiving of the three".

The other beta blockers are tagged on their own. Esmolol was changed in v0.18a to neutral once flag on_niv is set and stays discouraged before it. Propranolol, labetalol bolus and labetalol drip are discouraged in every phase. Propranolol's note says any beta blocker should be "given after the mask is on". The audit lists the metoprolol inconsistency as an open item and suggests crediting it only once he is on the mask.

The engine cannot do that today. Covered siblings take the covering action's tag and flags, so metoprolol cannot have its own phase rule while it stays in the group. Taking it out of the group means a learner who uses only metoprolol, even correctly after the mask, is told they missed the rate-control critical action.
questions.current: AFRVR-binding-map.json rows[digoxin_bolus].also_covers = [amiodarone_bolus_infusion, metoprolol_bolus]. case_actions[digoxin_bolus].tag critical unconditionally. case_actions[esmolol_drip].tag neutral when "flag on_niv set", else discouraged. propranolol_bolus, labetalol_bolus and labetalol_drip discouraged unconditionally (case_2_actions.py).

quotes.text: Acceptable approaches include digoxin, appropriately selected beta blockade when physiologically tolerated, or IV amiodarone.

quotes.source: audit v0.18a Open items: AFRVR metoprolol before the mask
quotes.text: The rate-control group credits metoprolol as critical even before positive pressure, while esmolol then is discouraged

Your own brief says aggressive beta blockade in active pulmonary edema is not the goal, and the case cannot express "acceptable, but the least comfortable of the three, and worse before the breathing is supported" as a tag.

options.label: Keep metoprolol credited in every phase
options.detail: Metoprolol before the mask earns the critical credit. The caveat lives only in the shared debrief note.
options.tradeoff: No false negatives and no engine work. Inconsistent with esmolol's new tag and with propranolol's own note, and it credits beta blockade before oxygenation is supported, which the case's own notes advise against and the seed's "when physiologically tolerated" arguably excludes.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off, and record that the esmolol v0.18a tag was accepted as is.

options.label: Split metoprolol out, tag it like esmolol
options.detail: Metoprolol becomes its own case action: discouraged before the mask, neutral after. It still slows the rate and counts toward the two-dose tally.
options.tradeoff: Consistent beta-blocker teaching with no engine change. A learner who uses only metoprolol, even after the mask, is reported as missing the critical rate-control act, which is a false negative.
options.implementation: AFRVR-binding-map.json: remove metoprolol_bolus from digoxin_bolus.also_covers. case_2_actions.py: add metoprolol_bolus with the esmolol tag rules, flags rate_control_given, RATE_CONTROL_REPEAT, RATE_CONTROL_HR_EFFECTS, RATE_CONTROL_ALERT and follow-up second_rate_control_dose. Change expectation_label and the digoxin prompt text to drop metoprolol. Update the "Coverage: metoprolol" scenario.

options.label: Conditional coverage (audit default)
options.detail: Metoprolol satisfies the critical act only once flag on_niv is set. Before that it is tagged discouraged and does not satisfy it.
options.tradeoff: Expresses exactly what the seed says. Needs an engine, validator and matrix change to allow a condition on a coverage entry, which touches every pack that uses coverage.
options.implementation: Engine: allow {"id": ..., "when": condition} inside also_covers, and have the debrief and matrix read it. Binding map: metoprolol_bolus covered when "flag on_niv set". case_2_actions.py: a metoprolol_bolus case action for the uncovered state, tagged discouraged, with the same flags and effects as in B.

questions.reasoning: The seed accepts beta blockade only when physiologically tolerated, and every other beta blocker in the case already follows that rule, so metoprolol is the outlier. Conditional credit fixes it without the false negative that B creates for a learner who gives metoprolol correctly after the mask. The strongest argument against C is cost: it is an engine change for one drug in one case, and B gets most of the teaching value today if you accept the false negative.
questions.evidence: My recollection is that the 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF guideline advises caution with IV beta blockers in decompensated heart failure and lists amiodarone and digoxin as options there, but I have not checked the class or the exact wording (from memory, verify). No trial compares these agents in a patient in this exact state.
sources: audit v0.18a Open items: AFRVR metoprolol before the mask
audit v0.18a Fixes made: AFRVR row 2 (esmolol neutral once on the mask, beta blocker teaching)

brief: Metoprolol shares digoxin's coverage group, so it earns critical rate-control credit in every phase, even before the mask.
Esmolol is discouraged until the mask is on. Propranolol and labetalol are always discouraged.
The engine cannot give metoprolol its own phase rule inside the group.
short.now: Digoxin, amiodarone or metoprolol satisfy critical rate control at any time. Esmolol neutral only after the mask.

opts.A: Metoprolol before the mask earns full credit. The caveat lives only in the debrief note.
opts.B: Discouraged before mask, neutral after. Metoprolol-only learners are told they missed critical rate control.
opts.C: Counts as critical only after the mask. Needs an engine change affecting every pack using coverage.

short.why: The seed accepts beta blockade only when tolerated, and every other beta blocker already follows that rule. C avoids B's false negative. Against this, engine work for one drug, and B gets most of the value today.

resolved.decision: Metoprolol is its own action: discouraged before the mask, credited as critical rate control only after it.

questions.title: Should the case prompt and reward a second digoxin dose within a minute?
questions.question: Digoxin counts toward the same two-dose rule as the other agents, so the nurse offers "another dose" 55 seconds after it and a second digoxin push controls the rate. The case's own notes say digoxin loads over hours. Which should win?
questions.context:
Every rate-control route shares one counter. The flag that turns the phase over is granted on the second administration of any of them. After the first dose, a follow-up obligation fires at 55 seconds: "Do you want me to draw up another dose?" It is discharged only by a second dose.

The v0.18a audit added text saying digoxin is the exception to this tempo. The follow-up debrief note and cardiology's third tier now say digoxin is loaded over hours. The mechanics did not change. A learner who gives digoxin, hears the prompt and gives digoxin again sees the rate controlled ten seconds later, which is the opposite of what the note says.

A mechanical fix is not simple. digoxin_bolus is the covering action for amiodarone and metoprolol, and covered siblings take its flags, so digoxin cannot get its own tempo without the same engine change as AFRVR-04 or a restructure of the group.

Cardiology's second tier, heard after one dose, also says "the answer is another dose of the same thing rather than a second drug" and "Give it again".

quotes.text: Digoxin is the exception to the tempo: its loading doses are spaced over hours, and a partial response in the first minutes is expected rather than a reason to redose.
He's slower than he was but he's still running fast. Do you want me to draw up another dose?

options.detail: Digoxin behaves like the other agents in the simulator. The debrief note explains that real digoxin is slower.
options.tradeoff: No work. The simulator rewards exactly what the note says not to do, and learners remember what worked on screen.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off.

options.label: Give digoxin its own tempo
options.detail: One digoxin dose counts as a full load, with a longer delay before the rate falls (for example 60 s). No redose prompt after digoxin.
options.tradeoff: Mechanics match the note. Needs per-route fields inside the coverage group or a restructure, and makes digoxin a one-click answer.
options.implementation: Engine: allow per-route flags_set_repeat and a digoxin-specific flag inside also_covers (same change family as AFRVR-04 C). case_1_shell.py: two extra transitions on the digoxin flag with after_seconds 60. follow_ups[second_rate_control_dose].applies_when: add AND NOT the digoxin flag.

options.label: Change the words, keep the mechanics
options.detail: The nurse's follow-up asks whether you want to give more or add something, rather than "another dose". The debrief note says the realistic second step after digoxin is waiting or adding amiodarone.
options.tradeoff: Cheap and removes the explicit prompt to redose digoxin. The simulator still rewards a second digoxin push.
options.implementation: case_2_actions.py FOLLOW_UPS second_rate_control_dose: nurse_prompt to "He's slower than he was but he's still running fast. Do you want to give more, or add something?". Edit the debrief note paragraph on digoxin. Update packet §2.2. Also edit consult_cardiology rule index 1 (flag rate_control_given set tier) so it does not advise an immediate second digoxin dose.

questions.reasoning: I am not certain here. The cleanest clinical answer is B, but it needs engine work and it turns digoxin into the easiest path through the case. C removes the part that is plainly wrong (a nurse prompting a second digoxin load one minute after the first) at almost no cost. The strongest argument against C is that the mechanics still reward the second digoxin push, so the note and the screen continue to disagree.
questions.evidence: My recollection is that IV digoxin has an onset of roughly 30 minutes or more with peak effect over hours, and that loading is split over several hours (from memory, verify). The case already states this in its notes.

questions.title: Should diltiazem stay discouraged after the ultrasound shows an EF of 30 to 35 percent?
questions.question: Diltiazem is discouraged both before and after the cardiac ultrasound has resulted. CHFE tags diltiazem harmful. Should the post-ultrasound rule change?
questions.context:
This is the decision the seed calls the central teaching point. Before the ultrasound, diltiazem is a defensible first move and a deduction. After it, the seed calls continued diltiazem a management error. The case has two tag rules that make this distinction visible in the matrix, and both resolve to discouraged.

In this engine "harmful" always halts the case. The five tiers have nothing between discouraged and harmful, so the case cannot say "error, but keep going". The seed's wrong path two describes a patient who keeps going after this error (HR 95 to 105, SBP 100 to 110, ongoing edema), which a halt would cut off. The engine also scores one entry per action, tagged from the last administration, so diltiazem given before and again after the ultrasound appears once.

The debrief note now says the 2023 guideline recommends against IV non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers in significant LV systolic dysfunction "as a harm recommendation". The audit lists this as an open item because CHFE makes diltiazem harmful.

The patient does not necessarily crash.

quotes.text: Keep discouraged, or harmful once the ultrasound has resulted

questions.title: Should magnesium replacement be critical, as the seed wrote it, rather than recommended?
questions.question: The seed's critical action four bundles the loop diuretic with addressing hypomagnesemia. The case tags magnesium replacement recommended. Should it be critical?
questions.context:
His magnesium is 1.6 mg/dL against an authored interval of 1.7 to 2.2. Magnesium is not on the basic chemistry panel, so the learner has to order it. Replacement covers both catalog magnesium entries and moves the level to 2.1 on repeat.

The model tagged replacement recommended for an engine reason. The engine fixes the set of critical actions a phase expects on entry to that phase, so a critical tag that applies only after the level has resulted cannot appear in the missed list. An unconditional critical tag would tell a learner who never ordered the level that they missed a critical action.

The counterargument is that checking and correcting electrolytes in new AF with heart failure is expected practice, so a learner who never ordered the level has missed something real. There is no nurse prompt for magnesium today.

questions.title: Should a crystalloid bolus end the case, or send him into respiratory failure?
questions.question: A crystalloid bolus halts the case in every phase except stabilized and intubated. Is a single bolus in this patient harmful enough to halt, or should it cause a deterioration he can be rescued from?
questions.context:
The seed named no harmful action. The model added one so the halted phase is reachable: any crystalloid bolus (saline or Ringer's, 1 L or 500 mL, and since v0.18a D5 NS) in a man with an EF of 30 to 35 percent and flooded lungs. The v0.18a audit rewrote the halt. The halt reason now says he needed emergency intubation, not that he died, and the halted phase now shows his own numbers (AF at 150, BP 104/62, RR 40, SpO2 76) instead of a generic peri-arrest picture. The authoring rules say harmful is for genuine lethality.

The case already has a respiratory failure phase and an intubated phase. A bolus could move him into respiratory failure instead of ending the run, so the learner has to rescue him. That works where he is not on the mask. On the mask (breathing_supported) the respiratory failure phase would exit at once, so there a vital effect would have to carry the harm.

questions.title: Is synchronized cardioversion rightly discouraged when AF is driving acute heart failure?

Cardiology's advice in the case agrees: "I would not cardiovert him today". Cardioversion needs sedation first, and it triggers a 90-second anticoagulation follow-up.

questions.title: Does every cited reference say what the case claims it says?
questions.question: Check each reference and each named guideline claim in the debrief notes against its source.
questions.context:
Every reference in the case carries "[UNVERIFIED in this pack, confirm before release]". The interface strips the marker, so the learner sees a clean citation.

**Cited in references:** 3CPO (Gray et al., NEJM 2008), the Cochrane review of NIV in cardiogenic pulmonary edema (Berbenetz et al., 2019), DOSE (Felker et al., NEJM 2011), RACE II (Van Gelder et al., NEJM 2010), LOMAGHI (Bouida et al., Acad Emerg Med 2019) and the 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF guideline (Joglar et al., Circulation 2024). The v0.18a audit corrected the guideline's citation year.

**Named in notes with no reference entry:** the 2024 ESC AF guideline (cardioversion after 24 hours), the AHA tachycardia algorithm (acute heart failure as a cardioversion criterion), and heart failure guidelines allowing nitrates alongside diuretics.

**Specific claims to check:** diltiazem note says the 2023 guideline recommends against IV non-dihydropyridine CCBs in significant LV dysfunction "as a harm recommendation". The design teaches that one IV dose is a trial and that a partial response calls for another dose rather than a switch to diltiazem. At arrival 160 becomes 138 after one dose. On the mask 152 becomes 130. The phase turns over only on the second administration. A nurse obligation fires 55 seconds after the first dose and is discharged only by a second.

The debrief reports the obligation as open if the learner never gives a second dose. In Normal mode the 55 seconds becomes 165.
questions.current: RATE_CONTROL_HR_EFFECTS minus 22 (key rate_control_hr_partial). RATE_CONTROL_REPEAT after_administrations 2. follow_ups[second_rate_control_dose].deadline_seconds 55 (case_2_actions.py).

quotes.text: One administration of any rate-controlling agent takes twenty-two beats off the ventricular rate, so 160 becomes 138 and stays there
Twenty-two beats, two doses, and fifty-five seconds are all authored figures.

options.label: Keep 2 doses, 22 beats, 55 s
options.detail: As authored.
options.tradeoff: Teaches redosing after a partial response. The numbers are invented and the redose prompt is identical for every agent (see AFRVR-05).
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off.

options.label: One adequate dose
options.detail: A single dose controls the rate after the delay. No redose obligation.
options.tradeoff: Simpler and closer to many real single-dose responses to metoprolol. Loses the partial-response lesson the case was built around.
options.implementation: case_2_actions.py: remove flags_set_repeat from the four rate-control actions and add rate_control_adequate to flags_set. Delete follow_ups second_rate_control_dose. Update narration and packet §2.2.

options.label: Two doses, smaller partial response, later prompt
options.detail: One dose takes 12 beats off (160 to 148). The nurse asks at 90 seconds.
options.tradeoff: Makes the partial response look more like a partial response and gives the learner time to decide. A smaller fall may read as a failed drug, the error the design tries to prevent.
options.implementation: case_2_actions.py: RATE_CONTROL_HR_EFFECTS minus 22 to minus 12, and the minus 13 failure effect adjusted to keep about 131. follow_ups second_rate_control_dose deadline 55 to 90. Update packet §2.2.

questions.reasoning: The two-dose design carries a specific teaching point and the numbers are plausible for display, so there is no clear gain from changing them. The strongest argument against is that 55 seconds leaves little time before the nurse prompts, which measures reading speed as much as judgment.
questions.evidence: No data fix these numbers. They are display choices.

The design teaches that a partial response calls for another dose, not a switch to diltiazem.
The redose prompt at 55 seconds becomes 165 in Normal mode.
short.now: At arrival 160 becomes 138 after one dose. On the mask 152 becomes 130. Two doses turn the phase.

opts.A: Teaches redosing. Numbers are invented and the redose prompt is identical for every agent.
opts.B: A single dose controls the rate after the delay. Loses the partial-response lesson.
opts.C: One dose takes 12 beats off, prompt at 90 s. May read as a failed drug.

short.why: The two-dose design carries a specific teaching point and the numbers are plausible for display. Against this, 55 seconds leaves little time before the prompt, measuring reading speed as much as judgment.

resolved.decision: Keep. No change.

questions.title: Should any two nodal blockers, even diltiazem then a beta blocker, count as two doses?
questions.question: All six rate-control routes share one tally, so diltiazem followed by metoprolol, or metoprolol followed by amiodarone, controls the rate. Is that what you meant?
questions.context:
Digoxin, amiodarone, metoprolol, esmolol, propranolol and diltiazem all add to rate_control_doses. Any two doses set the flag. Two diltiazem doses also control the rate, which the seed's wrong path two needs.

The v0.18a follow-up note now warns against one specific pair: "an intravenous beta blocker given shortly after intravenous diltiazem, which stacks two negatively inotropic nodal blockers". The tally treats that pair as success, and nothing scores it as a problem. Metoprolol cannot be tagged separately while it is covered by digoxin (see AFRVR-04).
questions.current: flags_set_repeat {flag rate_control_adequate, after_administrations 2, counter rate_control_doses} on digoxin_bolus (covering amiodarone and metoprolol), diltiazem_bolus, esmolol_drip and propranolol_bolus (case_2_actions.py RATE_CONTROL_REPEAT).

quotes.text: One combination to avoid is an intravenous beta blocker given shortly after intravenous diltiazem, which stacks two negatively inotropic nodal blockers.
Two attempts at nodal blockade are two attempts whichever drugs they were, and a resident stuck at 138 because they varied the agent would be a bug rather than a lesson.

options.label: Keep one shared tally
options.detail: Any two doses of any agents control the rate.
options.tradeoff: No learner is stuck at 138 for switching agents. The combination the note warns against goes unscored.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off.

options.label: Shared tally, penalize beta blocker after diltiazem
options.detail: Esmolol, propranolol (and metoprolol, if split out per AFRVR-04) are discouraged when flag ccb_given is set.
options.tradeoff: Scores the specific error the note names. Metoprolol needs the AFRVR-04 change first.
options.implementation: case_2_actions.py: add {"when": "flag ccb_given set", "value": "discouraged"} as the first tag rule on esmolol_drip and propranolol_bolus, and on metoprolol if it becomes its own action. Regenerate the matrix.

options.label: Per-agent tallies
options.detail: Only a second dose of the same agent controls the rate.
options.tradeoff: Teaches "same drug again" literally. The packet calls this a bug, and it blocks realistic add-on therapy such as digoxin then amiodarone.
options.implementation: case_2_actions.py: give each action its own counter in flags_set_repeat. Rework scenarios "Coverage: amiodarone ... two agents count as two doses".

questions.reasoning: A shared tally matches the clinical reading that two attempts at nodal blockade are two attempts, and it keeps wrong path two working. B is worth adding later if you adopt AFRVR-04's split. The strongest argument against A is that the note names a dangerous pairing and the score ignores it.

brief: All six rate-control routes share one tally. Any two doses control the rate.
The follow-up note warns against a beta blocker shortly after diltiazem, which stacks negative inotropes.
The tally counts that pair as success, and nothing scores it.
short.now: Digoxin, amiodarone, metoprolol, esmolol, propranolol and diltiazem share one counter. Any two doses control the rate.

opts.A: No learner stuck at 138 for switching agents. The warned combination goes unscored.
opts.B: Esmolol and propranolol discouraged after diltiazem. Metoprolol needs the AFRVR-04 split first.
opts.C: Only a second dose of the same agent works. Blocks add-ons like digoxin then amiodarone.

short.why: Two attempts at nodal blockade are two attempts, and a shared tally keeps wrong path two working. B can follow an AFRVR-04 split. Against this, the note names a dangerous pairing the score ignores.

resolved.decision: Keep one shared tally. No change.

questions.title: Should the rate-control delay note be rewritten, since it argues against a second dose?
questions.question: The debrief note on the rate-control transition says the delay stops a learner giving a second dose, in a case that requires one. Should it be rewritten?
questions.context:
This note is shown in the debrief timeline when the rate falls. It fires only after the second dose, because that is what grants the flag. Its reasoning dates from before the two-dose design: it says the delay prevents a second dose "because the first one appeared not to work", and that the nurse's line "will actually stop somebody redosing".

It also says "None of the three agents this case accepts" while the transition is triggered by six routes, including diltiazem, esmolol and propranolol. The nurse's narration on the same transition is "That second dose has done it", which contradicts the note beside it.

quotes.text: The reason it is not instant is that a resident who watches the number change on the same click as the injection learns that rate control is a button, and then gives a second dose because the first one appeared not to work.
That second dose has done it.

options.detail: As authored.
options.tradeoff: No work. The learner reads that a second dose is a mistake right after a second dose worked.
options.implementation: No change.

options.label: Rewrite to match the design
options.detail: Claude drafts: one dose is a partial response, a second dose of a reasonable agent controls the rate, onset is compressed to seconds here and takes minutes to hours in reality, and diltiazem also slows the rate but is the wrong drug once the EF is known.
options.tradeoff: Coherent with the rest of the case. You need to approve new learner-facing text.
options.implementation: case_1_shell.py RATE_CONTROL_NOTE: replace the text. Regenerate the case JSON and timeline.

options.detail: The timeline shows the rate change with no note.
options.tradeoff: Removes the contradiction without new text. Loses a place to explain compressed onset.
options.implementation: case_1_shell.py: drop debrief_note from both rate-control transitions.

questions.reasoning: The note contradicts the mechanics and the narration next to it, and the compressed-onset point is worth keeping. The strongest argument against B is that it is more learner-facing text to sign off, and C removes the error at no cost.

questions.title: Is a 20/10 mmHg fall the right visible cost of diltiazem?
questions.question: Diltiazem lowers the pressure by 20 systolic and 10 diastolic, starting 15 seconds after the first dose and never wearing off. Is that what you meant?
questions.context:
The seed says diltiazem must not produce a dramatic collapse, and that in wrong path two the systolic sits at 100 to 110 with a heart rate of 95 to 105. The effect does not stack, so two doses still lower the pressure by 20.

Resulting pressures: arrival 112/68, breathing_supported 106/66, stabilized 104/64 (heart rate 104, which matches wrong path two), rate_controlled_congested 98/60, respiratory_failure 98/60. The last two sit just under the seed's 100 to 110.
questions.current: case_actions[diltiazem_bolus].vital_effects: systolic_bp minus 20 (key ccb_systolic) and diastolic_bp minus 10 (key ccb_diastolic), onset_seconds 15, no duration, no phase guard (case_2_actions.py).

quotes.text: The simulation must not produce a dramatic hypotensive collapse.
Instead: heart rate 95 to 105, systolic pressure 100 to 110, persistent pulmonary edema, ongoing oxygen or NIV requirement, possible worsening heart failure symptoms.

options.label: Keep 20/10
options.detail: As authored.
options.tradeoff: Matches wrong path two in the stabilized phase. Slightly under 100 in the two congested phases.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off.

options.label: Reduce to 15/8
options.detail: Every phase stays at or above 100 systolic.
options.tradeoff: Fits the seed's stated range everywhere. Less visible, which weakens the "watch the pressure" lesson.
options.implementation: case_2_actions.py diltiazem_bolus: systolic delta minus 15, diastolic minus 8. Update the effect note and packet §2.3.

options.label: Larger fall after a second dose
options.detail: A second diltiazem dose adds a further 10 systolic, so continued use visibly costs more.
options.tradeoff: Makes continuing the drug look worse, which is the error the seed names. Needs a dose-dependent effect the engine may not support, since effects are keyed per action.
options.implementation: Engine or authoring change: a second effect granted on the second administration (for example via a flag set by flags_set_repeat on a diltiazem-only counter) with systolic minus 10. Update packet §2.3.

questions.reasoning: The numbers land on the seed's wrong path two where it matters most (on the mask, after the ultrasound), and the congested phases are only two points under the seed's range. The strongest argument against is that a fall that does not grow with continued use undersells the specific error the seed names, which C addresses at an engineering cost.
questions.evidence: The size of the fall is a teaching choice. Real responses to IV diltiazem vary widely.

brief: The seed says no dramatic collapse. Wrong path two has systolic 100 to 110, heart rate 95 to 105.
The fall does not stack, so two doses still lower systolic by 20.
Stabilized reads 104/64. The two congested phases read 98/60, just under the seed's range.
short.now: Diltiazem lowers BP 20/10 from 15 s after the first dose and never wears off.

opts.A: Matches wrong path two when stabilized. Slightly under 100 in the two congested phases.
opts.B: Every phase stays at or above 100 systolic. Weakens the watch-the-pressure lesson.
opts.C: A second dose drops systolic 10 more. The engine may not support dose-dependent effects.

short.why: The numbers land on wrong path two where it matters most, and the congested phases sit only two points under. Against this, a fall that never grows undersells continued use, the error the seed names.

resolved.decision: A second diltiazem dose takes a further 10/5 mmHg off the pressure.

questions.title: Should nitroglycerin be a neutral optional adjunct, with the high-dose bolus discouraged?

questions.title: Are the CHA2DS2-VASc count and the anticoagulant advice in the note right?
questions.question: The anticoagulation note counts CHA2DS2-VASc as four, or five with the vascular point, and says heparin is often the practical first choice while he is on the mask. Does it teach the right thing, and should it address bleeding risk as the seed asks?
questions.context:
The v0.18a audit found that the old note left out the heart failure the ultrasound had just shown. The note now counts heart failure, hypertension, age 65 to 74 and diabetes as four, and says vascular disease would make five depending on whether moderate non-obstructive plaque on CT counts. Cardiology says "at least four".

On agent: a DOAC is preferred and can start once he can swallow, and heparin is often more practical while he is on a mask. Apixaban, enoxaparin and heparin all satisfy the critical action.

The seed's critical action six is to assess thromboembolic and bleeding risk. The note says nothing in his history contraindicates anticoagulation but does not name a bleeding-risk assessment.

While he is on a mask and may still need a tube, a heparin infusion is often the more practical first choice.

questions.title: Is "do not give a third dose" the right advice after two doses in this patient?
questions.question: Cardiology and the redose note tell the learner that a rate still fast after two doses is being driven by the decompensation and should not get a third. Is that what you would say?
questions.context:
Cardiology answers in three stages keyed on rate control: before any dose it warns that one dose will not be enough, after one dose it says give another dose of the same drug and avoid diltiazem, and after two it moves on to anticoagulation, the bed and a formal echo.

The one-dose answer and the redose follow-up note both add a stopping rule. In the simulator the rate always comes down after the second dose, so a learner never sees the refractory situation. They only read the advice.

The packet names this as the claim most worth your eye.
questions.current: content_keys.consultants.consult_cardiology rule 1 (ECG and ultrasound resulted AND flag rate_control_given set) and follow_ups[second_rate_control_dose].debrief_note, third paragraph.

quotes.text: If the rate is still fast after two adequate doses, that is information rather than a reason for a third: a ventricular rate that will not come down in acute decompensated heart failure is usually being driven by the decompensation, and the treatment is the pulmonary edema and the hypoxemia rather than more nodal blockade in a ventricle that is already struggling.
That last teaching point is the one most worth your eye

options.label: Keep the stopping rule
options.detail: Two adequate doses, then treat the lung and the congestion.
options.tradeoff: Teaches not to chase the number. "Usually" is a strong word for a claim with no trial behind it.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off.

options.label: Soften to "reassess before a third"
options.detail: Treat the edema and hypoxemia first, and if the rate is still fast once those are addressed, a further dose or a second agent (for example amiodarone) may be reasonable.
options.tradeoff: Keeps the priority right without an absolute rule. Slightly less memorable.
options.implementation: Edit the third paragraph of follow_ups[second_rate_control_dose].debrief_note (case_2_actions.py FOLLOW_UPS) and the second paragraph of consult_cardiology rule 1 (content_keys generator).

options.label: Remove the stopping advice
options.detail: Cardiology after one dose says give another dose and avoid diltiazem, nothing more.
options.tradeoff: Avoids an unsupported claim. Loses a useful lesson about treating the number versus the patient.
options.implementation: Delete the "Know when to stop" paragraphs in both places.

questions.reasoning: The priority it teaches (lung and congestion before more nodal blockade) is sound, but the absolute form overstates what is known and could discourage a reasonable add-on such as amiodarone. The strongest argument against B is that residents often do chase the number, and a crisp rule may protect patients better than a hedged one.
questions.evidence: This is clinical reasoning without trial support. I know of no trial that defines when to stop escalating rate control in acute decompensated HFrEF.

brief: Cardiology and the redose note say a rate still fast after two doses should not get a third.
The note says the decompensation usually drives it. The packet flags this claim as most worth your eye.
The rate always falls after two doses, so learners only read it.
short.now: Cardiology's one-dose answer and the redose note both advise against a third dose.

opts.A: Treat lung and congestion after two doses. Usually is strong without trial support.
opts.B: Edema and hypoxemia first, then a further dose or amiodarone may be reasonable.
opts.C: Cardiology says only give another dose and avoid diltiazem. Loses a useful lesson.

short.why: Treating lung and congestion before more nodal blockade is sound, but the absolute rule overstates what is known and may deter amiodarone. Against this, residents chase the number, and a crisp rule may protect better.

resolved.decision: Softened to reassess before a third dose.

questions.title: Does each cardiology and critical care answer fit every state that triggers it?
questions.question: Read each consultant tier against the matrix rows that select it and confirm the answer is right in every combination.
questions.context:
Cardiology now has seven tiers, not the five the packet describes. Critical care has four. The combinations most likely to be wrong:

1. Cardiology rule 1 (one dose given): "another dose of the same thing rather than a second drug" then "Do not let a partial response push you toward diltiazem". If the first dose was diltiazem, the learner is told to repeat diltiazem and to avoid it in the same breath. It also says "still up around 140" when the monitor may read 130 (on the mask) or 144 (in respiratory failure).
2. Cardiology rule 3 (ultrasound resulted, ECG not yet): the packet calls this the tier most likely to be wrong. It says stay away from diltiazem and send the ECG.

questions.title: Is 'the mask moves the number, the nitrate moves the lung' a claim you will sign?
questions.question: The saturation ladder gives positive pressure a display-only +4 and gives the nitrate a +3 baseline gain, while other parts of the case say the mask alone takes the edema from severe to moderate. Which version of the mechanism should the case teach?
questions.context:
Every non-terminal phase authors the unsupported saturation, and the mask adds 4 points on top while he is not intubated. The authored baselines are 85 on arrival, 85 on the mask alone, 88 on a nitrate alone, 90 with both, 90 after diuresis and 80 when he tires. On screen that reads 85, 89, 88, 94, 94, and 80 or 84.

The notes turn that arithmetic into a mechanism claim: the mask improves the number and the work of breathing, and only afterload reduction empties the lung. The packet itself calls this a simplification, because positive pressure also lowers preload and left ventricular transmural pressure.

The case is not internally consistent on this point. The `niv_supported` phase is labeled moderate edema, its lung ultrasound reads "moderate" and its chest exam improves, yet its saturation baseline is identical to arrival. Learning objective 3 also says the mask "recruits flooded alveoli", which is a lung effect. Because the mask cannot come off before intubation, the split between baseline and effect is invisible on the monitor. What the learner meets is the framing in the notes and the debrief.

The timed debrief note in `niv_supported` also has a garbled repeated clause ("positive pressure looks like an answer because the saturation on the screen improves, and positive pressure looks like the whole answer because the saturation on the screen improves"). That needs fixing whichever option you pick.
questions.current: phases[].vitals.oxygen_saturation = 85, 85, 88, 90, 90, 80 (presentation, niv_supported, nitrate_responding, stabilizing, improving, impending_respiratory_failure) and case_actions[catalog_id=niv_bipap_cpap].vital_effects[0] adds +4 while NOT flag intubated set. phases_note states the mask moves the number and not the baseline.

quotes.source: CHFE-review-packet.md addendum 'what changed when the two treatments were separated'
quotes.text: The mask moves the number by four and the baseline by nothing. The nitrate moves the baseline by three with nothing on the patient's face.

It is also a simplification: positive pressure does reduce preload and left ventricular transmural pressure, so the honest version is that the mask moves the lung a little and the model gives it none of that movement.

Separate what positive pressure does from what a vasodilator does. The mask recruits flooded alveoli, unloads the work of breathing and modestly lowers preload and left ventricular afterload; a nitrate lowers the arterial pressure driving the edema much further. Neither alone finishes this patient.

options.label: Keep numbers and framing as authored

short.now: Monitor 85 arrival, 89 mask, 88 nitrate, 94 both. Notes say the mask moves the number, the nitrate the lung.

questions.title: Should furosemide move the saturation by nothing inside this case?
questions.question: Giving the diuretic lowers heart rate, pressure and respiratory rate but leaves the saturation exactly where it was. Do you accept zero as the oxygenation effect of diuresis within an eight to ten minute encounter?
questions.context:
Furosemide moves him from `stabilizing` to `improving`. Heart rate goes 104 to 92, pressure 144/84 to 132/80, respiratory rate 22 to 18, and the saturation baseline stays at 90 (94 on screen). Given before the mask and nitrate, it changes no vital at all, because `presentation` has no transition on the diuretic.

The intended lesson is sequencing: the resident who gives the diuretic first and watches the monitor sees nothing happen. The packet's own counterargument is that a man four kilograms over his dry weight does oxygenate better after diuresis, so 'furosemide does nothing to the sat' is true only inside the case's time window.

This part of packet section 4.0 is still current. The nitrate half of that section was overtaken in v0.15.
questions.current: case_actions[catalog_id=furosemide_iv] has no vital_effects and carries no_vital_effect_note. phases[id=improving].vitals.oxygen_saturation = 90, the same as stabilizing.

quotes.text: Diuresis in a patient four kilograms above his stated dry weight, five days off his loop diuretic, does improve oxygenation. The case now says it improves it by zero.
A resident who gives the diuretic first and watches the number sees nothing happen. That is the lesson.

options.label: Keep zero, no change
options.detail: Diuretic first produces no visible change. Diuretic after the mask and nitrate improves every vital except the saturation.
options.tradeoff: The sequencing lesson is visible, not only told. Risks teaching that diuresis does not help oxygenation at all.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off.

options.label: Give the improving phase a small saturation gain
options.detail: You pick a gain you can defend at about ten minutes, for example one or two points on the improving baseline.
options.tradeoff: More honest about diuresis. Blurs the sequencing signal slightly, and the number is still a teaching choice rather than a measurement.
options.implementation: Set phases[id=improving].vitals.oxygen_saturation to your value (and case_complete if you want the handoff snapshot to match). Update phases_note and furosemide_iv.no_vital_effect_note.

options.label: Keep zero on the monitor, state the time horizon
options.detail: The monitor is unchanged, and the furosemide debrief note adds one sentence saying the oxygenation benefit of diuresis arrives over hours, beyond this encounter.
options.tradeoff: Keeps the visible lesson and stops the learner generalizing it. Costs a sentence in an already long note.
options.implementation: Add one sentence to case_actions[catalog_id=furosemide_iv].debrief_note (Claude drafts, you approve). No numeric change.

questions.reasoning: The visible 'nothing happens' is the most effective way the case teaches sequencing, and a one or two point gain would not change practice. The risk is the over-generalization the packet names, and one sentence in the note addresses it. The strongest argument against C is that IV furosemide has a described early venodilating effect, so zero may be wrong even at ten minutes and B would be more accurate.
questions.evidence: Early venodilation after IV furosemide before diuresis is described in older small hemodynamic studies, and a transient neurohormonal vasoconstrictor response has also been reported (from memory, verify). Neither supports a specific saturation change at ten minutes.

brief: Furosemide lowers heart rate, pressure and respiratory rate but leaves saturation at 90 (94 on screen).
Given before the mask and nitrate, it changes no vital. That is the sequencing lesson.
The packet notes a man four kilograms over dry weight does oxygenate better after diuresis.
short.now: Furosemide has no saturation effect. The improving phase baseline stays 90, same as stabilizing.

opts.A: Diuretic first shows no change. Risks teaching that diuresis does not help oxygenation at all.
opts.B: You pick a small gain, such as one or two points. Blurs the sequencing signal slightly.
opts.C: Monitor unchanged. One debrief sentence says the oxygenation benefit of diuresis arrives over hours.

short.why: The visible 'nothing happens' teaches sequencing best, and one sentence prevents over-generalizing. But IV furosemide may have an early venodilating effect, so zero may be wrong even at ten minutes.

questions.title: Are the 240, 240 and 300 second deterioration clocks defensible?
questions.question: Without both treatments he tires into `impending_respiratory_failure` after 240 s with neither, 240 s on the mask alone, or 300 s on the nitrate alone, and that phase never ends the case. Do you sign these deadlines and the non-lethal design?
questions.context:
Three time-guarded transitions arrive at `impending_respiratory_failure` (HR 126, BP 176/98, RR 38, SpO2 80, drowsy, alertness 2). The venous gas there is pH 7.21, pCO2 68. The patient stops answering history questions. Both treatments together return him to `stabilizing`, and intubation leads to post-intubation hypotension. No clock ever reaches a terminal phase, so a resident who does nothing sits in this phase indefinitely.

Each rule carries 'AUTHOR SIGNATURE REQUIRED'. The model chose the numbers as a teaching tempo. The niv_supported clock is the most aggressive clinically: a patient on CPAP or BiPAP without a nitrate often improves in practice, and NIV failure is usually judged over a longer window than four minutes.

Default difficulty (Normal) triples prompt deadlines but not these clocks. In Normal mode the nitrate is first asked for at 180 s and the NIV escalation (90 s authored) arrives at 270 s, after the 240 s deterioration. Default difficulty is a platform decision, but it changes how fair these clocks are.

Post-intubation hypotension also has no clock: a resident who never starts a pressor stays at 74/46 until handoff.
questions.current: phases[id=presentation].transitions[4] (240 s, NOT on_niv AND NOT nitrate_given), phases[id=niv_supported].transitions[3] (240 s, NOT nitrate_given), phases[id=nitrate_responding].transitions[3] (300 s, NOT on_niv), all to impending_respiratory_failure, which is non-terminal with one non-tube exit (on_niv AND nitrate_given).

quotes.text: AUTHOR SIGNATURE REQUIRED. The claim is that a sixty-five year old man in hypertensive acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema at a saturation of 85 percent and a respiratory rate of 32 begins to tire inside four minutes if nothing is done. Four minutes is compressed against real disease tempo the way every deadline in these packs is. The guard names both treatments so that either one alone stops it, which is the fairness claim: a learner who did something is not punished for not doing everything.

quotes.source: CHFE-review-packet.md addendum, 'Three deadlines, none of them yours'
quotes.text: 240, 240 and 300 seconds are mine.
Neither can kill the patient: no transition in this case reaches a terminal phase on the clock, and the only terminal phases are the handoff and a harmful action.

options.label: Keep 240/240/300, non-lethal
options.detail: Delay costs the history and forces an airway decision, but never kills him.
options.tradeoff: Keeps the medical-student-safe design and a clear cost of delay. Compresses real NIV-failure tempo hard, most of all for the mask-only clock.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off on each author_rationale (replace 'AUTHOR SIGNATURE REQUIRED' with your initials and date).

options.label: Lengthen the clocks
options.detail: For example keep 240 s with neither treatment, and lengthen mask-only and nitrate-only to values you choose.
options.tradeoff: Closer to real disease and fairer under Normal-mode prompt tripling. Weakens the felt cost of partial treatment in a ten-minute case.
options.implementation: Edit after_seconds in phases[id=niv_supported].transitions[3] and phases[id=nitrate_responding].transitions[3] (and presentation[4] if you change it). Rerun engine/deterioration_timeline.py and the CHFE scenarios.

options.label: Keep the clocks, add a lethal end
options.detail: A further timed transition from impending_respiratory_failure (and optionally from post_intubation_hypotension without a pressor) to halted after a duration you choose.
options.tradeoff: Makes inaction truly consequential. Conflicts with medical_student in target_level and needs a timeout_reason that attributes the arrest to omission.
options.implementation: Add timed transitions with measured_from phase_entry to 'halted' plus a timeout_reason, update phase_notes.deterioration_path, and update the engine assertion that no clock reaches a terminal phase.

questions.reasoning: The clocks are a teaching tempo, and the non-lethal design suits the stated learner range. I am least confident about the mask-only clock, which asserts NIV failure in four minutes in a patient who would often improve on CPAP alone. The strongest argument against A is exactly that clock plus Normal-mode prompt tripling, which together can make a learner who did the right first thing deteriorate before the nurse escalates.
questions.evidence: No trial measures time to NIV failure without a nitrate in this phenotype at minute scale. 3CPO patients on standard oxygen alone mostly avoided intubation (from memory, verify), which argues these clocks are compressed.

brief: He tires into impending respiratory failure after 240 s with neither, 240 s mask-only, 300 s nitrate-only.
That phase never ends the case, even if nothing is done.
Mask-only clock is most aggressive. In Normal mode the NIV escalation prompt arrives at 270 s, after deterioration.
short.now: Clocks at 240, 240 and 300 s lead to HR 126, SpO2 80, pH 7.21. None is lethal.

opts.A: Delay costs the history and forces an airway decision, never death. Compresses real NIV-failure tempo.
opts.B: You choose longer mask-only and nitrate-only clocks. Weakens the felt cost of partial treatment.
opts.C: Inaction eventually halts the case after a duration you choose. Conflicts with targeting medical students.

short.why: The clocks are a teaching tempo and the non-lethal design suits the learner range. Against it, the mask-only clock plus Normal-mode prompt tripling can make a learner who did the right first thing deteriorate before the nurse escalates.

questions.title: Is the nitrate dosing and evidence note right as rewritten?
questions.question: The v0.18a audit rewrote the nitroglycerin note to cite GALACTIC, ELISABETH and an ESC 2021 downgrade, and to describe high-dose practice. Is the dosing and evidence summary what you want a learner to take away?
questions.context:
The infusion's button reads 'start 50 to 100 mcg/min, titrate'. The note says emergency practice commonly starts at 100 mcg/min or more, titrates toward 200 to 400 mcg/min, and sometimes gives an IV bolus of 400 to 1000 mcg first. The two overlap at 100 but give different impressions of a starting dose.

The note frames the benefit as faster relief of the crisis rather than proven survival, citing Cotter 1998 for a vasodilator-forward strategy and GALACTIC and ELISABETH as neutral on longer-term outcomes. Only Cotter and the 2022 AHA guideline appear in the references list. GALACTIC, ELISABETH and ESC 2021 are named in text only, from model memory.

This is audit Fixes-made row 'Physiology wording, furosemide dose, nitrate evidence...' and needs sign-off.
questions.current: case_actions[catalog_id=nitroglycerin_infusion].display_name = 'Nitroglycerin infusion, start 50 to 100 mcg/min, titrate'. debrief_note as quoted. references: Cotter 1998 (checked), Heidenreich 2022 (unverified).

quotes.text: larger recent strategy trials (GALACTIC, JAMA 2019; ELISABETH, JAMA 2020) found no improvement in longer-term outcomes and ESC 2021 downgraded intravenous vasodilators from IIa to IIb, so the justification is faster relief of the crisis rather than proven survival benefit.

Doses are far higher than anti-anginal doses: emergency practice commonly starts at 100 mcg/min or more and titrates every few minutes toward 200 to 400 mcg/min, sometimes after an intravenous bolus of 400 to 1000 mcg.
Physiology wording, furosemide dose, nitrate evidence, troponin wording, Nohria framework, carvedilol continued

options.detail: Button says 50 to 100 start, note describes common high-dose practice and neutral outcome trials.
options.tradeoff: Accurate framing of weak evidence, and the numbers overlap. A learner may still leave unsure what to start at.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off. Add GALACTIC, ELISABETH and ESC 2021 to the references list marked for verification.

options.label: Commit to high-dose SCAPE framing in both places
options.detail: Button and note both teach a high starting rate with rapid escalation and an optional bolus.
options.tradeoff: One clear message matched to SCAPE teaching in many EDs. The supporting evidence for high-dose nitrate strategies is observational and small, so this states practice more firmly than the data.
options.implementation: Change display_name to your wording (for example 'start 100 mcg/min or more, titrate rapidly'), edit the dosing sentence, keep the evidence sentence.

options.label: Conservative guideline-style dosing

options.tradeoff: Closest to generic guideline dosing and least likely to be read as a protocol. Undersells the high-dose approach many EM physicians use for SCAPE.
options.implementation: Change display_name and the dosing sentence to your numbers. Remove the bolus sentence here and in case_actions[catalog_id=nitroglycerin].debrief_note if you want consistency.

Moving the button to high-dose language would harden a practice supported mainly by observational data. The strongest argument against A is that a learner reading 50 on the button and 100 or more in the note gets a mixed message on the one number they will act on.
questions.evidence: GALACTIC (Kozhuharov, JAMA 2019) and ELISABETH (Freund, JAMA 2020) were neutral on their primary outcomes (from memory, verify). ESC 2021 gives IV vasodilators class IIb (from memory, verify). High-dose nitroglycerin series in SCAPE are observational (from memory, verify).

brief: The note says practice commonly starts at 100 mcg/min or more. The two overlap but read differently.
The note frames benefit as faster crisis relief, not proven survival.
GALACTIC, ELISABETH and ESC 2021 appear in text only, from model memory.
short.now: Button starts 50 to 100 mcg/min. Note titrates toward 200 to 400, sometimes after a 400 to 1000 mcg bolus.

opts.A: Button and note unchanged. Honest on weak evidence, but learners may be unsure of starting dose.
opts.B: Both teach a high start, rapid escalation, optional bolus. States practice more firmly than the data.
opts.C: Both teach a lower start and stepwise titration, no bolus. Undersells the high-dose approach for SCAPE.
