questions.title: Should one sublingual tablet or a bolus count the same as a nitrate infusion?
questions.question: Any nitrate (0.4 mg sublingual, IV bolus, nitroprusside or the infusion) sets the same permanent flag and moves the phase for good, but only the nitroglycerin infusion satisfies the critical nitrate action. Is that the right split?
questions.context:
Since v0.18a the IV nitroglycerin bolus and nitroprusside 'act'. All four nitrate routes set `nitrate_given`, a permanent flag, so a single sublingual tablet moves him to `nitrate_responding` or `stabilizing` and he never slides back as it wears off. The same flag also rescues `impending_respiratory_failure` together with the mask.

Scoring differs from physiology. `nitroglycerin_infusion` is critical in every phase before a nitrate has been given, so it is on the expected list of every run. The sublingual note calls its credit 'partial'. Nitroprusside, a sustained titratable vasodilator, is only recommended, so a learner who chooses it misses the critical nitrate.

Two mechanical gaps follow. Nitroprusside sets `nitro_infusion_running`, but the catalog's 'Stop Nitroprusside' button is unbound, so it does not set `nitro_stopped`, and after intubation the only exit is pressing 'Stop the nitroglycerin infusion' for a drug that is not running. The blood-pressure-cycling follow-up fires only for the nitroglycerin infusion, although the nitroprusside note says it needs an arterial line.
questions.current: nitroglycerin_sublingual, nitroglycerin (IV bolus), nitroprusside_drip and nitroglycerin_infusion all set nitrate_given. Only nitroglycerin_infusion is tagged critical (presentation, niv_supported, nitrate_responding, impending_respiratory_failure). Others default to recommended. stop_nitroprusside has no binding in CHFE-binding-map.json.

quotes.text: `nitroglycerin_infusion` is critical in every phase where it has not been given, so it is on the expected list of every run.
Credit here is partial: the right idea, an incomplete execution.

PDE5 inhibitor question added. IV nitroglycerin bolus and nitroprusside act. Post-intubation hypotension escapable without a running nitrate. Push-dose epinephrine no longer counts as a running pressor

options.label: Keep as authored
options.detail: Any route moves the physiology for good. Only the infusion satisfies the critical action.
options.tradeoff: Simple and forces the titratable drug. A single tablet producing a lasting cure is unrealistic, and choosing nitroprusside is scored as a miss.
options.implementation: No change except binding stop_nitroprusside to nitroglycerin_stop via also_covers in CHFE-binding-map.json so the post-intubation exit works. Record sign-off.

options.label: Any sustained vasodilator satisfies the critical action
options.detail: The nitroglycerin infusion or nitroprusside satisfies the critical nitrate. Sublingual and bolus still move the phase and stay recommended.
options.tradeoff: Scores the clinical decision (sustained afterload reduction) rather than the drug. Keeps the unrealistic lasting effect of one tablet.
options.implementation: Bind nitroprusside_drip into the critical action (move it under nitroglycerin_infusion via also_covers, or give nitroprusside_drip the same critical tag rules). Bind stop_nitroprusside to nitroglycerin_stop. Add nitroprusside_drip to follow_ups[id=bp_cycling_after_nitrate].triggered_by.

options.label: Make short-acting nitrates wear off
options.detail: Sublingual and bolus set an expiring flag. Without an infusion by the time it expires, he returns to the untreated edema phase.
options.tradeoff: Most realistic, and teaches why the infusion matters without scoring alone doing it. Needs timed mechanics, new transitions and a duration you sign, and more to review.
options.implementation: Replace nitrate_given on nitroglycerin_sublingual and nitroglycerin with an expiring flag (duration you choose), add return transitions from nitrate_responding and stabilizing guarded on NOT nitro_infusion_running, and include B's binding fixes.

questions.reasoning: The clinical decision is sustained afterload reduction, and nitroprusside meets it, so scoring it as a missed critical action is hard to defend. B also fixes the stuck post-intubation exit. The strongest argument against B is that it leaves the one-tablet cure in place, which C fixes at a real authoring and review cost.
questions.evidence: Sublingual nitroglycerin acts within minutes and lasts roughly 20 to 30 minutes (from memory, verify). Nitroprusside is listed as an alternative vasodilator in heart failure guidance (from memory, verify).

brief: All four nitrate routes, even one 0.4 mg sublingual tablet, permanently move the phase.
Only the nitroglycerin infusion satisfies the critical nitrate. Nitroprusside, a sustained vasodilator, is only recommended.
The Stop Nitroprusside button is unbound, so exiting after intubation needs the nitroglycerin stop button.
short.now: Any nitrate sets a permanent flag. Only the nitroglycerin infusion is critical. Others are recommended.

opts.A: Stop button fixed. One tablet still cures for good, and nitroprusside scores as a miss.
opts.B: Nitroprusside now counts. Stop button and BP follow-up fixed. One tablet still has a lasting effect.
opts.C: Tablet and bolus wear off. Without an infusion he returns to untreated edema. More to review.

short.why: The clinical decision is sustained afterload reduction, and nitroprusside meets it, so scoring it a miss is hard to defend. B also fixes the stuck post-intubation exit. Against it, the one-tablet cure remains.

questions.title: Should every IV beta blocker halt the case in every live phase?
questions.question: The audit extended the metoprolol halt to labetalol (bolus and drip), esmolol and propranolol, with one halt reason, in every phase including after he has improved. Do you sign that?
questions.context:
The sinus tachycardia of 118 is set to bait IV rate control. Before v0.18a only metoprolol was guarded, so labetalol, the drug most likely to be reached for as 'blood pressure control', was an unscored route to the same harm. Now `metoprolol_iv` covers `labetalol_bolus`, `labetalol_drip`, `esmolol_drip` and `propranolol_bolus`, and all halt with the same reason.

The tag is unconditional, so the halt applies in `improving` (HR 92, BP 132/80) as well as on arrival. The audit softened other halts 'where he was no longer at risk' but not this one.

The authoring guide reserves harmful for genuine lethality. Guidelines advise against starting or up-titrating beta blockade in acute decompensation, but a single IV dose being fatal is a teaching exaggeration. In AFRVR, esmolol is neutral once the patient is on the mask, so the same act scores differently across cases (a platform policy item).
questions.current: case_actions[catalog_id=metoprolol_iv].tag = [{when: null, value: harmful}], expectation_label names metoprolol, labetalol, esmolol or propranolol. CHFE-binding-map.json row metoprolol_iv also_covers labetalol_bolus, labetalol_drip, esmolol_drip, propranolol_bolus.

quotes.text: Only metoprolol was guarded: labetalol, esmolol and propranolol were unscored routes to the same harm

You gave an intravenous beta blocker to a patient in acute decompensated heart failure whose cardiac output depended on his heart rate and endogenous adrenergic drive; acute beta blockade dropped stroke volume and rate together, and he progressed to cardiogenic shock and arrested.
Reserve `harmful` for genuine lethality

options.label: Keep: all IV beta blockers halt in every phase
options.detail: Any IV beta blocker at any point ends the run with the cardiogenic shock halt reason.
options.tradeoff: The case's central trap, taught at maximum strength with no escape route. Overstates single-dose lethality, most of all once he has improved.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off.

options.label: Halt while decompensated, discouraged once improving
options.detail: Harmful in presentation, niv_supported, nitrate_responding, impending_respiratory_failure, stabilizing and post_intubation_hypotension. Discouraged in improving and intubated_stabilized.
options.tradeoff: Matches the audit's 'softened where no longer at risk' logic used for pressors and fluid. Adds rule complexity and a learner could read discouraged-late as permission.

options.label: Discouraged, with a deterioration instead

options.implementation: Change metoprolol_iv.tag to discouraged, remove halt_reason, add transitions 'flag beta_blocker_given set' to your chosen phase in each live phase, update debrief_configuration and scenarios.

questions.evidence: ACC/AHA and ESC heart failure guidance advise against initiating or increasing beta blockers during acute decompensation (from memory, verify). No trial measures immediate harm from a single IV dose in this phenotype.

brief: Sinus tachycardia of 118 baits IV rate control. Labetalol, esmolol and propranolol now halt like metoprolol.
The halt applies in every phase, including improving at HR 92, BP 132/80.
The guide reserves harmful for genuine lethality. A single fatal IV dose is a teaching exaggeration.
short.now: Any IV beta blocker is harmful and halts the case in every phase with a cardiogenic shock reason.

opts.B: Discouraged in improving and intubated stabilized phases. More rules, and late use may read as permission.

questions.title: Should a single dobutamine order still halt the case?
questions.question: Dobutamine halts the case with sustained VT in all six non-intubated phases and is neutral after intubation. Keep it harmful, make it discouraged, or model it as a deterioration?
questions.context:
He is warm, well perfused and hypertensive, so there is nothing for an inotrope to fix. The packet and the debrief note both call this the most debatable harmful designation in the case: the evidence against inotropes concerns outcomes over an admission, not immediate arrest.

The dobutamine debrief note still contains reviewer-facing text that a learner will read: it ends by saying 'the reviewing physician should decide whether it should instead be a deterioration path'. The audit removed reviewer wording from other notes but not this one.

After intubation dobutamine is neutral, while the norepinephrine note says an inotrope alone would drop the pressure further in that phase.
questions.current: case_actions[catalog_id=dobutamine_infusion].tag: neutral in post_intubation_hypotension, harmful in presentation, niv_supported, nitrate_responding, stabilizing, improving, impending_respiratory_failure, default neutral. halt_reason describes VT and collapse.

quotes.text: Modelling a single order as immediately fatal is a teaching-emphasis choice, not an evidence claim.

This is the most debatable harmful designation in the case: the physiological argument is strong, but calling a single dobutamine order immediately lethal is a modeling choice made for teaching emphasis, and the reviewing physician should decide whether it should instead be a deterioration path.

options.detail: Any dobutamine before intubation ends the case with sustained VT.

questions.title: Is the crystalloid tagging right, now that its own note contradicts it?
questions.question: Any crystalloid bolus halts before intubation and is discouraged after it, but the debrief note still says it 'remains harmful' after intubation. Which tagging do you want, so the note can be made to match?
questions.context:
The fluid bolus is the commonest reflex in a tachycardic unwell patient, and the case uses one action to cover all four catalog boluses (NS and LR, 1 L and 500 mL). Before v0.18a it halted in every phase. The audit softened it to discouraged in `post_intubation_hypotension` and `intubated_stabilized`, under the heading "halts softened where he was no longer at risk". The packet (section 4.4) had already argued that a fluid challenge in post-intubation hypotension is a common and often reasonable reflex.

The debrief note was not updated and still teaches that fluid remains harmful after intubation. The packet (section 4.4) is also stale on this point.

The halt still applies in `stabilizing` and `improving`, where the audit made pressors discouraged because he was 'no longer at risk'. A 500 mL bolus in the improving phase halting with 'he arrested' is the weakest part of the current rule.

quotes.text: Note that this remains harmful in the post-intubation hypotension phase: the hypotension there is vasodilation and reduced venous return in a fluid-overloaded patient, and the treatment is a vasopressor and stopping the nitrate, not volume.

questions.title: Should vasopressors halt in the hypertensive phases, and via every route?

questions.context:
No one is likely to start a pressor at 188/104. The packet already questioned whether halting for it is more punitive than instructive. The audit then softened both to discouraged in `stabilizing` and `improving`.

Only two catalog routes are guarded. The catalog also offers an epinephrine drip, dopamine drip, phenylephrine bolus and drip, and vasopressin bolus and drip. None is bound in CHFE, so each gets a neutral tag and a generic note in every phase. The sign-off checklist asks that every harmful and discouraged action cover every catalog route to the same act.

The intubation note tells the learner to have a vasopressor drawn up before induction. In `impending_respiratory_failure` (BP 176/98), starting norepinephrine just before intubation halts the case.

questions.title: Once he is tiring, is 'mask or tube, both recommended' right?
questions.question: In `impending_respiratory_failure` both NIV and intubation are tagged recommended and neither is critical, while the exam there says he is no longer clearing secretions. Do you sign this airway teaching?
questions.context:
Before v0.18a, intubating a man who could no longer protect his airway was scored as an avoidable error. The audit made both the mask and the tube recommended once he is tiring and rewrote the intubation note.

In this phase he is drowsy (alertness 2), pCO2 68 on the venous gas, saturation 80. A mask plus a nitrate returns him directly to `stabilizing` (mild edema) the moment both are in place. If he reached this phase already on the mask, a nitrate alone rescues him.

The airway exam in this phase reads 'Patent, but no longer speaking or clearing secretions.' Inability to clear secretions is a common relative contraindication to NIV, which sits awkwardly beside a recommended mask trial and an instant full recovery on it.

questions.title: Should every intubation produce post-intubation hypotension (74/46)?
questions.question: Intubation from any live phase sends him to `post_intubation_hypotension` at 74/46, with or without a nitrate running. Is certain collapse the right model?
questions.context:
The engine has no probability, so the choice is between always and never. The packet argued for always, on the anticipation lesson in learning objective 7. It also offered a gate: collapse only when a nitrate infusion is running at intubation.

His pre-intubation shock index is about 0.63 and he is hypertensive, so profound collapse is less likely without a vasodilator running. The phase description still blames 'ongoing nitrate vasodilation' even when no nitrate was given. The transition's author note still calls him 'preload-dependent', wording the audit removed from the learner-facing descriptions.

Since v0.18a the exit no longer requires stopping a nitrate that is not running (see the post-intubation exit question).

quotes.text: Post-intubation hypotension is common but not universal, and this patient's pre-intubation shock index is around 0.63, which is not high-risk.
You may prefer to gate it on the nitrate infusion being running, which would be a small change to one transition condition.

Intubation in a preload-dependent, vasodilated patient predictably drops the blood pressure. Modeled as certain here for teaching; see review packet, this is the most debatable transition in the case.

questions.context:
The v0.18a audit added `propofol_infusion` as its own case action so propofol could be discouraged while he is hypotensive. Its default rule is recommended, and unlike the post-intubation sedation action it has no 'flag intubated set' prerequisite. The catalog only requires IV access.

So in `presentation` (SpO2 85, RR 32, pCO2 54) the learner can start a propofol infusion and the case scores it as recommended. It also sets the `post_intubation_sedation` flag. This looks like an unintended side effect of the audit fix rather than a design choice.

Nothing in the review packet discusses it, because it postdates the packet.

quotes.text: Sedation after intubation is required, and propofol is a reasonable agent once the pressure has recovered. While he is hypotensive, sedate with ketamine or small doses of fentanyl, then change agents once he is on a stable pressor dose.

questions.title: Which vasopressors should end post-intubation hypotension?
questions.question: He leaves `post_intubation_hypotension` only when a norepinephrine infusion is running and no nitrate infusion is running. Push-dose epinephrine does not count, and an epinephrine drip, vasopressin, phenylephrine or dopamine do nothing. Which agents should count?
questions.context:
Since v0.18a the exit is 'pressor running AND (nitrate stopped OR no nitrate infusion running)', so a patient intubated without a nitrate needs only the pressor. Push-dose epinephrine no longer counts as a running pressor.

Only `norepinephrine_infusion` sets `pressor_running`. A learner who chooses an epinephrine infusion or vasopressin, both defensible in some hands, stays at 74/46 with no feedback. There is no clock in this phase, so nothing else happens until handoff. The norepinephrine note justifies preferring it over epinephrine with a randomized trial stopped early.

Stopping the nitrate is critical here (prompt at 25 s) and norepinephrine is critical (prompt at 40 s).
questions.current: phases[id=post_intubation_hypotension].transitions[0].when = 'flag pressor_running set AND (flag nitro_stopped set OR NOT flag nitro_infusion_running set)'. pressor_running is set only by norepinephrine_infusion. epinephrine_push_dose sets push_dose_epi_given and is recommended here.

Norepinephrine is generally preferred over epinephrine in cardiogenic shock, where a randomized comparison was stopped early for a higher rate of refractory shock in the epinephrine arm.

options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off. Consider a nurse line on other agents so the learner is not stuck without explanation.

options.detail: Any of these sets pressor_running and restores him. Norepinephrine stays critical, the others recommended or neutral.
options.tradeoff: Credits agents a reasonable EM physician might choose, while norepinephrine remains the taught first choice. Epinephrine in cardiogenic states carries the concerns the note describes.
options.implementation: Add a case action bound to epinephrine_drip with also_covers vasopressin_drip that sets pressor_running, tagged recommended in post_intubation_hypotension. Coordinate with the vasopressor-before-hypotension question, which proposes the same binding.

options.implementation: Same binding as B, also covering phenylephrine_drip and dopamine_drip, with phenylephrine and dopamine tagged discouraged in this phase.

Norepinephrine remains the only critical agent. The strongest argument against B is simplicity: A gives one right answer and the note explains it, and B adds a binding and tags to review.

Levy 2018 (JACC) epinephrine versus norepinephrine in post-MI cardiogenic shock was stopped early for refractory shock (from memory, verify).

questions.title: Are nitrates after intubation tagged right: halting, then discouraged?
questions.question: Any nitrate halts the case in `post_intubation_hypotension` and is discouraged in `intubated_stabilized` (108/68 on norepinephrine). The packet had made both harmful. Which do you want?
questions.context:
The packet (section 5.2) records a defect where the nitrate fell through to recommended in `intubated_stabilized` and was fixed by making it harmful there too. The v0.18a audit then softened it to discouraged, as part of 'halts softened where he was no longer at risk'.

All four nitrate routes carry the same rule. The sublingual halt reason describes an arrest after a sublingual tablet in a sedated, intubated patient, a route that is not realistic in that state.
questions.current: nitroglycerin_infusion, nitroglycerin_sublingual, nitroprusside_drip, nitroglycerin (bolus): harmful in post_intubation_hypotension, discouraged in intubated_stabilized.

quotes.text: Extended the harmful condition to both phases.
You gave sublingual nitroglycerin to a patient who was already hypotensive after intubation; further vasodilation dropped his coronary perfusion pressure and he arrested.

options.label: Keep: halt while hypotensive, discouraged once on a pressor
options.detail: A nitrate at 74/46 ends the case. Restarting one at 108/68 on norepinephrine costs points.
options.tradeoff: Halts where the harm is immediate and softens where it is an error of judgment. Restarting a vasodilator in a pressor-dependent patient is still a serious error.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off. Optionally block nitroglycerin_sublingual when flag intubated set with a nurse message.

options.label: Halt in both intubated phases
options.detail: Restore the packet's design.
options.tradeoff: Strongest teaching that a pressor-dependent patient gets no vasodilator. Claims lethality at 108/68 on a pressor, which is weaker.
options.implementation: Change the intubated_stabilized rule to harmful in all four nitrate actions and extend halt reasons to mention the pressor.

options.label: Discouraged in both intubated phases
options.detail: No nitrate halts. The debrief carries the lesson.
options.tradeoff: Consistent with the tag guide's lethality bar. At 74/46 a vasodilator is plausibly lethal, and C loses that signal.
options.implementation: Change the post_intubation_hypotension rule to discouraged in all four actions and remove their halt_reasons.

questions.reasoning: The tag should follow the risk: at 74/46 a vasodilator plausibly causes arrest, at 108/68 on a pressor it is a clear error but not an immediate death. Blocking the sublingual route in an intubated patient is a sensible extra. The strongest argument against A is that the packet's defect fix made both harmful for a reason, and an error in a pressor-dependent patient is dangerous enough that some would halt it.

brief: At 74/46 after intubation, any nitrate halts the case.
At 108/68 on norepinephrine, the audit softened it to discouraged. The packet had made both harmful.
The sublingual halt reason describes a tablet in a sedated, intubated patient, which is unrealistic.
short.now: All four nitrate routes harmful in post-intubation hypotension, discouraged in intubated stabilized.

opts.A: At 74/46 it halts, at 108/68 it costs points. Restarting on a pressor remains serious.
opts.B: Restores the packet's design. Strongest lesson, but claims lethality at 108/68 on a pressor.
opts.C: No nitrate halts, the debrief teaches. Loses the signal at 74/46, where arrest is plausible.

short.why: The tag follows the risk. At 74/46 a vasodilator plausibly causes arrest, at 108/68 on a pressor it is a clear error but not immediate death. Against it, the packet's fix made both harmful for a reason.

questions.title: Consultants give pre-intubation advice for an intubated patient: fix how?
questions.question: In `intubated_stabilized` (and partly in `impending_respiratory_failure`) cardiology and critical care fall through to rules written for the awake patient on a mask. How should these be fixed?
questions.context:
Both consultants have a phase rule only for `post_intubation_hypotension`. Everything else resolves on flags and studies, and flags are permanent.

In `intubated_stabilized`, with the ECG and troponin resulted, cardiology says to keep going with positive pressure and the nitrate, to admit him somewhere monitored, and that they will see him on the ward round. The patient is intubated on norepinephrine with the nitrate stopped. Critical care, because `on_niv` and `nitro_infusion_running` stay set after intubation, says the treatment is right and to keep the mask on and keep titrating the nitrate. Without those flags it asks whether he is on positive pressure yet.

In `impending_respiratory_failure` with the mask on and no nitrate, critical care says 'good, the mask is the right move' about a man tiring under it. This is the same class of defect as the four the packet fixed during drafting.
questions.current: content_keys.consultants.consult_cardiology rule 0 and consult_critical_care rule 0 are 'phase is post_intubation_hypotension'. No rule for intubated_stabilized or impending_respiratory_failure.

quotes.text: | «any other phase» | yes | yes | rule 1 (flag on_niv set AND flag nitro_infusion_running set) | plausible |

quotes.text: He will need a bed that can keep the mask on and keep titrating the nitrate, so that is us or the coronary care unit depending on who has space.
Keep going with positive pressure and the nitrate, diurese him properly, and keep his carvedilol going at his home dose once he is taking tablets, since he is warm and perfusing.

options.tradeoff: Each consultant says the right thing in every reachable state. Four new pieces of consultant text to review.
options.implementation: Insert rules 'phase is intubated_stabilized' and 'phase is impending_respiratory_failure' at the top of content_keys.consultants.consult_cardiology and consult_critical_care, then regenerate the matrix.

options.tradeoff: Fewer new lines. The existing text is about a patient who just dropped his pressure, which reads oddly once he is stable on a pressor, and the impending phase stays unfixed.
options.implementation: Edit the when and value of rule 0 in both consultants.

options.label: Leave as is
options.detail: Rarely reached states keep their current replies.
options.tradeoff: No work. A learner who consults after intubating hears advice that is clinically wrong for the patient in front of them.
options.implementation: No change.

questions.reasoning: Both phases are reachable in ordinary play, and the current replies contradict the patient's state, which is exactly the matrix failure the sign-off checklist asks you to rule out. Critical care says keep the mask on and keep titrating the nitrate, because those flags stay set.
Tiring on the mask without a nitrate, critical care still praises the mask.
short.now: Both consultants have a dedicated rule only for post-intubation hypotension. Other phases fall through to awake-patient rules.

opts.A: Four new consultant replies, drafted by Claude, for your review. Right advice in every reachable state.
opts.B: Post-intubation text also covers the stable phase. Reads oddly there, and the tiring phase stays unfixed.
opts.C: No work. Learners who consult after intubating hear clinically wrong advice.

questions.title: Should asking about PDE5 inhibitors before a nitrate be scored?

questions.context:

Nitrates are not gated on it and the debrief does not flag its absence. In real SCAPE care, many clinicians ask this in seconds or give the first dose before asking in a patient at low risk of use. The note's instruction is therefore stronger than what the scoring checks.
questions.current: interview.topics[topic=pde5_inhibitor_use], interview.must_ask includes pde5_inhibitor_use, interview.key_topics includes it. No case action or prerequisite references it.

questions.title: Is the rewritten furosemide dose teaching right for a 40 mg-only button?
questions.question: The only diuretic button is furosemide 40 mg IV (a catalog fixed dose), and the audit-rewritten note says 40 mg is the floor for a man on 40 mg daily and 80 mg is equally defensible. Is that the teaching you want?
questions.context:
The note cites DOSE and says guidelines advise an IV dose at least equal to the total daily oral dose, with 1 to 2.5 times the usual range. He takes 40 mg daily, so 40 mg IV meets the floor.

The catalog carries the dose in the entry name, so the learner cannot choose 80 mg. The catalog's fixed furosemide dose is an open platform item. Diuretic is critical in `stabilizing` and recommended elsewhere, and its prompt fires 60 s after `stabilizing` begins.

options.detail: The button is the floor dose, the note says so and names 80 mg as defensible.
options.tradeoff: Honest about the limitation. A learner can never choose the dose the note says is equally good.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off. Leave the fixed dose to the catalog rename pass.

questions.title: Is morphine correctly tagged discouraged?

questions.title: How should the critical adherence question be credited?
questions.question: Asking about medication adherence is critical in every phase and is credited only through the free-text matcher or a volunteered answer. Keep it, accept the precipitant at handoff (the audit's default), or change it?
questions.context:
The audit (v0.18a) listed this as open: a critical action depends on the free-text matcher. Its suggested default is also to accept the precipitant named at handoff. The handoff currently takes a disposition and diagnoses from the catalog, with no precipitant field.

The explanation reasons that NIV plus a titrating vasoactive infusion needs a unit that can continue both. That is institution-dependent, and the case says so. The care setting (cardiology, critical care and interventional cardiology in house) is authored per case because the correct disposition depends on it.

Several explanations assume a nitrate infusion is running. A learner who used only sublingual or bolus nitrates, or who has come off the mask, reads an explanation that does not match their run. The observation-unit explanation says he required a vasoactive infusion.

questions.title: Does the case play correctly start to finish, including a halt?
questions.question: The sign-off checklist requires the case to be played in the interface. Please play it and say whether anything looked wrong.
questions.context:
How to check. Use the local build `build/simulator.html`, which has a review speed control at the bottom right (1x to 16x, keys [ and ]). Play at least four runs.

Run 1, intended path: monitor, IV, mask, nitrate infusion, ECG, film, gases, labs, ask about his tablets, furosemide once 'responding', urine output, hand off to ICU. Watch the saturation reach 94.
Run 2, a halt: give IV metoprolol or labetalol. Read the halt reason and the debrief.
Run 3, do nothing for four minutes: confirm the move to 'tiring', then rescue with mask plus nitrate and confirm the return to 'responding'.
Run 4, intubate: induction and paralytic, tube, then stop the nitrate and start norepinephrine, then sedation. Try propofol before intubation, and try a consult in the intubated stable phase.

The validator and the matrix read the case file only. Neither can see what the interface does not render.

questions.title: Where should the hepatojugular reflux appear in the neck exam?
questions.question: After the audit's neck exam change, hepatojugular reflux appears only in the intubated phases, and not in the awake patient whose JVP reaches the jaw sitting up. Is that right?
questions.context:
The catalog has no discrete HJR maneuver, so it was folded into the neck exam. The packet says it happens automatically whenever the neck is examined, which is no longer true: the awake finding is 'JVP to the angle of the jaw sitting upright, at least 14 cm. Trachea midline.' The intubated finding adds 'Hepatojugular reflux positive.'

questions.title: Should the arrival seizure stay escapable with bicarbonate plus a benzodiazepine?
questions.question: The source says the seizure happens regardless of performance. The case now lets a resident avoid it by giving sodium bicarbonate and a benzodiazepine (or propofol) before about 230 seconds. Keep the escape, delete it, or tie it to the ECG?
questions.context:
Dr Medwid wrote the seizure as scripted natural history: it happens at four minutes whatever the resident does. On Aakash Setty's instruction of 5 September 2026 the arrival phase gained an arrow to the narrowing phase. If bicarbonate and an anticonvulsant are both on board, she moves to `stabilizing` ten seconds later and never convulses. The 240-second seizure rule itself is unchanged and unguarded.

Since v0.18a the anticonvulsant half of the guard is a benzodiazepine OR a propofol bolus OR a propofol infusion. The guard does not look at the ECG. A resident who gives bicarbonate empirically, before any tracing, escapes as well. The case's own `intended_path_note` says the opposite, so that note is wrong whichever option you choose.

Consequences you are signing. The intended path is now arrival, narrowing, stabilized, so the seizure teaching (about a third of the case, per the packet) is off the best path. There is a ten-second dead zone: the escape needs ten seconds to mature, so a pair completed at 235 seconds still seizes. No nurse prompt asks for a benzodiazepine or bicarbonate in the arrival phase (the benzodiazepine prompt is guarded to the seizing and wide-complex phases, the bicarbonate prompt to seizing, post-ictal and wide-complex), so the escape needs both drugs unprompted.

The case itself calls the pharmacology weak: a patient with a large diphenhydramine ingestion may seize through an adequate benzodiazepine dose. Preventing the seizure outright is a teaching choice, not physiology.

What remains a teaching choice rather than a physiological certainty is that the combination PREVENTS the seizure rather than making it less likely.
A resident who seized has not necessarily done anything wrong, because the escape needs the ECG ordered, resulted, read and acted on inside about 230 seconds, and most runs will not manage it.

questions.title: Is physostigmine harmful in every wide-QRS phase and only discouraged once stabilizing?
questions.question: The v0.18a audit made physostigmine halt the case in the arrival, seizing, post-ictal and wide-complex phases whether or not the ECG was read, and discouraged (no consequence) in the stabilizing and stabilized phases. Is that the right line?
questions.context:
The author's instruction was that physostigmine is harmful and leads back to a seizure requiring bicarbonate. The engine cannot do both: a harmful tag halts the case at once and bypasses every transition. The first conversion split it on the ECG: harmful before the tracing resulted, discouraged with a seizure ten seconds later after it. The v0.18a audit rated that a critical error, because it scored reading the wide QRS and then giving physostigmine more leniently than giving it blind.

**The packet is stale here.** Packet §2.1, the §2.0a physostigmine gap and the §2.9 point about the five-second ECG window all describe the old split. The seizure arrow was removed in v0.18a.

One inconsistency in the current line. The stabilizing phase's own ECG reads QRS 104 ms, and learning objective 2 defines sodium-channel blockade as a QRS above 100 ms. The case's toxicologist says not to give physostigmine while the QRS is anything other than normal. Yet physostigmine in `stabilizing` is only discouraged and does nothing. The debrief note says the halt applies while the QRS is wide, which is not true of this phase.

The halt reason now reads as bradycardia, then seizure, then arrest. Packet §11 asked whether it should use the narrative's bradycardia-and-seizure or the scenario flow's arrest. It now uses both. See DIPH-46 for that wording.

questions.question: The source narrative says the examinee should recognize the lack of an R wave in aVR, while three other source passages say the terminal R is the finding. The case authors it present at 5 mm with R/S above 0.7. Is that right?
questions.context:
This is one of the three source contradictions the seed resolved by drafting assumption (§9.2). The whole ECG teaching rests on it: the arrival tracing (as described by cardiology), the objective, the debrief notes and the physostigmine note all name the terminal R in aVR.

Values now authored across the tracings: arrival 5 mm, seizing 6 mm, wide-complex 7 mm, arrival after bicarbonate 3 mm, stabilizing 2 mm, stabilized 1 mm. The arrival tracing itself is an image with no words, so the 5 mm reaches a resident only through the cardiology consult or the debrief. None of these numbers is in the source.

If 'the lack of' is right, every tracing, the ECG debrief note, the cardiology consult, objective 2 and the physostigmine note need rewriting.
questions.current: content_keys.imaging.ecg_12_lead text reports carry a terminal R in aVR in the seizing (6 mm), wide-complex (7 mm), arrival-after-bicarbonate (3 mm), stabilizing (2 mm) and stabilized (1 mm) rules. The arrival rule is an image with no text, and the pulseless_vt report does not mention aVR. content_keys.consultants.consult_cardiology reads 'terminal R wave about 5 millimeters, R to S ratio over 0.7' for the arrival tracing. metadata.learning_objectives[1] names a terminal R wave in aVR.

quotes.text: The examinee should recognize the lack of a significant R wave in lead aVR and should also note a wide complex rhythm.
There may be a large terminal R in lead AVR.
Terminal R wave in lead aVR. Increased R-to-S ratio in aVR.

options.label: Present at 5 mm, as authored
options.detail: The narrative's 'lack of' is treated as a slip. Every tracing and consult keeps the terminal R.
options.tradeoff: Agrees with three of four source statements and with standard teaching. The 5 mm is invented.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off in DIPH-review-packet.md and DIPH-review-matrix.md. Amend DIPH-SEED.md §9.2 to record the author's confirmation.

options.label: Present, but described qualitatively
options.detail: Keep the finding but drop invented millimeter values: 'prominent terminal R wave in aVR, R/S greater than 0.7'.
options.tradeoff: Removes invented precision the source never gave. Loses the link to the >3 mm threshold the source itself cites, which is a useful anchor for learners.
options.implementation: Edit content_keys.imaging.ecg_12_lead report strings, consult_cardiology texts and case_actions[ecg_12_lead].debrief_note in case_2_actions.py and the builder that writes content_keys. Keep the >3 mm threshold sentence in the physostigmine note.

options.label: Absent, as the narrative says
options.detail: The QRS width alone carries the sodium-channel teaching. aVR is described without a terminal R.
options.tradeoff: Follows one sentence of the source. Contradicts the source's own teaching text and standard toxicology teaching, and requires rewriting every tracing, the objective and several notes.
options.implementation: Rewrite every ecg_12_lead report, consult_cardiology, consult_toxicology, metadata.learning_objectives[1], and the ecg_12_lead and physostigmine debrief notes. Amend DIPH-SEED.md §3.6 and §9.2.

questions.reasoning: Three of the four source statements, and standard teaching, say the terminal R in aVR is a marker of sodium-channel blockade, so 'the lack of' is most plausibly a slip. Keeping a number also ties to the >3 mm threshold the source quotes for withholding physostigmine. The strongest argument against is that 5 mm is invented and the author may have meant something specific. Only she can say what the narrative sentence meant.
questions.evidence: R in aVR of 3 mm or more predicted seizures or dysrhythmia in TCA overdose (Liebelt et al. 1995, from memory, verify). Diphenhydramine produces the same ECG pattern in case reports (from memory, verify). No source gives this patient's values.

brief: The source narrative says 'lack of a significant R wave in aVR.' Three other passages describe a terminal R.
Every tracing, the objective, the consult and debrief notes rely on the terminal R.
None of the millimeter values come from the source.
short.now: Cardiology reads a 5 mm terminal R in aVR, R/S over 0.7. Later tracings range 1 to 7 mm.

opts.A: Treats 'lack of' as a slip. No tracing changes, but the 5 mm is invented.
opts.B: Drops millimeter values for 'prominent terminal R, R/S greater than 0.7'. Loses the >3 mm anchor.
opts.C: QRS width alone carries the teaching. Every tracing, the objective and several notes need rewriting.

short.why: Three of four source statements and standard teaching support a terminal R, so 'lack of' is most plausibly a slip. A number also ties to the >3 mm threshold. Against, 5 mm is invented.

questions.title: What should replace the arrival ECG image that shows about 165/min, not 135?
questions.question: The v0.18a learner review found the arrival twelve-lead image shows a rate near 165 per minute, while the case says sinus tachycardia at 135. Replace the image, return to a text report, or change the numbers?
questions.context:
The arrival ECG is the pivot of the case, and it is the one study a resident must read unaided: it resolves to a picture with the caption 'Twelve-lead ECG' and no text. The monitor, the presenting vitals, the EMS handover ('130 to 140') and the cardiology consult all say 135.

The seed never settled which of the two source tracings is the arrival one: 'That the remaining image is the arrival tracing rather than the repeat' is listed as still a drafting assumption. Both source tracings are wide-complex. The second was removed from the narrowing phase because it did not look narrow. A rate near 165 fits neither the arrival phase (135) nor the seizing phase (150) exactly, and fits the wide-complex phase (180) no better.

Provenance of the image is also open (see DIPH-16). A text report removes that question for this image.
questions.current: content_keys.imaging.ecg_12_lead default rule: `{kind: image, image: diph-ecg-arrival, caption: Twelve-lead ECG}`. Presentation vitals HR 135 (case_1_shell.py PHASES presentation).

quotes.text: DIPH's arrival ECG image shows a rate near 165 per minute while the case says 135
Replace the image, or return to a text report
That the remaining image is the arrival tracing rather than the repeat.

options.label: Return the arrival ECG to a text report
options.detail: The resident gets a written report: sinus tachycardia 135, QRS 132 ms, terminal R in aVR, rightward terminal axis, QTc 495, no ST elevation.
options.tradeoff: Removes the contradiction and the provenance risk at once, and puts 132 ms back on screen. Loses the skill of reading a tracing unaided, which the case was redesigned around.
options.implementation: content_keys.imaging.ecg_12_lead: replace the default image rule with a report rule using the numbers in consult_cardiology. Move media/diph-ecg-arrival.jpg to cases/DIPH/assets/. Update imaging.authoring_note, seed §9.10 and packet §2.9. Rebuild (the build inlines media/ whole).

options.label: Keep the image and change the case to match it
options.detail: Presenting heart rate becomes about 165 in the arrival phase, monitor, handover and every text that says 135.
options.tradeoff: Keeps the picture. Overrides the author's own presenting heart rate of 135, which is her value, and ripples through the vitals, exam lines, consults and scenarios.
options.implementation: Edit case_1_shell.py presentation HR, patient.ems_handover_text, content_keys.exam.exam_card default, consult_cardiology, and seed §3.2 and §3.3. Rerun all scenarios.

options.label: Source a replacement tracing that matches
options.detail: Find a licensed or original twelve-lead showing sinus tachycardia near 135 with QRS about 130 ms and a terminal R in aVR.
options.tradeoff: Best teaching result if a suitable tracing exists. Needs sourcing, licensing and a physician read of the new image before release.
options.implementation: Add the new file to cases/DIPH/media/, point the default rule's image at it, record its provenance in provenance.unused_source_material, and move the old file to assets/. Until then, apply option A.

questions.reasoning: A tracing that contradicts the monitor on the case's pivot teaches the wrong habit, and a text report fixes that today without overriding an author value. It also closes the provenance question for this image and restores the 132 ms. The strongest argument against is that the case was deliberately built so the resident reads the tracing, and text does the reading for them. Option C restores that if a matching tracing can be found and licensed.

questions.title: Is the chemistry bicarbonate of 13 right, with the source's CO2 of 34 an error?
questions.question: The source chemistry gives CO2 34 mEq/L and its gas gives HCO3 13. The case carries 13 in both. Is 13 correct, and do you accept that with the author's chloride of 109 the anion gap is only 13?
questions.context:
This is the seed's §9.4 drafting assumption. With sodium 135 and chloride 109, a bicarbonate of 34 gives an anion gap of minus 8, which is impossible, so the case treats 34 as a transcription error.

A second-order issue the packet does not raise. With 13, the gap is 13, close to normal on most assays. The bicarbonate has fallen by about 11 while the gap has risen little, so most of the acidosis is non-gap (hyperchloremic). Nothing in the case explains a non-gap acidosis, and the lactate of 3.1 is the stated cause. The case's own comment acknowledges this.

The post-bicarbonate chemistry (Na 141, K 3.1, Cl 107, HCO3 21) is model output and is covered in DIPH-19.
questions.current: content_keys.labs.basic_chemistry_chem_7 default rule: Na 135, K 3.8, Cl 109 (flagged), HCO3 13 (flagged), BUN 12, Cr 0.8, glucose 120.

quotes.text: A bicarbonate of 34 gives an anion gap of negative 8, which is not a number a patient can have.
A metabolic acidosis with an anion gap of 13, near normal, so the lactate explains only part of the fall in bicarbonate.

options.label: Keep 13 and the author's chloride of 109
options.detail: Bicarbonate 13 in the chemistry and the gas. Anion gap 13.
options.tradeoff: Consistent with the pH and changes only the one impossible value. Leaves an unexplained non-gap component a sharp resident may ask about.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off in DIPH-review-packet.md and DIPH-review-matrix.md. Amend DIPH-SEED.md §9.4 with the author's confirmation.

options.label: Keep 13 and lower the chloride so the gap is raised
options.detail: Chloride about 102, giving a gap near 20 that fits lactate, ketosis (urinalysis ketones 1+) and a seizure-prone agitated patient.
options.tradeoff: Makes the acid-base story coherent. Changes a second author value that is not itself contradictory.
options.implementation: content_keys.labs.basic_chemistry_chem_7 default: Cl 102, set abnormal false, rewrite the comment. Post-bicarbonate panel: adjust Cl to keep its gap plausible. Seed §3.6.

options.label: Keep the source's 34 and remove the acidosis
options.detail: Chemistry CO2 34. The gas is rewritten to a near-normal or alkalotic picture.
options.tradeoff: Honours the chemistry figure. Overrides the author's pH 7.28, HCO3 13 and lactate-driven acidosis, and removes the acidemia that the seizure and bicarbonate teaching depend on.
options.implementation: Rewrite content_keys.labs.arterial_blood_gas and venous_blood_gas defaults and every note that cites pH 7.28 or bicarbonate 13 (chemistry, gas, seizure note, intubation note). Large change.

questions.reasoning: Thirteen is the only value consistent with the author's pH, gas bicarbonate and lactate, and changing one impossible number is the smallest defensible correction. The non-gap component is real but minor and does not change management. The strongest argument against is that a learner doing the arithmetic finds an acidosis that does not fit its stated cause, which option B would fix at the cost of a second author value.
questions.evidence: Arithmetic only. Anion gap reference ranges vary by analyser (from memory, verify).

brief: Source chemistry gives CO2 34, but its gas gives HCO3 13. The case uses 13 in both.
With sodium 135 and chloride 109, 34 gives an impossible gap of minus 8.
With 13 the gap is only 13, so most of the acidosis is non-gap and unexplained.
short.now: Chemistry shows Na 135, Cl 109, HCO3 13. Gas bicarbonate is also 13. Anion gap 13.

opts.A: Changes only the impossible 34. The non-gap component stays unexplained.
opts.B: Chloride about 102, gap near 20, fitting lactate and ketosis. Changes a second author value.
opts.C: Gas rewritten near-normal or alkalotic. Overrides pH 7.28 and removes the acidemia the teaching needs.

short.why: Thirteen is the only value consistent with the author's pH, gas bicarbonate and lactate, and it changes just one impossible number. Against, a learner doing the arithmetic finds an acidosis that does not fit its stated cause.

questions.title: Should the arrival gas keep pCO2 28, changed by v0.18a from the author's 34?
questions.question: The author's gas is pH 7.28, pCO2 34, HCO3 13. The v0.18a audit changed the pCO2 to 28 so the three values agree. Accept the change, or restore 34 and adjust another value?
questions.context:
The three source values cannot all be true. By the Henderson-Hasselbalch relation, pCO2 34 with HCO3 13 gives a pH near 7.20, and pH 7.28 with pCO2 34 needs an HCO3 near 15. The audit kept pH and HCO3 and moved pCO2 to 28, which is also what Winter's formula predicts for full compensation (1.5 x 13 + 8 = 27.5).

**The packet is stale here.** Packet §1 lists 'the gas' among values carried unchanged, and seed §3.6 still lists pCO2 34. The case's own verify note on this panel still says all five values are the author's. The arterial gas action's own debrief note is also stale: it still reads pCO2 34 and "partly compensated".

Clinically, pCO2 34 with pH 7.20 would mean inadequate respiratory compensation, which fits an agitated patient about to seize and supports the case's teaching that ventilation matters. pCO2 28 means she is compensating fully at a respiratory rate of 25.
questions.current: content_keys.labs.arterial_blood_gas default rule: pH 7.28, pCO2 28, pO2 94, HCO3 13, lactate 3.1. Comment: 'The pCO2 is revised from the source's 34 to 28 so that the three values agree.' Venous gas default: pH 7.25, pCO2 31, HCO3 13.

quotes.text: An appropriately compensated metabolic acidosis on room air. The pCO2 is revised from the source's 34 to 28 so that the three values agree.
The five values are the author's.
Arterial blood gas pH 7.28, pCO2 34 mmHg, pO2 94

options.label: Keep pCO2 28
options.detail: Compensated metabolic acidosis, as now.
options.tradeoff: Internally consistent and keeps the author's pH and bicarbonate. Changes an author value, so the verify note and seed must say so.
options.implementation: Keep values. In case_2_actions.py, edit the arterial_blood_gas debrief note to read pCO2 28 and "an appropriately compensated metabolic acidosis". Rewrite the verify note to say four values are the author's and pCO2 was revised. Amend DIPH-SEED.md §3.6 and packet §1. Rebuild.

options.label: Restore pCO2 34 and set pH 7.20
options.detail: A mixed metabolic and relative respiratory acidosis.
options.tradeoff: Keeps the author's pCO2 and bicarbonate and strengthens the ventilation teaching. Overrides the author's pH, and a pH of 7.20 is a sicker arrival patient than the source describes.
options.implementation: content_keys.labs.arterial_blood_gas default: pCO2 34, pH 7.20, comment rewritten. Recalculate the venous gas default to match. Update every note citing pH 7.28 (the arterial_blood_gas and basic_chemistry_chem_7 debrief notes in case_2_actions.py, and the seizing phase's 120 s author_rationale in case_1_shell.py).

options.label: Restore pCO2 34 and set HCO3 15
options.detail: pH 7.28, pCO2 34, HCO3 15 in the gas, and 15 in the chemistry.
options.tradeoff: Keeps the author's pH and pCO2. Overrides the bicarbonate that DIPH-05 just defended and lowers the anion gap to 11.
options.implementation: content_keys.labs.arterial_blood_gas, venous_blood_gas and basic_chemistry_chem_7 defaults: HCO3 15. Update the chemistry comment, seed §3.6 and every note that cites 13.

questions.reasoning: Keeping the pH and the bicarbonate preserves the two numbers the case teaches from, and 28 is what full compensation predicts. The strongest argument against is that it silently overrides a physician's value and makes the patient look better compensated than an agitated, pre-seizure patient might be, which option B would show. Whatever you choose, the verify note that calls all five values the author's must change.
questions.evidence: Henderson-Hasselbalch and Winter's formula arithmetic. No clinical evidence question.
sources: audit v0.18a Fixes made: DIPH row 5 (gases)

brief: The author's pH 7.28, pCO2 34 and HCO3 13 cannot all be true. v0.18a changed pCO2 to 28.
28 is what full compensation predicts. 34 would mean inadequate compensation, fitting an agitated patient about to seize.
The verify note still calls all five values the author's.
short.now: Arterial gas pH 7.28, pCO2 28, pO2 94, HCO3 13, lactate 3.1. Described as appropriately compensated.

opts.B: Mixed metabolic and relative respiratory acidosis. Overrides the author's pH for a sicker arrival patient.

questions.title: Should flumazenil halt the case only after a benzodiazepine has been given?
questions.question: The seed made flumazenil harmful always. The v0.18a audit made it harmful only once a benzodiazepine is on board and discouraged before. Is that right, and is the halt reason accurate?
questions.context:
Before a benzodiazepine, flumazenil has little to reverse, and the main risk is unmasking a proconvulsant co-ingestant. After a benzodiazepine, it removes the drug controlling her agitation and seizure risk. The audit split the tag along that line.

**The packet and seed are stale here.** Seed §3.4 lists flumazenil as harmful 'always', and packet §11 asks you to confirm it is 'genuinely lethal'.

The halt reason says she arrested 'with a QRS that had never been treated'. That is false for a resident who gave bicarbonate first, for example in the stabilizing or stabilized phase, where benzo_given is usually set.
questions.current: case_actions[flumazenil].tag (case_2_actions.py act("flumazenil")): harmful when `flag benzo_given set`, otherwise discouraged.

quotes.text: Precipitates seizure in an undifferentiated overdose, in a patient who is going to seize anyway
She had a prolonged seizure that would not respond to a benzodiazepine, because you had just blocked the receptor it works at, and she arrested with a QRS that had never been treated.

options.label: Keep the split, fix the halt reason
options.detail: Harmful after a benzodiazepine, discouraged before. The halt reason no longer claims the QRS was untreated.
options.tradeoff: Matches the pharmacology. A resident who gives flumazenil to a benzodiazepine-naive, about-to-seize patient loses one point only.
options.implementation: case_2_actions.py act("flumazenil"): replace 'and she arrested with a QRS that had never been treated' with wording true in every phase, for example 'and the acidosis of the seizure widened her QRS until she arrested'. Rebuild.

options.label: Harmful always, as the seed had it
options.detail: Any flumazenil halts the case.
options.tradeoff: Simplest rule and matches the seed. Overstates the harm when no benzodiazepine is on board.
options.implementation: case_2_actions.py act("flumazenil"): ALWAYS("harmful"). Fix the halt reason as in A. Update the 'no benzodiazepine' scenario to expect halted.

options.label: Discouraged always
options.detail: Flumazenil never halts, costs one point and carries the note.
options.tradeoff: Consistent with how the case treats other drugs whose harm is real but not reliably lethal. Understates the danger of reversing the one drug controlling her seizures.
options.implementation: case_2_actions.py act("flumazenil"): ALWAYS("discouraged"), remove halt_reason. Update both flumazenil scenarios.

questions.reasoning: The split tracks the actual mechanism of harm, and the halt reason needs fixing in any case because it is false on the bicarbonate paths. The strongest argument against is that flumazenil in an undifferentiated overdose that includes a proconvulsant is dangerous even without prior benzodiazepines, which is why the seed made it always harmful.
questions.evidence: Seizures after flumazenil in mixed overdoses, especially with TCAs, are described in case series and reviews (from memory, verify). Evidence for lethality specifically is limited.
sources: audit v0.18a Fixes made: DIPH row 4

brief: The seed made flumazenil always harmful. The v0.18a audit split it on whether a benzodiazepine was given.
Before a benzodiazepine, the main risk is unmasking a proconvulsant co-ingestant. After, it removes her seizure control.
The halt reason says the QRS was never treated, false on bicarbonate paths.
short.now: Flumazenil is harmful (halts the case) after a benzodiazepine, discouraged before.

opts.A: Halts after a benzodiazepine. Before one, giving it costs one point only.
opts.B: Any flumazenil halts the case. Overstates harm when no benzodiazepine is on board.
opts.C: Never halts, costs one point with a note. Understates reversing the drug controlling her seizures.

short.why: The split tracks the actual mechanism of harm, and the false halt reason needs fixing anyway. Against, flumazenil in an undifferentiated overdose with a proconvulsant is dangerous even without prior benzodiazepines.

questions.title: Should the urine drug screen result turn antibiotics, acyclovir and LP to discouraged?
questions.question: Empirical antibiotics and acyclovir are recommended on arrival and become discouraged once the urine toxicology screen has resulted, and the lumbar puncture follows the same switch. The audit suggests removing that rule. What should the switch be?
questions.context:
The source's Part 1 asks for a sepsis bundle at time zero and Part 2 never mentions sepsis. The conversion tagged for the moment: recommended on arrival, discouraged after the first hard evidence of a toxidrome, with the urine screen as the proxy because the engine cannot see what the resident has worked out.

The audit's objection: the screen does not detect diphenhydramine. In this case it returns a false-positive tricyclic, which is no evidence against meningitis. A febrile 40.1 C eighteen year old with a white count of 16 who has had cultures drawn is still reasonably covered. Discouraging antibiotics after a screen result can teach that stopping empirical cover is the right move once any tox result is back.

Current tags outside the arrival phase before the screen: antibiotics and acyclovir neutral. Isolation is recommended on arrival and neutral after, with no screen rule. The LP is discouraged during seizing and the wide-complex phase regardless.
questions.current: case_actions[ceftriaxone] and [acyclovir].tag (case_2_actions.py): discouraged when `study urine_tox_screen resulted`, recommended when `phase is presentation`, otherwise neutral. case_actions[lumbar_puncture].tag: discouraged when screen resulted, discouraged in seizing or wide-complex, otherwise neutral. Vancomycin and cefepime share the ceftriaxone tag through coverage (DIPH-binding-map.json).

quotes.text: Once resulted it turns the infection workup to discouraged, though it does not detect diphenhydramine
Sepsis bundle should be be initiated with IV fluid bolus and possible antibiotics
The switch point is a drafting judgement.

options.label: Keep the screen as the switch
options.detail: Antibiotics, acyclovir and the LP become discouraged once the screen has resulted.
options.tradeoff: Marks continuing the infectious workup after a tox result as an error. Uses a proxy that neither detects the drug nor excludes infection.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off in DIPH-review-packet.md and DIPH-review-matrix.md.

options.label: Remove the screen rule (audit default)
options.detail: Antibiotics and acyclovir recommended on arrival, neutral afterwards. LP discouraged in seizing and wide-complex, neutral otherwise.
options.tradeoff: Never penalises empirical cover. Loses the explicit teaching that chasing the infectious workup instead of the ECG is the error, which then lives only in the debrief notes.
options.implementation: case_2_actions.py: delete the `study urine_tox_screen resulted` rule from ceftriaxone, acyclovir and lumbar_puncture. Rewrite the ceftriaxone note's 'Tagged discouraged once the toxicology screen has resulted' paragraph and the acyclovir note. Update DIPH-SEED.md §3.4 and §9.7.

options.label: Switch on the ECG result instead
options.detail: Antibiotics and acyclovir become neutral (not discouraged) once the ECG has resulted, and the LP discouraged once the ECG shows a wide QRS.
options.tradeoff: Uses the evidence the case actually pivots on. Still a proxy, and a wide QRS does not exclude meningitis either.
options.implementation: case_2_actions.py: replace the screen rule with `study ecg_12_lead resulted` valued neutral for antibiotics and acyclovir, and discouraged for lumbar_puncture. Rewrite the notes. Update scenarios.

questions.reasoning: Empirical cover in a febrile, delirious young adult is defensible at any point until an alternative is secure, and a screen that cannot detect the drug is not that alternative. Removing the rule stops the case from penalising safe practice, and the debrief notes still teach that the infectious workup must not delay the ECG. The strongest argument against is that the case loses its only scored signal for anchoring on sepsis.
questions.evidence: Standard immunoassay tricyclic screens cross-react with diphenhydramine on some platforms (from memory, verify). No evidence base for the proxy itself.
sources: audit v0.18a Open items: DIPH urine drug screen

brief: The urine tox screen result is the case's proxy for the resident recognizing the toxidrome.
The screen misses diphenhydramine and returns a false-positive tricyclic, no evidence against meningitis.
She is 40.1 C, white count 16, cultures drawn.
short.now: Antibiotics and acyclovir recommended on arrival, then neutral. Once the urine screen results, they and the LP are discouraged.

opts.A: Continuing the workup after the screen scores as an error. The screen excludes no infection.
opts.B: Empirical cover is never penalized. Teaching against chasing infection over the ECG moves to debrief only.
opts.C: Antibiotics and acyclovir go neutral after the ECG results. LP discouraged once QRS is wide.

short.why: Empirical cover in a febrile, delirious young adult is defensible until an alternative is secure, and a screen that cannot detect the drug is not one. Against, the case loses its only scored signal for anchoring on sepsis.

questions.title: Should a seizure treated with bicarbonate but no anticonvulsant ever progress?
questions.question: If a resident gives bicarbonate during the seizure but no benzodiazepine or propofol, she seizes indefinitely with no further deterioration. Is that acceptable?
questions.context:
The seizing phase has two exits besides handoff: an anticonvulsant ends it at once, and 120 seconds with no anticonvulsant AND no bicarbonate leads to the wide-complex rhythm. A resident who gives only bicarbonate satisfies neither, so the patient stays in `seizing` (HR 150, SpO2 84, T 40.4) until the case ends. The nurse asks for a benzodiazepine at 15 and 60 seconds in Easy mode (45 and 180 in the default Normal mode) and then stops asking.

The v0.18a audit made this path more common: bicarbonate alone in the wide-complex phase now returns her to `seizing` after ten seconds, where she then stays.

**The packet is stale here.** Packet §2.4 describes the seizing deadline as '120s with no benzodiazepine'. The deterioration timeline also shows the old guard.

Clinically, an untreated generalized seizure beyond five minutes is status epilepticus, with worsening acidemia, hyperthermia and hypoxia. The case's own notes say the seizure widens the QRS again.
questions.current: phases[seizing].transitions (case_1_shell.py): `SEIZURE_STOPPED` to post_ictal instantly. `NOT SEIZURE_STOPPED AND NOT flag bicarb_given set` after 120 s from phase entry to wide_complex_tachycardia. No rule covers bicarbonate given without an anticonvulsant.

quotes.text: The convulsion goes on producing heat and acid, and both will widen the QRS again.
two minutes of untreated convulsion in an acidaemic patient with a QRS of 132 ms widens the complex to a ventricular rhythm

options.label: Keep: no further deterioration
options.detail: She keeps seizing, the monitor holds, and the resident is prompted twice for a benzodiazepine.
options.tradeoff: Simple and avoids a loop. Teaches, by omission, that an untreated seizure is stable once bicarbonate is in.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off in DIPH-review-packet.md and DIPH-review-matrix.md.

options.label: Add a one-time relapse to the wide-complex rhythm

questions.context:
`SEIZURE_STOPPED` is `flag benzo_given set OR action propofol_bolus taken OR action propofol_infusion taken`. Midazolam counts through lorazepam coverage, including when given for induction. A benzodiazepine ends the seizure instantly: the case does not model a delay.

In the wide-complex phase, bicarbonate with an anticonvulsant goes to `stabilizing` after ten seconds. Bicarbonate without one goes to `seizing` after ten seconds, with the narration 'She's still fitting, though.' A resident who then gives a benzodiazepine passes through post-ictal to stabilizing.

Levetiracetam is tagged neutral everywhere and does not stop the seizure. Its note says going past a benzodiazepine is the error, which argues for discouraged before a benzodiazepine. Ketamine (an induction agent with anticonvulsant properties) does not count either.

questions.title: Is 120 seconds of untreated stable VT before pulseless arrest the right deadline?
questions.question: In the wide-complex phase (HR 180, BP 95/60), 120 seconds with no bicarbonate ends the case in pulseless VT. This is the number that lets the case kill the patient. Keep it?
questions.context:
The direction is the author's: without bicarbonate the patient develops stable VT, then pulseless VT. The number is a drafting judgment. The do-nothing path reaches arrest at eight minutes: seizure at 4, wide-complex at 6, arrest at 8.

Fairness: in Easy mode bicarbonate is prompted at 25 and 90 seconds in this phase (and at 25 and 90 in seizing and post-ictal). In Normal mode, the default, those become 75 and 270 seconds, so only one prompt fires before the 120-second arrest (see ALL-02). The phase's own terminal_opt_in_rationale says 20 and 70 seconds, which is wrong and should be corrected whichever option you choose.

Nothing can be done in `pulseless_vt`: the engine ends the case five seconds after entry, so defibrillation and further bicarbonate are out of reach.

questions.context:
This is not in the source. It was added on Aakash Setty's instruction on 5 September 2026 to teach that a standard wide-complex algorithm is the trap. The audit's open item calls it 'as the author designed'. 'Author' there most likely means the platform author, not Dr Medwid, whose document never mentions amiodarone.

The case's own note states the evidence is weaker than for procainamide: mechanistic reasoning and case experience. So the case punishes most severely the drug it says it is least sure about. The arrow is placed first so that bicarbonate and amiodarone in the same batch still arrest her.

questions.title: Which of the twelve critical actions are the seed's five?
questions.question: The seed supplied five critical actions, but no file in the repository lists which five, and the case now tags twelve actions critical. Which should stay critical?
questions.context:
The packet and the case provenance both say the seed author supplied "the five critical actions". Neither the packet nor MGCA-SEED.md names them, so nobody can currently check whether the model and the v0.18a audit kept the seed's list, added to it, or removed from it.

The case now tags twelve actions critical in at least one phase: insert_iv (arrival only), the crystalloid bolus, hydrocortisone, ceftriaxone (cefotaxime covered), norepinephrine (meningococcal branch and frank shock only), isolation precautions, public health notification, fingerstick glucose (arrival only), the chemistry panel (arrival only), lactate (arrival only), blood cultures, and the critical care consult.

Scoring matters here. Per authoring requirements 13.0, a critical action is worth two points on its tab and a recommended one is worth one, so every extra critical tag dilutes the ones that decide the outcome. Critical is defined as "The patient does badly without it". Blood cultures, the lactate and the consult are good practice but the patient does not do worse in this case without them.

One specific risk: the seed's constraint that the lumbar puncture "happens only if the patient is not hypotensive" reads as though the seed expected an LP in the non-hypotensive state. The v0.18a audit made the LP never critical. If the LP was one of the seed's five, that audit fix departs from the seed (see MGCA-09).

The patient does badly without it. Omission costs

options.detail: Every action listed stays critical in the phases where it is now critical.
options.tradeoff: No edits and a broad definition of good care. Dilutes the score, and a resident who skips blood cultures but treats perfectly is told they missed a critical action.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off, and record which five were the seed's in provenance.author_supplied.

options.label: Only the seed's five stay critical
options.detail: The seed author names the five. The other seven move to recommended.
options.tradeoff: Restores seed fidelity exactly and sharpens the score. Needs you to recall the seed list, and may drop isolation and notification from critical if they were not in it.

options.tradeoff: Keeps the two actions that protect other people as critical. Still departs from a strict seed reading, and the chemistry panel is the route to the adrenal diagnosis, which some reviewers would keep critical.
options.implementation: As B, excluding place_patient_on_isolation_precautions and consult_public_health_authorities from the demotion.

The strongest argument against: the chemistry panel is how the resident finds the adrenal crisis, and demoting it may soften the case's central lesson.

questions.title: Are the 240, 210 and 300 second deterioration deadlines defensible?
questions.question: The case moves her to a worse phase after 240 s without hydrocortisone or an antibiotic, to frank shock 210 s later, and to arrest 300 s after that. Do you accept these numbers as the case's clinical claims?
questions.context:
The seed defined the six states and the triggers between them. The clocks were added by the model after the engine gained time-guarded transitions. They are compressed against real disease tempo, the same way the five-second laboratory turnaround is.

What happens now: from arrival, 240 s without hydrocortisone moves her to adrenal_crisis (this rule is checked first), and 240 s without an antibiotic moves her to progressive_meningococcemia. From either branch, 210 s more without the missing drug moves her to frank_septic_shock. From frank shock, 300 s without antibiotic, glucocorticoid and vasopressor all in place ends the case in cardiac_arrest. A passive run arrests at 750 s against an estimated runtime of 600 s.

At the authored (easy) prompt deadlines, ceftriaxone is prompted at 45 s and 90 s and hydrocortisone at 70 s and 140 s, all well before 240 s. The design note suggests a deadline about three times the prompt deadline, and this case is deliberately more generous. In the default Normal mode prompts are tripled and deterioration is not, which is covered in MGCA-07.

What you are signing is the relative order and the rough proportion. The two first-hop clocks are equal, and you could reasonably argue that untreated adrenal crisis with hypoglycemia decompensates faster than untreated bacteremia, or the reverse. No evidence maps real hours to simulator seconds.

quotes.text: Those numbers are compressed against real disease tempo, in the same way the five-second laboratory turnaround is, and they are model output.
A completely passive run arrests at 750 seconds against an estimated runtime of 600.
Progression of an untreated adrenal crisis into refractory shock. Shorter than the presentation timer because she is already further along.

The meningococcemia case runs at 240 seconds against a 45-second antibiotic prompt and a 90-second escalation, which is a ratio of about five and is on the generous side deliberately, because it is the first case to use the feature.

options.tradeoff: Tested, generous in easy mode, and the ordering matches the seed's states 2 and 3. Tight against the 600 s runtime and against Normal-mode prompts.

options.implementation: Set after_seconds to 300 in phases[presentation].transitions[4] and [5], and 240 in phases[adrenal_crisis].transitions[3] and phases[progressive_meningococcemia].transitions[3]. Update phase_notes.time_guarded_transitions, debrief_configuration.cross_cutting_teaching_points[5] ("Four minutes" and "twelve and a half minutes"), metadata.estimated_runtime_seconds (suggest 720). Rerun validator, scenarios, and regenerate the deterioration timeline.

options.detail: Adrenal clock unchanged. The antibiotic clock from arrival lengthens to 300 s, reflecting a view that the hypoglycemic adrenal crisis is the faster killer in minutes.
options.tradeoff: Makes the two deficits carry different urgency, which the case currently does not express. The clinical basis for either ordering is weak, and it gives a resident more slack on the antibiotic, the action with the largest effect on outcome.

questions.reasoning: The relative ordering is sound, the numbers are openly declared as compression, and the easy-mode prompt margins are wide. The real fairness problem is that Normal mode triples prompts but not clocks, and that is better fixed in the prompts or the default difficulty than by stretching every clock. The strongest argument against: a passive arrest at 750 s already exceeds the 600 s runtime estimate, which suggests the clocks are tighter than the case's own pacing assumes.
questions.evidence: No evidence maps disease hours to simulator seconds. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 recommends antimicrobials immediately, ideally within one hour, for possible septic shock (packet §9, checked against source). Adrenal crisis guidance recommends immediate parenteral hydrocortisone without waiting for confirmation (Endocrine Society primary adrenal insufficiency guideline 2016, from memory, verify).

questions.title: Is adrenal crisis 90 seconds after fluid without hydrocortisone the right model?
questions.question: The v0.18a audit changed the fluid-without-hydrocortisone trigger from instant to a 90 s delay measured from the fluid. Do you accept that, or should the branch work differently?
questions.context:
The seed's state 2 trigger is fluid or dextrose given without glucocorticoid. Until 28 Sep the fluid half fired in the same second as the fluid, so the monitor showed the pressure falling the moment the fluid went in. The educator review called this finding M1 and the audit drafted a 90 s delay.

What happens now: after a crystalloid bolus without hydrocortisone, the case waits 90 s. If hydrocortisone arrives inside that window, she does not enter adrenal_crisis. If not, she moves to adrenal_crisis (HR 136, BP 88/54 from 124, 99/63) with a narration. The 240 s arrival clock still applies independently.

The packet's §4 paragraph on this ("the adrenal crisis branch will be entered by most good runs") was written for the instant version and is stale. With the delay, a resident who gives fluid and then hydrocortisone within 90 s avoids the branch. The branch still discriminates partly on sequence, because a resident who gives fluid first and reads the chemistry later will usually enter it.

Two things to weigh. The narration says the pressure came down after the fluid, which is true of the numbers but can still read as the fluid causing the fall. And giving hydrocortisone inside the window before the antibiotic currently sends her instantly into the meningococcal branch, which is MGCA-04.

M1. MGCA punished fluid before hydrocortisone in the same second

v0.18a. Was instantaneous, which taught that the fluid itself caused the hypotension. A 90 second delay measured from when the fluid was given keeps the lesson (glucocorticoid is the missing piece) without punishing the conventional sequence of fluid first.
She's had the fluid and her pressure's come down, not up. She's still cold and she's harder to rouse.
So the branch discriminates on order rather than on competence

options.tradeoff: Keeps the seed's trigger, removes the same-second punishment, and rewards giving hydrocortisone alongside fluid. The 90 s is a teaching number with no clinical basis.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off. Update MGCA-review-packet.md §4 to describe the delay.

The strongest argument against: the resident who follows a conventional sepsis sequence (fluid, then labs, then targeted treatment) still enters the branch most of the time, and some will read that as being punished for correct sepsis care.
questions.evidence: Fluid does not lower blood pressure in adrenal insufficiency. The fall is the untreated disease. Hydrocortisone is given on suspicion alongside fluid (Endocrine Society 2016, from memory, verify). No source supports any specific delay: 90 s is a teaching device.

questions.title: Should hydrocortisone before the antibiotic worsen her in the same second?
questions.question: Giving hydrocortisone (with fluid) before the antibiotic moves her instantly into progressive_meningococcemia with worse vitals, the mirror image of the defect the audit fixed on the adrenal side. Should this transition be delayed too?
questions.context:
The seed's state 3 trigger is glucocorticoid and volume given, antibiotic not. The audit added a 90 s delay to the adrenal trigger but left both routes into the meningococcal branch instant.

What happens now: from arrival, fluid plus hydrocortisone without an antibiotic moves her at once to progressive_meningococcemia (HR 124 to 140, BP 99/63 to 84/50). From adrenal_crisis, hydrocortisone alone moves her at once to the same phase (HR 136 to 140, BP 88/54 to 84/50). Neither transition has a narration. On the monitor, hydrocortisone appears to make her worse.

A realistic sequence triggers this: fluid running, hydrocortisone pushed, ceftriaxone being drawn up 10 s later. She drops into the meningococcal branch and returns to improving when the ceftriaxone lands.

The scoring consequence is inferred from the spec, not tested. Authoring requirements 13.0 scores critical actions "expected on that tab in the phases the run visited", and norepinephrine is critical in progressive_meningococcemia. A run that passes through that phase for a few seconds is therefore likely to be scored as missing a critical vasopressor. Platelets and other phase-keyed labs drawn in that window also show the progressive values.
