questions.title: Should dextrose without hydrocortisone trigger adrenal crisis, as the seed says?
questions.question: The seed's state 2 trigger is fluid or dextrose without glucocorticoid. The case only triggers on fluid. Should dextrose trigger it too?
questions.context:
The seed says state 2 (adrenal crisis progression) is entered when fluid or dextrose is given and glucocorticoid is not. The case file implements the fluid half only. D50 sets dextrose_given and a 90 s dextrose_recent flag, and no transition reads either flag.

What happens now to a resident who gives D50 and nothing else: the glucose reads 131 for 90 s, falls back, and the adrenal branch arrives only when the 240 s arrival clock expires. Several texts in the case still describe dextrose as a trigger, so the file contradicts itself.

Clinically, dextrose does not accelerate adrenal crisis, and neither does fluid. Both triggers are teaching devices for "treated the numbers, not the cause". D50 is tagged recommended here, so a dextrose trigger would move her to a worse phase after a correct symptomatic action, which is the same tension as the fluid trigger.

questions.title: In Normal mode, is she ever warned about hydrocortisone before frank shock?
questions.question: In adrenal_crisis the first hydrocortisone prompt is suppressed by the three-prompt cap, and in Normal mode its escalation lands at 420 s against a 210 s exit. Do you accept that, or change the prompts?
questions.context:
The validator's fairness rule checks that a prompt naming the missing drug precedes every deterioration by at least 20 s. It checks the authored (easy) deadlines only.

In adrenal_crisis, first warnings compete for three slots. The generated timeline orders them ceftriaxone 45 s, norepinephrine 45 s, crystalloid 55 s, so the hydrocortisone first warning at 70 s is suppressed. The escalation at 140 s is exempt from the cap and fires. The timeline does not say whether prompts for actions already taken still take a slot, so in a run where ceftriaxone and fluid are done the first warning may survive.

Normal mode is the default and multiplies every prompt deadline by three while leaving the 210 s exit alone. The hydrocortisone escalation moves to 420 s and never fires. Before the exit, the only first warnings a Normal-mode resident can hear in that phase are for ceftriaxone and norepinephrine (135 s) and fluid (165 s), when those are still outstanding. A resident who gave fluid early may also have left arrival before the 210 s Normal-mode hydrocortisone prompt there. The packet asked you to accept this for "hard mode", which is now called Normal and is the default.

Whether Normal should stay the default is a platform decision. This question is about what MGCA does with its own prompts.

questions.title: Can she reach a resolution phase without ever receiving fluid?
questions.question: The seed's improving state requires antibiotic, glucocorticoid and volume. Two clock routes reach improving with no fluid ever given, and frank shock's exit and arrest guard disagree about fluid. Should every resolution route require volume?
questions.context:
From arrival, improving needs all three: antibiotic, glucocorticoid and fluid. But the branches do not check fluid. A resident who does nothing for 240 s enters adrenal_crisis by the clock, then gives hydrocortisone (instantly to progressive_meningococcemia) and ceftriaxone (instantly to improving). No fluid was given, yet the phase label reads "Responding to antibiotics, hydrocortisone and volume". The same happens through progressive_meningococcemia entered by the 240 s antibiotic clock.

A second inconsistency: adrenal_crisis with a pressor running, then ceftriaxone, then hydrocortisone, goes to improving (the reverse order reaches stabilized_shock), whose description says perfusion was restored without a vasopressor.

A third: from frank_septic_shock the only exit to stabilized_shock requires all four (antibiotic, hydrocortisone, pressor and fluid), while the arrest clock only checks the first three. A resident who gives three but no fluid neither improves nor arrests and stays in frank shock until handoff. The crystalloid prompt has no guard and fires in every phase, so the resident is prompted. The seed table defines stabilized shock by antibiotic, glucocorticoid and vasopressor only. The fluid requirement on this exit is the case's addition, even though its author_note calls it the seed's rescue.

questions.title: Is norepinephrine critical only in the meningococcal branch and frank shock?
questions.question: The audit made norepinephrine critical only in progressive_meningococcemia and frank shock, recommended in adrenal_crisis, and discouraged on arrival and once improving. Do you accept those phase tags?
questions.context:
Norepinephrine is now critical in progressive_meningococcemia (BP 84/50, MAP about 61) and frank_septic_shock (70/42, MAP about 51), recommended in adrenal_crisis (88/54, MAP about 65) and in stabilized_shock, and discouraged on arrival (99/63, no fluid yet) and in improving.

The note's reasoning: norepinephrine is indicated once hypotension persists after adequate volume, and in adrenal crisis catecholamines work poorly without cortisol. The critical tag in the meningococcal branch assumes she has had fluid and a glucocorticoid. Hydrocortisone is always given on entry to that phase, but fluid is not on the clock routes (see MGCA-08).

Two problems to weigh. The meningococcal branch exits to improving on the antibiotic alone, so a resident who gives ceftriaxone promptly never needs the pressor, yet the phase visit likely makes it an expected critical action (see MGCA-04). And the adrenal_crisis tag of recommended sits beside a nurse prompt for norepinephrine in that phase.

questions.question: After 300 s in frank shock without antibiotic, hydrocortisone and vasopressor all in place, the case ends in cardiac arrest with no action from the resident. Do you intend this?

The validator forbids ending a case by the clock unless the transition opts in explicitly. MGCA opts in. The arrest is its own terminal phase with a timeout_reason, so the debrief attributes it to omission. Since v0.18a an arrest run shows "not scored" and the audit drafted a corrected arrest debrief note (listed under "arrest debrief").

The packet says the seed asked for progression toward peri-arrest on failure to intervene. A full arrest is one step beyond that wording. The seed's state 4 is frank septic shock, and the arrest phase itself is model-added.

What you sign: that a completely passive resident sees her arrest at 12:30, that the timeout_reason and debrief note are true, and that this is an educational choice you are willing to own.

questions.title: Should insulin halt the case in every phase, including after hydrocortisone?
questions.question: Both insulin routes are harmful in every phase and the halt reason says her glucose was 53 with no cortisol. Once hydrocortisone is in, her glucose is 84 to 98. Should insulin still end the case there?
questions.context:
The teaching is sound for arrival and the adrenal branch: insulin to shift a potassium of 5.4 in a patient with a glucose of 47 to 53 and no cortisol can produce a profound hypoglycemia.

The tag is unconditional. In progressive_meningococcemia, improving and stabilized_shock hydrocortisone has always been given and the glucose is 88 to 98. In frank shock after hydrocortisone it is 84. The halt reason still states a glucose of 53 and no cortisol. Also, in practice insulin for hyperkalemia is given with dextrose, and the catalog offers insulin without dextrose, so a resident may intend both.

Authoring §7.3 reserves harmful for genuine lethality.

Reserve `harmful` for genuine lethality

options.detail: Any insulin at any point ends the case.
options.tradeoff: Simple and memorable. The halt reason is false after hydrocortisone, and a lethal halt for insulin at a glucose of 96 overstates the risk.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off.

options.detail: Harmful while steroid_given is unset. Discouraged afterwards, with a note that the potassium falls with hydrocortisone and volume.

B keeps the halt where the halt reason is true. The strongest argument against: any insulin for a potassium of 5.4 with a normal ECG is the wrong reflex, and a resident who does it late has still made the conceptual error the case teaches.

questions.title: Which antibiotics should satisfy the critical antibiotic action?
questions.question: Ceftriaxone or cefotaxime now satisfies the critical action. Cefepime, meropenem, piperacillin-tazobactam, penicillin G and ampicillin also rescue her but do not satisfy it. Is that the right line?
questions.context:
The v0.18a audit (educator finding C4) added cefotaxime to the critical expectation, since the case's own note calls it interchangeable. It also retagged piperacillin-tazobactam, penicillin G and ampicillin from their previous tags to neutral.

What happens now: seven agents set abx_given and move her toward improving. Only ceftriaxone and cefotaxime count as the critical "Third-generation cephalosporin". Cefepime and meropenem are recommended, the other three neutral. Vancomycin and doxycycline are recommended and do not rescue her. A resident who gives meropenem alone is rescued and is told they missed a critical action.

Authoring §7.3 defines critical as an action whose omission harms the patient. Meropenem's omission does not harm her if ceftriaxone is given, and ceftriaxone's omission does not harm her if meropenem is given.

MGCA-binding-map.json rows[ceftriaxone].also_covers [cefotaxime]. cefepime, meropenem recommended. piperacillin_tazobactam, penicillin_g, ampicillin neutral. All seven set abx_given.

Adequate and unnecessarily broad. It treats the organism
Seven antibiotics do satisfy the requirement, so a resident who chooses any reasonable agent is not stranded.

options.detail: Seven agents rescue the physiology, only ceftriaxone or cefotaxime earns the critical credit.
options.tradeoff: Teaches the guideline empiric choice clearly. Tells a resident who gave meropenem that they missed the most important action.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off. Correct packet §7.5.

options.label: Any active agent satisfies it
options.detail: All seven rescuing agents also satisfy the critical expectation. Preference is taught in notes and by recommended versus neutral tags.
options.tradeoff: Matches the definition of critical. Removes the scoring signal for choosing the guideline agent.
options.implementation: Add the five agents to MGCA-binding-map.json rows[ceftriaxone].also_covers or an engine-level satisfier list. Note: also_covers copies ceftriaxone's tag and note onto the covered agent (CHANGELOG, also_covers fix), so their own notes would need merging. Update expectation_label to "An antibiotic active against Neisseria meningitidis".

options.label: Add cefepime and meropenem only
options.detail: Third-generation cephalosporins plus the two broad agents with reliable CSF penetration satisfy it. Penicillin G, ampicillin and piperacillin-tazobactam still rescue her without the credit.
options.tradeoff: Credits the defensible empiric alternatives while keeping penicillin and piperacillin-tazobactam as teaching points. Still a line drawn by judgment.

Penicillin G is still active but is no longer an empiric choice given reported reduced susceptibility, and piperacillin-tazobactam has unreliable CSF penetration, so leaving them uncredited is defensible. The strongest argument against: the engine's also_covers mechanism replaces each covered agent's own tag and note, so C needs either note merging or an engine change.
questions.evidence: IDSA bacterial meningitis guideline 2004 lists third-generation cephalosporins as standard for N. meningitidis, with penicillin G or ampicillin when susceptible, and meropenem among alternatives (from memory, verify). Reduced penicillin susceptibility in N. meningitidis is reported in the US (MMWR, from memory, verify).

brief: Seven antibiotics rescue her, but only ceftriaxone or cefotaxime earns the critical credit.
A resident who gives meropenem alone is rescued and told they missed a critical action.
Critical means omission harms her. Meropenem and ceftriaxone each make the other's omission harmless.
short.now: Ceftriaxone or cefotaxime critical. Cefepime, meropenem recommended. Piperacillin-tazobactam, penicillin G, ampicillin neutral. All seven rescue.

opts.B: All seven rescuing agents earn the credit. Loses the scoring signal for the guideline agent.
opts.C: Penicillin G, ampicillin and piperacillin-tazobactam still rescue without credit. Still a judgment line.

questions.title: Are the glucocorticoid alternatives tagged right after the audit?
questions.question: Methylprednisolone is now neutral and rescues her. Dexamethasone is discouraged but also rescues her. Oral prednisone is discouraged and does not rescue her. Do you accept these three?
questions.context:
Hydrocortisone is critical in every phase. The v0.18a audit retagged methylprednisolone to neutral. Dexamethasone is discouraged. Both set steroid_given, so both move her out of the adrenal branch. Oral prednisone sets only oral_steroid_attempted, so the deficit stays open (packet §7.5).

The distinction the case draws: hydrocortisone has meaningful mineralocorticoid activity at stress doses, methylprednisolone has little, dexamethasone none. Her sodium 128 and potassium 5.4 are partly mineralocorticoid problems. Methylprednisolone and dexamethasone both rescue the physiology, and neither earns the critical credit.

Dexamethasone's note gives a second reason: residents reach for it by association with adjunctive dexamethasone in pneumococcal meningitis, which she does not have.

Etomidate inhibits 11-beta-hydroxylase, and a single dose suppresses cortisol synthesis for a day or two. In this patient the adrenals have already failed and she needs hydrocortisone whatever induction agent is used.

The audit retagged it neutral. The note still calls it "the single most instructive drug choice in this case" and says a reduced dose of either etomidate or ketamine is defensible. Ketamine is recommended. Intubation itself is discouraged in every phase.

The packet (§7.3) still describes etomidate as discouraged and is stale on this point.

questions.title: Should intubation always cause instant frank shock, and be discouraged even at GCS 9?
questions.question: Intubating on arrival or in either branch moves her instantly to frank shock regardless of resuscitation, and intubation is discouraged in every phase including frank shock with GCS 9. Is that what you want to teach?
questions.context:
From presentation, adrenal_crisis and progressive_meningococcemia, the intubated flag moves her at once to frank_septic_shock. The author note calls this "Modeled as certain here for teaching".

The intubation note gives a correct sequence for when intubation is needed: volume in, vasopressor running, hydrocortisone given, reduced-dose induction. The engine ignores that sequence. A resident who resuscitates fully and then intubates still collapses.

The tag is discouraged in every phase (two rules, both discouraged). In frank_septic_shock she is obtunded (GCS 9), RR 32, SpO2 95 percent, and the note's argument ("She is maintaining her own airway, saturating 98 percent on room air") describes arrival only. Frank shock also has no intubation-dependent exit, so intubating there changes nothing except the figure and the interview.

When intubation is genuinely needed, the order is: volume in, vasopressor running or drawn up, hydrocortisone given, reduced-dose induction agent, and someone watching the pressure rather than the tube.

questions.title: Should beta blockers and diltiazem halt the case in every phase?
questions.question: All six rate-control routes are harmful in every phase, with halt reasons that cite no cortisol and a rate of 124. Should they still halt once she is improving on hydrocortisone?
questions.context:
The lesson is sound for the shocked phases: her tachycardia is compensation, and blocking it in vasodilatory shock can collapse her output.

The tags are unconditional. In improving she has HR 110, BP 110/70 and has had hydrocortisone. The halt reasons say she had "no cortisol to support vascular tone", which is false in progressive_meningococcemia, improving and stabilized_shock, where hydrocortisone is always in. The diltiazem halt names a rate of 124.

Authoring §7.3 reserves harmful for genuine lethality.

options.detail: Any rate control at any point halts.
options.tradeoff: Simple and consistent with the teaching point. Halt reasons are partly false after hydrocortisone.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off.

options.label: Harmful except in improving
options.detail: Halts in every shocked phase. Discouraged in improving. Halt reasons drop the cortisol clause or make it conditional.
options.tradeoff: Keeps the lethal lesson where she is shocked. Adds a rule to six actions.
options.implementation: For each of the six: tag [{when: "phase is improving", value: discouraged}, {when: null, value: harmful}]. Reword halt reasons to "in septic shock" without the cortisol clause and without a fixed rate. Regenerate matrix.

options.detail: Unconditional harmful, but halt reasons no longer mention cortisol or a fixed rate.
options.tradeoff: Makes every halt reason true with text edits only. Still claims lethality in improving.
options.implementation: Edit the six halt_reason strings. Regenerate matrix.

questions.reasoning: In improving she is normotensive on hydrocortisone, and a lethal halt for a beta blocker there overstates the harm. In every other phase the halt is defensible. The strongest argument against: rate control for sinus tachycardia in sepsis is always the wrong reflex, and a softer tag late in the case may teach that it becomes acceptable.
questions.evidence: Rate control of compensatory sinus tachycardia in septic shock is harmful in principle. Esmolol in selected septic shock patients after resuscitation has been studied (Morelli 2013, from memory, verify), which shows harm is not certain once stabilized.

In improving she has HR 110, BP 110/70, and has had hydrocortisone.
Halt reasons cite no cortisol, false wherever hydrocortisone is in. Diltiazem's names a rate of 124.

opts.B: Halt reasons drop or condition the cortisol clause. Adds a rule to six actions.
opts.C: Halt reasons drop cortisol and fixed-rate wording. Still claims lethality in improving.

questions.title: Is potassium chloride genuinely lethal enough to halt the case?

questions.context:
Her potassium is 5.0 to 5.9 across phases with an AKI. Giving potassium is clearly wrong. The question is whether a single catalog dose would plausibly kill her in minutes, which is what a halt claims.

The note suggests the likely route to the error is reflex electrolyte replacement after fluid. Authoring §7.3 says to reserve harmful for genuine lethality and to use discouraged when the evidence is weaker.

quotes.text: the serum potassium rose to a level that produced a wide-complex bradyarrhythmia and she arrested.

options.label: Keep harmful
options.detail: Any IV potassium halts.
options.tradeoff: Makes a never-event memorable. Overstates the effect of a standard rider in most phases.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off.

options.label: Discouraged everywhere
options.detail: No halt. The note explains mineralocorticoid deficiency and AKI.
options.tradeoff: Honest about dose-dependent risk. Loses the halt as a teaching moment.
options.implementation: case_actions[potassium_chloride_kcl].tag: unconditional discouraged, remove halt_reason, keep note. Regenerate matrix.

options.label: Harmful only when potassium is 5.5 or higher
options.detail: Harmful in adrenal_crisis, progressive_meningococcemia and frank_septic_shock (5.6 to 5.9). Discouraged elsewhere.
options.tradeoff: Ties the halt to the phases where the number is highest. The threshold is arbitrary and the clinical error is the same at 5.4.
options.implementation: tag: [{when: "phase is adrenal_crisis OR phase is progressive_meningococcemia OR phase is frank_septic_shock", value: harmful}, {when: null, value: discouraged}]. Regenerate matrix.

questions.reasoning: A single 10 to 20 mEq dose raises serum potassium modestly in most patients, and an arrest in minutes at a starting value of 5.4 is not the expected outcome, so the halt overstates the claim. The strongest argument against: with no aldosterone and an AKI there is no floor under the potassium, and some reviewers would rather over-teach a potentially fatal reflex.

A halt claims one catalog dose would plausibly kill her in minutes.
Authoring rules reserve harmful for genuine lethality, discouraged for weaker evidence.
short.now: IV potassium is harmful in every phase. The halt describes a wide-complex bradyarrhythmia and arrest.

opts.A: Any IV potassium halts. Memorable never-event, but overstates a standard rider in most phases.
opts.B: No halt, the note explains mineralocorticoid deficiency and AKI. Loses the halt as a teaching moment.
opts.C: Halts in adrenal crisis, meningococcal branch and frank shock (5.6 to 5.9). Threshold is arbitrary.

short.why: A single 10 to 20 mEq dose raises potassium modestly in most patients, and arrest in minutes from 5.4 is not expected. Against it, without aldosterone and with an AKI, the potassium has no floor.

questions.title: Do the nurse prompts describe what is in front of her without giving away the answer?
questions.question: The audit reworded prompts to describe the current state. Some still imply a trajectory or state a number the monitor contradicts, and one names hydrocortisone. Keep or reword?
questions.context:
Authoring §9.5 forbids prompts that imply a trajectory. The packet checklist asks you to read every prompt for this, since no validator can.

Specific items. The hydrocortisone first prompt on arrival says her pressure "isn't holding", while the monitor shows the arrival values unchanged. The norepinephrine escalation says her mean pressure is under 65, which is true in the meningococcal branch (about 61) and frank shock (about 51) but not in adrenal_crisis (88/54, about 65). The norepinephrine first prompt says "after what she's had", which is false when adrenal_crisis was reached by the clock with no fluid given. The hydrocortisone escalation names the drug. The ceftriaxone escalation names ceftriaxone.

Authoring §9.5 also says prompts must be helpful and rescue a stuck learner. Naming the drug is that rescue, and the debrief records the action as prompted.

questions.title: How should path-dependent lab values be handled (platelets, CSF glucose)?
questions.question: Phase-keyed labs trend wrongly on some paths: platelets rise from 75 to 95 when progressive_meningococcemia resolves to improving, and CSF glucose is interpreted against a serum glucose of 53 even right after D50. Accept, patch, or restructure?
questions.context:
Content is keyed on phase, and improving can be reached from four phases. The packet recorded the platelet case as a residual limitation (OQ-2): a patient who reaches improving from the meningococcal branch sees platelets go from 75 to 95, which the disease does not do in minutes.

A second case the packet did not name: the LP is possible on arrival. If D50 was given first, the serum glucose reads 131 while the CSF glucose rule still reads 34 with a comment calculating the ratio against a serum glucose of 53. In reality CSF glucose lags serum by hours, so a low apparent ratio right after dextrose is expected and misleading, and the comment should say so.

Authoring §11.4 forbids faking a delta by gating on an unrelated flag. dextrose_given is a related flag, so gating the CSF comment on it is allowed.
questions.current: content_keys.labs.complete_blood_count_cbc: improving 95, progressive_meningococcemia 75. content_keys.labs.csf_glucose: default 34 with comment citing serum 53, no dextrose rule.

quotes.text: a patient who reaches `improving` from `progressive_meningococcemia` sees the platelet count go from 75 to 95, which the disease does not do.
Interpret against the simultaneous serum glucose of 53, giving a ratio of about 0.64, which is normal.

options.label: Accept both as residual
options.detail: No change.
options.tradeoff: No edit. Two paths show values that teach something false.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off.

options.label: Patch CSF only, accept platelets
options.detail: Add a CSF glucose rule for arrival after dextrose with a comment about lag. Platelets stay as authored for the intended path.
options.tradeoff: Fixes the misleading interpretation with a legitimate flag. Leaves the platelet rise on a minority path.
options.implementation: content_keys.labs.csf_glucose: insert before rule 1 a rule "flag dextrose_given set" with value 34 and a comment that CSF glucose lags serum by hours and the ratio is unreliable after a dextrose bolus. Regenerate matrix.

options.label: B plus split improving by predecessor
options.detail: Add a seventh clinical phase so improving from the meningococcal branch has its own lab values.
options.tradeoff: Correct on every path. Exceeds the six-phase ceiling in authoring §3.3 and duplicates most content.
options.implementation: Add phase improving_after_branch, route progressive_meningococcemia.transitions[2] to it, duplicate content rules with corrected platelets and coagulation. Needs a spec exception.

questions.title: Should MGCA demote its conditional and alternative recommended actions?
questions.question: A textbook MGCA run lists 35 recommendations as not done. Should MGCA stop tagging as recommended the alternatives and the actions that only make sense after a discouraged one, before the platform policy is written?
questions.context:
Fifty actions carry a recommended tag somewhere. Each is a point on offer on its tab (authoring §13.0), so a correct run that skips alternatives looks incomplete.

Two groups stand out. Actions that follow a discouraged act: ketamine, rocuronium, ketamine infusion and fentanyl (intubation is discouraged in every phase), and the six CSF tests (the LP is discouraged or neutral). The platform question on a tagging policy and an "acceptable" tier is separate. This question is what MGCA should do with its own tags.

questions.title: Have you played MGCA start to finish in the interface, including both branches?
questions.question: Play the case in the interface through the intended path, both deterioration branches, a harmful halt and the do-nothing arrest, and confirm what you see matches the file.
questions.context:
Neither the validator nor the review matrix can see a result the interface never renders or a rescue a resident cannot reach. The packet lists this as outstanding.

**How to do it.** Use the local build with the review speed control (bottom right, or the [ and ] keys, 1x to 16x). Suggested runs, each in Easy and one in Normal: (1) IV, ceftriaxone, fluid and hydrocortisone within 60 s, then hand off to ICU. (2) Fluid first, wait 90 s without hydrocortisone, confirm adrenal_crisis and the narration, then rescue. (5) Metoprolol on arrival for a harmful halt. (6) Try an LP in adrenal_crisis and read the blocked message. (7) Hydrocortisone then D50 on arrival, then a fingerstick (see MGCA-06).

In each run check the monitor against the narration, the figure against the status line, and the debrief timeline against what you did.

questions.title: Are reference intervals, abnormal flags and the blood gases right?
questions.question: Check the reference intervals and red flags, including the female ranges, the fibrinogen interval and the audit's corrected gas arithmetic.

options.tradeoff: Closes the checklist item. Costs your time on the check itself.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off.

options.label: I checked it: needs change (describe)
options.detail: You found something wrong and describe it in your answer.
options.tradeoff: Fixes a defect before learners see it. Needs a follow-up edit session.
options.implementation: Name the diagnosis or disposition and the change.

options.label: Ask Claude to pre-check first, then I confirm
options.detail: Claude checks every explanation against the case's own values and phases, then you confirm the verdicts.
options.tradeoff: Saves your time on mechanical checks. A model pre-check is not a physician check and can miss what only play reveals.
options.implementation: Claude runs the pre-check described in context, reports discrepancies, then you confirm or amend.

questions.reasoning: The verdicts are clinical judgments you can make quickly, and you already approved the list. The strongest argument against: calling step-down incorrect on the path where she never needed a pressor may be stricter than many hospitals practice.

brief: Meningococcemia is primary. Septic shock and adrenal crisis are acceptable primaries with qualification.
Bacterial meningitis is incorrect, and step-down is incorrect even on the improving path.
Hypoglycemia is both an incorrect primary and a credited additional diagnosis. Explanations remain AI-written.
short.now: ICU is the only correct disposition. Five additional diagnoses, list approved by the author on 5 September.

opts.A: Grades and explanations are right. Closes the item, costs your time.
opts.B: You describe the defect, fixed before learners see it. Needs a follow-up edit session.
opts.C: Claude checks every explanation against the case's values and phases, then you confirm verdicts.

short.why: The verdicts are clinical judgments you can make quickly, and you already approved the list. Against it, calling step-down incorrect when she never needed a pressor may be stricter than many hospitals practice.

questions.title: Should the platform adopt a written tagging policy and an "acceptable" tier?
questions.question: A textbook run of each case scores 35 to 64 percent on its action tabs because reasonable alternatives count as missed recommendations. Do you want a written tagging policy, and should it add a sixth tag, "acceptable", that is never counted as missed?
questions.context:
Every action a case references carries a tag rule list with one of five values: critical, recommended, discouraged, harmful, neutral. The debrief's four ordering tabs score a critical action at two points and a recommended one at one point, over everything expected in the phases the run visited. A discouraged action costs a point and a harmful halt zeroes the tab.

No document says what earns "recommended" rather than "neutral". The tagging was drafted case by case, mostly by a model. The count of case actions with at least one rule valued recommended is 43 of 89 in AFRVR, 26 of 68 in CHFE, 45 of 111 in DIPH and 50 of 124 in MGCA. When two drugs are both reasonable and a learner gives one, the other is listed as "not done" and costs a point.

The v0.18a educator review called this the largest open scoring problem. It made failed runs unscored but left the tier question to you. A tagging policy is also the place to settle the cross-case consistency question in ALL-08.
questions.current: Five tiers only (case-authoring-requirements.md section 7.3, scored per section 13.0). No written policy. Counts from each case JSON case_actions[*].tag.

quotes.text: The biggest one left is the score: after the fixes, each case's intended path still scores 35 to 64 percent on its action tabs, and a textbook MGCA run lists 35 recommendations as "not done", because acceptable alternatives count as missed recommendations.

quotes.source: audit-v018a.txt, Open items that need you, Tagging policy row
quotes.text: Write a one-page policy, add the tier, retag all four

A recommended tag therefore now carries weight it did not before: it is a point on offer, and a case that tags forty things recommended has diluted its critical actions. Tag recommended what you would actually want said in the debrief.

options.label: Written policy, retag with the existing five tiers
options.detail: A one-page policy defines each tier with examples. Recommended is kept for acts you would name in a debrief. Interchangeable alternatives are grouped with also_covers or listed as satisfiers, so doing one satisfies the expectation. All four cases are retagged against it.
options.tradeoff: No engine change. But a coverage group can only say "either one satisfies this". It cannot say "reasonable, not expected", so some reasonable choices drop to neutral and their teaching notes become harder to find.
options.implementation: New section 7.4 "Tagging policy" in docs/case-authoring-requirements.md. Retag CHFE-case.json and MGCA-case.json case_actions[*].tag and cases/AFRVR/case_2_actions.py and cases/DIPH/case_2_actions.py. Regenerate AFRVR and DIPH, rerun the four suites and all scenarios, and report the new intended-path scores.

options.label: Policy plus a new "acceptable" tier
options.detail: Same policy, plus a sixth tier. An acceptable action is reasonable but not expected. It is never listed as missed, earns no points and costs none, and its note appears in a debrief section such as "Reasonable choices you made". This is the audit's suggested default.
options.tradeoff: The clearest signal to a learner. It costs engine, validator and debrief work, and adds a sixth tier that every case and every reviewer must apply consistently.
options.implementation: Add "acceptable" to the tag enum in engine/validate_case.py, exclude it from the expected set in engine.js summaryScores, add the debrief section in engine/ui.js, update sections 7.3 and 13.0 of case-authoring-requirements.md, then retag the four cases as in A.

options.label: Score critical actions only
options.detail: The tab percentages count critical actions only, plus the discouraged and harmful penalties. Recommended actions stay listed under "Other actions worth doing" but carry no points.
options.tradeoff: Removes the dilution in one engine change with no retagging. The score becomes coarse (9 to 12 critical actions per case) and gives no credit for good supportive care.
options.implementation: engine.js summaryScores: numerator and denominator over critical actions only. Rewrite case-authoring-requirements.md section 13.0. No case edits.

questions.reasoning: The audit's numbers point to a structural gap: "reasonable but not required" has no tier, so a correct run cannot score well however it is retagged. An acceptable tier gives those choices a place and lets recommended mean "expected". The strongest argument against it is cost and consistency. It is a sixth tier to author and review in every case, and part of the dilution may be overtagging that a written policy alone (A) would fix more cheaply. If review time is short, do A first and add the tier only if scores stay low.
questions.evidence: There is no external evidence for this platform choice. The 35 to 64 percent figure comes from the v0.18a audit and was not re-measured for this question. The simulation assessment literature compares weighted checklists with global ratings, but none of it tests this tier design (from memory, verify).
sources: audit-v018a.txt Educator C5 and Open items

brief: A textbook run scores 35 to 64 percent on action tabs because reasonable alternatives count as missed.
No written rule says what earns recommended rather than neutral. A model drafted most tags.
When two drugs are reasonable and the learner gives one, the other costs a point.
short.now: Five tags (critical, recommended, discouraged, harmful, neutral). Critical earns two points, recommended one. No written policy.

opts.A: A policy defines each tier, and alternatives are grouped so either satisfies. Some drop to neutral.
opts.B: Reasonable choices never count as missed and get their own debrief section. Needs engine work.
opts.C: Scores count critical actions and penalties only. Coarser score, no credit for supportive care.

short.why: Reasonable but not required has no tier, so a correct run cannot score well however it is retagged. Against it, a sixth tier costs authoring and review, and a policy alone (A) may fix overtagging more cheaply.

questions.title: Which difficulty mode should be the default, given prompts can land after deterioration?
questions.question: Normal mode, the default, triples every prompt deadline but leaves deterioration deadlines unscaled. So in several cases the nurse's warning now arrives at or after the deterioration it was meant to prevent. Which default do you want?
questions.context:
A case authors prompt deadlines for Easy mode. Normal mode, where every case starts, multiplies every prompt, escalation and follow-up deadline by three. Time-guarded deteriorations are not scaled, on purpose, so the physiology is the same in both modes. The validator's fairness rule (a prompt must come at least 20 seconds before a deterioration) checks only the authored Easy deadlines.

Worked from the case JSON, in Normal mode:
- AFRVR: the positive-pressure prompt moves from 80 to 240 seconds, the same second as the 240-second slide into respiratory failure. The escalation moves to 600 seconds.
- CHFE: the mask prompt (45, escalation 90) becomes 135 and 270, and the nitrate prompt (60, escalation 140) becomes 180 and 420. The deterioration is at 240.
- MGCA: the antibiotic prompt (45, escalation 90) becomes 135 and 270, against a 240-second deterioration. In frank septic shock the pressor escalation moves from 100 to 300 seconds, the same second as the timed arrest.
- DIPH: in the wide-complex phase the bicarbonate prompt (25, escalation 90) becomes 75 and 270, against a timed pulseless VT at 120 seconds.

The DIPH and MGCA terminal opt-in rationales both justify a death on the clock by the prompts that precede it. In Normal mode some of those prompts never fire. The v0.14 reason for making Normal the default was that in Easy the prompt often arrives before the learner has finished thinking, so the debrief's "prompted" marker measures reading speed. The audit's randomized test mentions three difficulty modes, while the authoring document describes two. Confirm what the third is before you decide.
questions.current: difficulty.default is Normal (CHANGELOG v0.14). The Normal multiplier is 3 on prompts, escalations and follow-ups only (case-authoring-requirements.md section 9.7). Prompt deadlines are from each case JSON case_actions[*].prompt, and timed exits from phases[*].transitions[*].after_seconds.

quotes.text: The default Normal mode triples prompt deadlines, so some prompts arrive after the deterioration

quotes.source: audit-v018a.txt, Open items, Default difficulty row, suggested default
quotes.text: Easy for medical students and interns

The consequence is that in normal mode a resident can deteriorate a patient before the prompt that would have warned them has fired. That is the honest version of the question normal mode asks, and it is the strongest argument for setting your deadlines generously.
where a case uses deterioration on inaction, the deadline should be roughly three times the prompt deadline for the action that prevents it.

options.label: Keep Normal as the default, as authored
options.detail: The learner starts unaided and prompts come three times later. A frozen learner can reach a deterioration, or in DIPH and MGCA an arrest, before the warning.
options.tradeoff: Keeps the "independent versus prompted" report meaningful. But the default experience breaks the validator's own fairness rule, and the 3x convention in the decision record lands Normal prompts on the deterioration deadline.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off, and record that section 5.2 rule 2 is guaranteed in Easy mode only.

options.label: Make Easy the default, Normal an opt-in
options.detail: Every run starts with the authored deadlines. Normal becomes a labeled choice for senior learners. This is the audit's suggested default.
options.tradeoff: Every timed deterioration is preceded by its prompt. But the "prompted" marker measures reading speed again, which is the v0.14 reason for the change, and seniors must choose to make it harder.
options.implementation: Set difficulty.default to easy in engine/build_simulator.py SHARED. Update the splash wording in engine/ui.js, section 9.7 of case-authoring-requirements.md, and the mode sentence in the debrief.

options.label: Keep Normal, but never let a prompt pass its deterioration
options.detail: Normal still triples prompts, but in a phase with a time-guarded exit a prompt fires no later than 20 seconds before the exit whose guard it serves. Everywhere else, Normal is unchanged.
options.tradeoff: The fairness rule then holds in both modes, and Normal still gives less help elsewhere. It needs an engine change, and Normal gives more help in exactly the timed phases, which blurs what the mode means.
options.implementation: engine.js prompt scheduler: effective deadline = min(authored x multiplier, earliest time-guarded exit in the phase minus 20 s), for prompts on actions that set a flag the exit's guard requires unset (the same pairing validate_case.py uses for rule 2). Add a Normal-mode do-nothing walk to engine-tests.js and update section 9.7.

questions.reasoning: The prompt-before-deterioration rule is the platform's main fairness guarantee, and both terminal opt-ins in DIPH and MGCA rest on it. The default mode should not break it. C keeps that guarantee and keeps Normal meaning "less help" wherever no clock is running. The strongest argument against C is that it is an engine change with a less obvious meaning than B. B is simpler, matches the audit, and suits the medical students and interns that CHFE and MGCA target. If you prefer simplicity, choose B.
questions.evidence: There is no external evidence for this choice. The prompt and deadline figures above are computed from the case JSON files as they stand after v0.18c.
sources: audit-v018a.txt Educator M2 and Open items

brief: Normal mode, the default, triples prompt deadlines but leaves deterioration deadlines unscaled.
AFRVR's positive-pressure prompt moves to 240 seconds, the same second as the slide into respiratory failure.
DIPH and MGCA justify timed deaths by prompts that may never fire in Normal.
short.now: Normal is the default. Prompts, escalations and follow-ups are tripled. Deteriorations are not. Fairness rule checked in Easy only.

opts.A: Learners start unaided. A frozen learner can deteriorate, or arrest in DIPH and MGCA, unwarned.
opts.B: Every timed deterioration follows its prompt. The prompted marker again measures reading speed.
opts.C: In timed phases, prompts fire at least 20 seconds before the deterioration. Needs an engine change.

short.why: The prompt-before-deterioration rule is the main fairness guarantee, and the DIPH and MGCA terminal exits rest on it. C keeps it while Normal still means less help elsewhere. Against it, B is simpler and matches the audit.

questions.title: May an untreated patient sit in respiratory failure indefinitely?
questions.question: In AFRVR and CHFE, an untreated patient reaches a failure phase (saturation 80 to 82, drowsy or obtunded) and then stays there until the learner hands off. DIPH and MGCA end the case on the clock. Should the two respiratory cases also progress on the clock?
questions.context:
Time-guarded transitions let a case deteriorate when nothing is done. Ending a case on the clock needs an explicit opt-in and a rationale. The authoring guide says most cases should not use this.

Two cases opt in. DIPH moves from wide-complex tachycardia to pulseless VT after 120 seconds without bicarbonate. MGCA moves from frank septic shock to arrest after 300 seconds without antibiotics, hydrocortisone and a pressor.

Two cases stop short. In AFRVR, 240 seconds without positive pressure moves the patient to respiratory_failure: rate 166, 118/70, respiratory rate 38, saturation 82, alertness 1. In CHFE, 240 seconds without the mask or a nitrate moves him to impending_respiratory_failure: rate 126, 176/98, respiratory rate 38, saturation 80, alertness 2 (obtunded). Neither phase has a timed exit. A learner who does nothing more sees those numbers hold for as long as they wait, and can still complete the case with a handoff.

This is a platform policy question: when a failure phase is not survivable untreated, must the case say so on the clock? Your answer depends on ALL-02, because a new timed exit needs its prompt to survive whichever default mode you choose.

For AFRVR this plateau was the seed author's explicit instruction, recorded in packet §3. Option B would override a physician's instruction, which is why the recommendation below is the escalation option rather than a terminal exit.
questions.current: AFRVR phases[id=respiratory_failure].transitions and CHFE phases[id=impending_respiratory_failure].transitions have no after_seconds rule, only exits by intubation, positive pressure (plus nitrate in CHFE) or handoff. DIPH phases[id=wide_complex_tachycardia] and MGCA phases[id=frank_septic_shock] carry allow_time_to_terminal: true.

quotes.text: Exhausted after minutes of untreated work. Hypercapnic and drowsy with a saturation in the low eighties.
If the last row of it is a terminal phase, you have written a case that can kill the patient without the resident touching her, and that should be a decision you remember making.
Ending a case because nothing was done is the strongest statement this system can make
The do-nothing trajectory ends at respiratory failure and not in an arrest.

options.label: Keep as authored
options.detail: The two respiratory cases never end on the clock. The failure phase persists until the learner intubates, applies positive pressure or hands off.
options.tradeoff: Keeps the clock out of cases whose lesson is a treatment choice. But a learner may conclude that an obtunded, hypercapnic patient at a saturation of 80 is a stable plateau.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off for both cases.

options.label: Add a time-to-terminal exit to both failure phases
options.detail: After a deadline you set, an untreated failure phase moves to a new terminal phase (respiratory arrest) with its own timeout_reason, vitals, ECG block and debrief note. The existing positive-pressure and intubation prompts must fire first.
options.tradeoff: Consistent with DIPH and MGCA, and truthful about untreated respiratory failure. It adds a second way to die in each case, makes the ALL-02 decision binding, and needs a new do-nothing review of both deterioration timelines.
options.implementation: CHFE-case.json phases[id=impending_respiratory_failure].transitions: add a negative-guard rule on the airway flags (on_niv, intubated) with after_seconds set by you, allow_time_to_terminal true and terminal_opt_in_rationale, plus a new terminal phase respiratory_arrest. The same in cases/AFRVR/case_1_shell.py for respiratory_failure. Add prompts in each failure phase at least 20 s before the deadline, then regenerate and rerun both suites and the deterioration timelines.

options.label: Escalate without ending the case
options.detail: After a set time in the failure phase, the nurse escalates (for example asking whether to call anesthesia or set up for intubation) and the debrief reports how long the patient sat in respiratory failure. The vitals do not improve, and the case does not end on the clock.
options.tradeoff: Respects the AFRVR seed instruction and gives a stuck learner a realistic next step. The nurse's escalation partly hands the learner the answer, and the plateau still does not show progression to arrest.
options.implementation: Add a nurse prompt guarded on the failure phase with a deadline you set (AFRVR case_1_shell.py respiratory_failure, CHFE-case.json impending_respiratory_failure). Add a debrief line reporting time spent in the failure phase. Record the platform rule in case-authoring-requirements §5.2. Regenerate and rerun both suites and deterioration timelines.

questions.reasoning: C keeps the physician seed's explicit instruction for AFRVR while removing the worst part of the plateau, which is a learner who waits with no signal at all. B is the more truthful model of untreated hypercapnic failure and would make all four cases follow one rule, so it is a close call. The strongest argument against C is that a nurse suggesting the airway hands over the phase's key decision. Settle ALL-02 first, because any prompt here must fire in the default mode.
questions.evidence: Untreated hypercapnic respiratory failure with falling consciousness progressing to arrest within minutes to hours is standard clinical teaching, but no source gives a defensible deadline in seconds (from memory, verify). Any deadline you set is a teaching choice, and the rationale field should say so.

brief: Untreated AFRVR and CHFE patients reach a failure phase, saturation 80 to 82, drowsy or obtunded, and stay there.
DIPH and MGCA end the case on the clock. The AFRVR plateau was the seed author's explicit instruction.
short.now: Neither failure phase has a timed exit. The numbers hold until airway treatment or handoff.

opts.A: The failure phase persists until treatment or handoff. Learners may read it as a stable plateau.
opts.B: After a deadline you set, untreated failure becomes respiratory arrest. Overrides the AFRVR seed instruction.
opts.C: After a set time the nurse escalates, and the debrief reports time spent in failure.

short.why: C keeps the AFRVR seed instruction while ending the wait with no signal. B is more truthful about untreated failure, so it is close. Against C, the nurse's escalation hands over the phase's key airway decision.

questions.title: Should the catalog split arrest-dose epinephrine from push-dose epinephrine?
questions.question: One catalog button, "Epinephrine bolus", stands for both the cardiac arrest dose and push-dose pressor epinephrine, because doses are not implemented. Should it become two entries?
questions.context:
The catalog has epinephrine_bolus ("Epinephrine bolus", under Meds - Resuscitation, IV bolus), epinephrine_drip and epinephrine_intramuscular. The engine does not implement doses, so the button carries no amount.

Cases already use it in different senses. CHFE binds its own action epinephrine_push_dose to epinephrine_bolus. MGCA tags epinephrine_bolus recommended in frank septic shock, which only makes sense as a push-dose pressor. DIPH tags it discouraged. A learner who presses "Epinephrine bolus" for a hypotensive patient with a pulse cannot tell which drug the case thinks they gave, and a debrief that credits it could be read as crediting an arrest dose given to a patient with a pulse.

The v0.18a catalog review listed this as an open major finding. Ids are derived from names, so a rename or split touches every case that binds the id.
questions.current: catalog/action-catalog.json entries[id=epinephrine_bolus]: display_name "Epinephrine bolus", route_class iv_bolus, placement Meds - Resuscitation, no dose. Bound by CHFE (as epinephrine_push_dose, CHFE-binding-map.json), MGCA (recommended in frank_septic_shock) and DIPH (discouraged).

quotes.source: audit-v018a.txt, Open items, Catalog names row
quotes.text: 23.4 percent saline, Tdap, amphotericin formulation, aqueous penicillin G, arrest versus push-dose epinephrine. Ids derive from names, so a rename touches every case
The other seven majors (magnesium duplicates, formulation names, missing antidotes, epinephrine dose ambiguity, fixed furosemide dose, a 3 percent bolus) are open.

options.label: Keep one entry, cases explain in notes
options.detail: The button stays. Each case's debrief note says which use it is scoring.
options.tradeoff: No id changes. The learner still presses an ambiguous button, and a note read after the case cannot correct what the learner believed they were doing.
options.implementation: No catalog change. Add a sentence to the debrief_note of epinephrine_bolus in CHFE-case.json, MGCA-case.json and cases/DIPH/case_2_actions.py.

options.label: Split into two named entries
options.detail: Two entries: "Epinephrine IV/IO (cardiac arrest dose)" and "Push-dose epinephrine (dilute)". Each case retags the one it means and tags the other.
options.tradeoff: Removes the ambiguity where the learner acts. It costs an id map across three cases and a tag decision for the second entry in each.
options.implementation: catalog: replace entries[id=epinephrine_bolus] with epinephrine_arrest_dose and epinephrine_push_dose (iv_bolus, IV access prerequisite, Meds - Resuscitation and Meds - Vasoactive Agents). Id map in the rename pass. Rebind CHFE-binding-map.json, retag MGCA-case.json and cases/DIPH/case_2_actions.py, update voice aliases for "epi" and "push-dose epi", and rerun all suites.

options.label: Split, and warn when a case leaves the arrest dose untagged
options.detail: As B, plus a validator warning when a case has a phase with a pulse and does not tag the arrest-dose entry in it.
options.tradeoff: Makes the dangerous choice something each case must decide. The catalog still holds no appropriateness judgment, but the validator adds a rule that names one drug, which the design has so far avoided.
options.implementation: As B, plus a check in engine/validate_case.py that warns when epinephrine_arrest_dose is untagged or neutral in any non-terminal phase.

questions.reasoning: Epinephrine dosing errors between the arrest dose and pressor doses are a known source of harm, and a teaching tool should not blur them at the point of action. B fixes the ambiguity where the learner makes the choice. C adds a drug-specific validator rule that goes against the design's rule of keeping clinical judgment out of the engine. The strongest argument against B is the cost of the id change across three cases, which should be batched with the other renames in ALL-35.
questions.evidence: Epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO every 3 to 5 minutes in adult arrest is AHA ACLS guidance (from memory, verify). Push-dose epinephrine for peri-intubation or transient hypotension is supported mainly by observational data and expert practice, and errors from confusing concentrations are described in safety literature (from memory, verify).

brief: One button, Epinephrine bolus, covers both the arrest dose and push-dose pressor. Doses are not implemented.
CHFE binds push-dose epinephrine to it, MGCA tags it recommended in septic shock, DIPH tags it discouraged.
A debrief credit could read as an arrest dose given with a pulse.
short.now: One Epinephrine bolus entry, IV bolus, no dose. Push-dose in CHFE, recommended in MGCA, discouraged in DIPH.

opts.A: The button stays. Each case's debrief note explains which use it scored, after the fact.
opts.B: Two buttons, arrest dose and dilute push-dose. Costs an id map across three cases.
opts.C: Two buttons, plus a validator warning when a phase with a pulse leaves arrest dose untagged.

short.why: Arrest versus pressor dose errors are likely a known source of harm, so B fixes the ambiguity where the learner acts. C adds a drug-specific validator rule. Against B, the id change touches three cases, best batched with ALL-35.

questions.title: Do you sign off the hypertonic saline changes, its name and a 3 percent bolus?
questions.question: The concentrated hypertonic saline bolus now needs a central line. Its catalog name still says 25 percent, MGCA shows it as 23.4 percent, and there is no 3 percent bolus. How should the hypertonic saline entries read?
questions.context:
The v0.18a catalog review found that 25 percent saline could be given through a peripheral line. It rated this a critical error and fixed it in draft: the entry now requires central access, with a nurse message saying so.

Three things are still open. The name says 25 percent, while the commonly stocked US concentrate is 23.4 percent. MGCA already overrides the display name to "Hypertonic saline 23.4% bolus", but DIPH shows the catalog name "Hypertonic saline (25%) bolus", so the same button reads differently in two cases. And the catalog has a 3 percent infusion but no 3 percent bolus, the form used for symptomatic hyponatremia and raised intracranial pressure.

In the cases, MGCA tags both hypertonic entries discouraged. DIPH tags the concentrated bolus neutral, including after bicarbonate in the wide-complex phase.
questions.current: catalog/action-catalog.json entries[id=hypertonic_saline_25_bolus]: display "Hypertonic saline (25%) bolus", prerequisite "flag central_access set" with message "That concentration has to go through a central line. Do you want one placed?". entries[id=hypertonic_saline_3_infusion] needs any line. No 3 percent bolus entry. MGCA-case.json overrides the display name to 23.4 percent.

quotes.source: audit-v018a.txt, Physician section, Catalog critical finding
quotes.text: 25 percent hypertonic saline could be given through a peripheral line

quotes.source: audit-v018a.txt, Fixes made, Catalog row (Sign-off: Yes)
quotes.text: 25 percent saline needs a central line. Induction agents and paralytics set the intubation flags. Naloxone, glucagon and hydrocortisone need no line
That concentration has to go through a central line. Do you want one placed?

options.label: Rename to 23.4 percent, keep central line, add 3% bolus
options.detail: The concentrate becomes "Hypertonic saline 23.4% bolus" (central line). A new "Hypertonic saline 3% bolus" is added with any-line access. These are the audit's defaults.
options.tradeoff: Matches what US departments stock and what MGCA already shows. The rename touches every case that binds the id, and the new bolus needs a tag decision in each case.
options.implementation: catalog: rename hypertonic_saline_25_bolus to hypertonic_saline_23_4_bolus via the id map, keeping the central_access prerequisite. Add hypertonic_saline_3_bolus (iv_bolus, standard access prerequisite, Meds - Miscellaneous). Remove MGCA's display override. Retag in MGCA-case.json and cases/DIPH/case_2_actions.py, update voice aliases, rerun.

options.label: Sign off the central line, keep the 25 percent name
options.detail: Only the drafted safety fix is accepted. The name and the missing 3 percent bolus stay as they are.
options.tradeoff: Smallest change. The same button keeps two different names across cases, and a learner who wants a 3 percent bolus has no button for it.
options.implementation: No catalog change beyond the drafted prerequisite. Record sign-off. Either remove MGCA's display override or add the same one in cases/DIPH/case_2_actions.py so the two cases agree.

options.label: Remove the concentrate, add a 3 percent bolus
options.detail: Drop the concentrated bolus from the catalog altogether and offer 3 percent as a bolus and an infusion.
options.tradeoff: Removes a drug that ED learners rarely give and that is dangerous if mishandled. But it takes away a real option for herniation and for sodium loading in sodium-channel toxicity, which DIPH currently tags neutral.
options.implementation: catalog: delete hypertonic_saline_25_bolus and add hypertonic_saline_3_bolus. Remove the bindings in MGCA-case.json and cases/DIPH/case_2_actions.py, retag the new entry, update voice aliases, rerun.

questions.reasoning: The central-line requirement fixes a real hazard and should be signed. The 23.4 percent name matches what a US learner will meet. One consistent name across cases avoids a learner seeing two concentrations for one button. The 3 percent bolus fills a gap the catalog review flagged. The strongest argument against A is cost: a rename plus a new entry each need a tag decision in all four cases, so batch them with the other renames in ALL-35.
questions.evidence: 23.4 percent sodium chloride is the concentrate commonly used in US practice for intracranial hypertension and is generally given centrally. 3 percent boluses are used for severe symptomatic hyponatremia per expert consensus (from memory, verify). Peripheral 3 percent is increasingly accepted in observational studies (from memory, verify).
sources: audit-v018a.txt Physician, Fixes made (Catalog row 1) and Open items

brief: The concentrated hypertonic saline bolus now requires a central line, fixing a critical peripheral-line error.
Its name says 25 percent. MGCA shows 23.4 percent, DIPH shows 25 percent.
The catalog has a 3 percent infusion but no 3 percent bolus.
short.now: Hypertonic saline (25%) bolus needs a central line. MGCA tags it discouraged, DIPH neutral. No 3 percent bolus.

opts.A: Concentrate renamed 23.4 percent, still central. New 3 percent bolus via any line. Every case retags.
opts.B: Only the central-line fix is signed. The name stays 25 percent, and no 3 percent bolus.
opts.C: Concentrate removed, 3 percent as bolus and infusion. Loses an option for herniation and sodium loading.

short.why: The central line fixes a real hazard, 23.4 percent matches what US learners meet and gives one name across cases, and the 3 percent bolus fills a flagged gap. Against it, each change needs tag decisions in every case.

questions.title: How should references be verified before learners see them?
questions.question: Of 46 references across the four cases, 27 are marked unverified, and since v0.18a the display strips that marker, so a learner sees an unverified citation as if it were checked. Who checks references, and what may learners see in the meantime?
questions.context:
Debrief notes cite trials and guidelines. Most of these citations were written by a model. Each carries a marker in the case file, such as "[UNVERIFIED, confirm before release]" or "[PubMed record checked]". Counted from the case JSON, AFRVR has 9 references (9 unverified), CHFE 18 (9 unverified), DIPH 1 (1 unverified) and MGCA 18 (8 unverified).

In v0.18a the interface began stripping these markers from everything the learner reads, because a marker in a teaching note tells a learner to distrust it. The side effect is that an unverified reference now looks identical to a checked one. The audit also notes that the clinical pass was itself a model reading cases against guidelines, with some guideline classes and doses cited from memory.

A model can check a citation's existence, DOI and wording against web sources quickly. It cannot vouch that a paper supports the teaching claim as a physician would read it.
questions.current: Reference strings in each <CASE>-case.json (debrief_note references, rationale fields) carry verification markers. The markers are removed at display (CHANGELOG v0.18a, authoring section 13). No reference has a recorded physician check.

quotes.text: They are optional, and an unverified one is worse than none. A plausible-looking citation to a paper that does not say what is claimed will be believed.
Reference verification markers stay in the case file and are stripped from the display.

This pass was a model reading each case against guidelines, not a physician's review. Where a reviewer cited a guideline class or a dose from memory, the finding says so and needs checking against the source.

options.label: Physicians check every reference themselves
options.detail: Each case's reviewing physician opens every cited source and confirms it supports the sentence it is attached to.
options.tradeoff: The most reliable. It is also the most time-consuming, and 46 references is several hours spread across busy reviewers.
options.implementation: No tooling. Record each check in the case file by replacing the marker with "[verified by <initials>, <date>]", and list the results in each review packet's references section.

options.label: Claude pre-checks, physicians confirm, unverified hidden
options.detail: Claude checks each citation against PubMed or the publisher: that it exists, its details, and a verbatim passage that supports the claim. It produces a table. The physician confirms or rejects each row. Until a row is confirmed, the learner-facing note shows no citation.
options.tradeoff: Much faster for physicians, and learners never see an unconfirmed citation. It relies on Claude's quotes being exact and adds a display rule that hides content until sign-off.
options.implementation: Claude builds rv/reference-check-<CASE>.md with citation, source URL, verbatim supporting passage and a verdict. engine/ui.js hides any reference string whose marker is not a physician-verified marker. The review tool records the confirmations in the case file.

options.label: Claude verifies, physicians spot-check
options.detail: A reference Claude matches to a verbatim supporting passage is shown to learners. Physicians spot-check a sample, and only mismatches are escalated.
options.tradeoff: Fastest. But it lets a model decide what counts as support for a clinical claim, which is the judgment the authoring rules reserve for physicians.
options.implementation: As B for the table. Show references marked "[machine-verified]" and spot-check 20 percent at random, recorded in each packet.

questions.reasoning: Hiding unconfirmed citations restores the protection the stripped markers used to give, without printing a warning into teaching notes. Claude's pre-check does the mechanical part, and the physician keeps the judgment of whether the paper supports the claim. The strongest argument against B is that a model-produced quote could itself be wrong, so the physician must open the source for any row they are not sure of, not just read the table.
questions.evidence: There is no evidence base for this process choice. The reference counts are from a scan of the four case JSON files and may miss references embedded in free-text notes without a reference field.

brief: 27 of 46 references across the four cases are marked unverified. A model wrote most citations.
Since v0.18a the display strips the marker, so an unverified citation looks checked.
A model can confirm a citation exists, but not that it supports the teaching claim.
short.now: Verification markers stay in the case files but are stripped from display. No reference has a recorded physician check.

opts.A: Each reviewing physician opens every source. Most reliable, but several hours across busy reviewers.
opts.B: Claude builds a table with verbatim supporting passages. Physicians confirm rows. Unconfirmed citations stay hidden.
opts.C: References Claude matches to a passage are shown. Physicians spot-check a sample. A model judges support.

short.why: Hiding unconfirmed citations restores the protection the markers gave without warnings in teaching notes, and physicians keep the judgment of support. Against it, Claude's quotes could be wrong, so physicians must open any source they doubt.

questions.title: Do you sign off the catalog's default normal results and reference ranges?
questions.question: Any study a case does not author returns the catalog's default normal result, and those defaults and ranges were drafted by a model from general knowledge. How do you want them reviewed?
questions.context:
The learner sees the whole catalog of 300 actions. If a case does not author a study, ordering it returns the catalog default, which is normal. The authoring guide calls this the most dangerous property of the system. The v0.18a educator review found three unauthored studies in CHFE (cardiac ultrasound, blood gases, CT chest) returning normals that contradicted the diagnosis.

The defaults' values and reference ranges were drafted by a model, not taken from a laboratory reference. Known weak points listed in the catalog: arterial gas defaults assume room air, peak flow has no meaningful normal, and blood type and hCG are patient attributes rather than normals.

**How to check:** Claude exports every default result in the catalog (label, value, unit, range) into one table grouped by panel. You mark any range or value you would not accept for an adult US emergency department, and any default that would mislead in one of the four cases. Separately, for each case, Claude lists every study that would return a default (the debrief already lists these after a run). The case reviewer then confirms that none contradicts that case's diagnosis.
questions.current: catalog/action-catalog.json entries[*].default_result for every investigation and exam. known_gaps records that defaults were drafted by the AI from general knowledge and are unverified.

quotes.text: Anything the case does not author returns the catalog default, which is normal. This is the most dangerous property of the system.
Default normal results were drafted by the AI from general knowledge, not from a laboratory reference. Ranges are assay- and institution-specific and are unverified.
ABG defaults assume room air. On supplemental oxygen the same numbers are abnormal, and nothing in the schema knows that.

options.label: Confirmed as drafted
options.detail: You have read the default table and accept every value and range as a reasonable adult normal.
options.tradeoff: Closes the item. It is only as good as the read, and assay-specific ranges vary by institution.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off in catalog/action-catalog.json field_provenance and remove the known_gaps line.

options.label: Needs change: list the entries
options.detail: You name the defaults or ranges to change, and any study that should return "not applicable" or "not available" instead of a normal.
options.tradeoff: Fixes what you find. Any change to a default affects every case that does not author that study.
options.implementation: Edit entries[id=...].default_result per your list, rerun the four suites and the validator, and regenerate the review matrices.

options.label: Ask Claude to pre-check first, then I confirm
options.detail: Claude compares each default range with a named published reference (for example a standard laboratory reference table), flags the mismatches, and you review only the flagged rows plus the per-case default lists.
options.tradeoff: Cuts your reading to the disagreements. It depends on Claude citing a real, current reference for each range.
options.implementation: Claude produces rv/catalog-defaults-check.md with each default, the comparison source and quote, and a flag. You confirm, and the changes are applied as in B.

questions.reasoning: There are too many defaults for a full physician read to be a good use of time, and most will be uncontroversial. A pre-check that surfaces disagreements makes the review tractable. The per-case list of studies returning defaults is the part that most needs a physician, because only the case reviewer can see that a normal result contradicts the diagnosis. The strongest argument against C is that a published reference range is itself institution-specific, so agreement with one table is not proof of correctness.
questions.evidence: Reference intervals are assay- and laboratory-specific. No single universal table exists.

brief: Any study a case does not author returns the catalog default, which is normal.
A model drafted the defaults and ranges from general knowledge, not a laboratory reference.
The v0.18a review found three unauthored CHFE studies returning normals that contradicted the diagnosis.
short.now: Learners see all 300 catalog actions. Unauthored studies return unverified normal defaults. Arterial gas defaults assume room air.

opts.A: You accept every default value and range as a reasonable adult normal.
opts.B: You list defaults to change, or studies that should return not available.
opts.C: Claude compares ranges with a published reference. You review flagged rows and the per-case default lists.

short.why: Most defaults are uncontroversial, so a pre-check makes the review tractable, and the per-case lists get a physician's eye where it matters most. Against it, any published range is institution-specific, so agreement is not proof.

questions.title: Should the same act be scored the same way across cases unless a case says why?
questions.question: The same catalog action carries different tags in different cases, sometimes for good clinical reasons and sometimes by drafting accident. Do you want a platform baseline for common acts that a case may override only with a stated reason?
questions.context:
The v0.18a educator review (finding M6) found the same act scored differently across cases. Some examples from the current case JSON: AFRVR tags all twelve exam maneuvers it references recommended, while CHFE, DIPH and MGCA tag every exam neutral and score the physical through key_exams. Attaching the monitor is critical in AFRVR and recommended in MGCA. Consulting critical care is recommended in AFRVR and CHFE and critical in DIPH and MGCA. Labetalol and propranolol are discouraged in AFRVR and DIPH and harmful in MGCA.

Some of these differences are right: a beta blocker in a patient in septic shock with adrenal crisis is not the same act as in a hypertensive patient. Others look like drafting drift. The authoring guide lists unindicated antibiotics as a standard discouraged trap, yet CHFE leaves ceftriaxone neutral. The AFRVR diltiazem item (discouraged in AFRVR, harmful in CHFE) is in the AFRVR question bank.

A learner who plays several cases will notice when the same act is praised in one and ignored in another. Without a stated reason, they may conclude the scoring is arbitrary.
questions.current: No cross-case baseline exists. Tags are set per case in each <CASE>-case.json case_actions[*].tag (CHFE uses its own ids bound through CHFE-binding-map.json). AFRVR and DIPH now tag plausible traps discouraged after v0.18a.

quotes.text: Partly. Plausible traps are now tagged in AFRVR and DIPH. A written policy is open
Morphine in acute pulmonary edema, a bronchodilator for cardiac asthma, unindicated steroids or antibiotics, an unnecessary CT: these are `discouraged`.
Ceftriaxone, aspirin and the D-dimer stay neutral.

options.label: Case by case, with a reason when it differs
options.detail: Each case keeps its own tags. Where a common act is tagged differently from the other cases, its debrief note says why in one sentence.
options.tradeoff: Keeps the case author's judgment. Consistency then depends on someone comparing cases, which nobody currently does.
options.implementation: Add a cross-case tag table to each review matrix (generated by the matrix tool from all four packs) and add a reason sentence to each differing note in the case files.

options.label: Platform baseline, case overrides with a reason
options.detail: A short baseline table sets the default tag for universal acts: monitor, line, ECG, glucose, each exam, common consults, and the standard traps (unindicated antibiotics, steroids, CT). A case may override the baseline only with a recorded reason, which the validator requires.
options.tradeoff: Predictable for learners, and the reasons become reviewable. It needs a baseline you agree on and a validator rule, and some case teaching will move.
options.implementation: New section in the tagging policy (see ALL-01) with the baseline table. engine/validate_case.py warns when a case tag differs from the baseline without an override_reason field. Retag the four cases where they differ without reason.

options.label: Fixed global tags for universal acts
options.detail: Universal acts carry one tag everywhere and cases cannot change them.
options.tradeoff: The most consistent. It is also wrong where the patient genuinely differs, for example exams that carry a case's teaching, or a monitor attached late in a patient who is crashing.
options.implementation: Move the tags for the listed acts into catalog/action-catalog.json as tag defaults, remove them from the cases, and add an engine change so the catalog can carry a tag.

questions.reasoning: A baseline with reasoned overrides keeps real clinical differences while removing drift, and it makes each difference something a reviewer can check. It also gives the ALL-01 policy concrete content. The strongest argument against B is that it adds a validator rule and a new artifact that must be kept current as cases are added, and a physician must first agree the baseline itself.
questions.evidence: There is no external evidence for this choice. The examples are from the current case JSON files.

brief: The same act gets different tags across cases, sometimes for clinical reasons, sometimes by drafting drift.
A critical care consult is recommended in AFRVR and CHFE but critical in DIPH and MGCA.
Learners who play several cases may conclude the scoring is arbitrary.
short.now: No cross-case baseline. Each case sets its own tags. AFRVR tags exams recommended, the other three neutral.

opts.A: Tags stay per case, and differing notes give a one-sentence reason. Nobody compares cases today.
opts.B: A baseline table tags universal acts. Cases override only with a reason the validator requires.
opts.C: Universal acts carry one fixed tag everywhere. Wrong where the patient genuinely differs.

short.why: A baseline with reasoned overrides keeps real clinical differences, removes drift, and gives the ALL-01 policy concrete content. Against it, a physician must first agree the baseline, and it adds a validator rule and a table to maintain.

questions.title: Do you sign off the intubation drug flags, and add a crash-airway intubation?
questions.question: Intubation is blocked until an induction agent and a paralytic have been given. Since v0.18a, four induction agents (including midazolam) and two paralytics set those flags. Do you sign this off, and should there be an intubation entry for a patient in arrest that needs no drugs?
questions.context:
The catalog's intubation entry requires the flags sedation_given and paralytic_given. Before v0.18a some induction drugs did not set them, so a learner who gave the right drugs could still be refused. The fix makes etomidate, ketamine, propofol and midazolam set sedation_given, and succinylcholine and rocuronium set paralytic_given. Fentanyl does not set sedation_given, so fentanyl with a paralytic alone is refused.

The authoring guide says a crash airway in arrest does not need drugs, and lets a case waive the prerequisite. But the catalog has no separate arrest intubation, and the audit lists one as a needed addition. Today, a case that wants a learner to intubate during arrest must author a waiver.

Midazolam counts as an induction agent here. It is used for induction, less often in emergency RSI because of its slower onset and hypotension.
questions.current: catalog/action-catalog.json: intubate_rapid_sequence prerequisite "flag sedation_given set AND flag paralytic_given set". flags_set_default sedation_given on midazolam_bolus, etomidate_bolus, ketamine_bolus and propofol_bolus, and paralytic_given on succinylcholine_bolus and rocuronium_bolus. No arrest intubation entry.

quotes.text: The four induction agents and two paralytics set the flags the intubation prerequisite asks for.
A crash airway in a patient already in arrest does not require sedation and paralysis

quotes.source: audit-v018a.txt, Open items, Catalog additions row
quotes.text: Vitamin K, protamine, calcium gluconate, hydroxocobalamin, methylene blue, deferoxamine, antivenom, idarucizumab, desmopressin, a 3 percent bolus, an arrest intubation, a magnesium maintenance infusion

options.label: Sign off as drafted
options.detail: The six drug flags stand. There is no arrest intubation entry, and cases waive the prerequisite when they need to.
options.tradeoff: No further change. A future arrest case must remember to author the waiver, or a learner will be refused a crash intubation.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off.

options.label: Sign off, and add an arrest intubation entry
