options.detail: As drafted, plus a catalog entry "Intubate (crash, in cardiac arrest)" with no drug prerequisite. It sets intubated. Each case tags it (usually harmful or discouraged in a patient with a pulse).
options.tradeoff: Makes the crash airway a deliberate act rather than a waiver. Every case then needs a tag for the new entry, and a learner might press it in a patient with a pulse to skip the drugs, which the tag must catch.
options.implementation: catalog: add intubate_crash_arrest (stabilization, Intubation group, flags_set_default intubated, no prerequisite). Add it to SHARED.patient.deviceActions so the figure draws the tube. Tag it in all four cases (harmful or discouraged in any phase with a pulse) and rerun.

options.label: Remove the drug prerequisite and teach by tags
options.detail: Intubation is never blocked. Intubating without induction and paralysis is instead tagged harmful or discouraged in each case, with a note.
options.tradeoff: Closer to real life, where nothing physically stops you. But it loses the immediate blocked-action message the nurse gives today, which teaches sequencing at the moment it matters, and it needs a tag rule in every case.
options.implementation: catalog: remove default_prerequisites from intubate_rapid_sequence. Each case adds a tag rule on intubate_rapid_sequence for "NOT flag sedation_given set OR NOT flag paralytic_given set" in live phases, with a halt reason where harmful.

questions.reasoning: The drafted flags match standard RSI drug choices and should be signed. An arrest intubation entry avoids relying on each future case to remember a waiver. The strongest argument against B is the tag burden: every case must tag the new entry so that it cannot be used as a shortcut in a patient with a pulse, and a missed tag there would teach something unsafe.
questions.evidence: Etomidate, ketamine and propofol are standard RSI induction agents, and midazolam is an accepted but slower alternative. Succinylcholine and rocuronium are the standard paralytics (from memory, verify).
sources: catalog/action-catalog.json entries[id=intubate_rapid_sequence], induction and paralytic entries
audit-v018a.txt Fixes made (Catalog row 1) and Open items

brief: Intubation requires an induction agent and a paralytic. Six drugs now set those flags, including midazolam.
Fentanyl with a paralytic alone is refused.
A crash airway in arrest needs no drugs, but each case must author a waiver today.
short.now: Intubation is blocked until sedation and paralytic flags are set. No arrest intubation entry exists.

opts.A: The flags stand. Future arrest cases must remember the waiver, or learners are refused.
opts.B: New crash intubation with no drug prerequisite. Every case must tag it to block shortcuts.
opts.C: Intubation is never blocked, and tags penalize skipping drugs. Loses the nurse's immediate sequencing message.

short.why: The flags likely match standard RSI drugs, and an arrest entry stops relying on each case remembering a waiver. Against it, every case must tag the new entry, and a missed tag would teach something unsafe.

questions.title: May naloxone, glucagon and hydrocortisone be given with no IV line?
questions.question: Since v0.18a these three drugs no longer need vascular access, because each has a non-IV route. Do you sign that off?
questions.context:
Catalog drugs with an IV route need a line before the nurse will give them. The fix removed that requirement from naloxone, glucagon and hydrocortisone, whose route class is "unspecified". The reasoning: naloxone is given intranasally or IM, glucagon IM for hypoglycemia, and hydrocortisone IM in adrenal crisis when no line is available.

The catch is that one button now covers both routes. Glucagon for beta-blocker or calcium-channel-blocker toxicity is given IV in large doses, so a learner could give it that way with no line. MGCA's critical hydrocortisone can now be given before a line, which matches guidance on IM hydrocortisone in suspected adrenal crisis.
questions.current: catalog/action-catalog.json entries[id=naloxone_bolus], [id=glucagon], [id=hydrocortisone_bolus]: route_class "unspecified", default_prerequisites empty.

quotes.text: Naloxone, glucagon and hydrocortisone no longer require IV access.
route_class is derived, not transcribed. Entries marked 'unspecified' need author confirmation because the vascular-access prerequisite depends on it.

options.label: Sign off as drafted
options.detail: All three may be given without a line.
options.tradeoff: Matches the common non-IV uses and removes a false block in MGCA. It lets IV-only uses such as high-dose glucagon in toxicology through without a line, which no current case teaches.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off and set route_class to "any" in the three entries so the known_gaps line no longer applies to them.

options.label: Naloxone and hydrocortisone free, glucagon needs a line
options.detail: Glucagon goes back to needing IV access, while the other two stay line-free.
options.tradeoff: Fits glucagon's toxicology use. It blocks IM glucagon for hypoglycemia in a patient without a line, which is also a real use.
options.implementation: catalog: restore the standard access prerequisite on entries[id=glucagon] and set route_class iv_bolus. Rerun the suites.

options.label: Split each into route-specific entries
options.detail: Separate buttons for naloxone IN/IM and IV, glucagon IM and IV, and hydrocortisone IM and IV. Only the IV entries need a line.
options.tradeoff: The most accurate, and it lets a case teach route choice. It adds six entries, and every case must tag each one.
options.implementation: catalog: replace the three entries with six (non_iv and iv_bolus), add voice aliases, map old ids, retag MGCA hydrocortisone as a coverage group over both routes, rerun.

questions.reasoning: No current case turns on the route of these drugs. The drafted change removes a real false block for MGCA's critical hydrocortisone, and naloxone's usual ED route does not need a line. The strongest argument against A is glucagon: a future toxicology case would need C, or at least B, so revisit this when such a case is written.
questions.evidence: IM or subcutaneous hydrocortisone is recommended when IV access is delayed in suspected adrenal crisis. Intranasal and IM naloxone are standard. Glucagon for beta-blocker toxicity is given IV (from memory, verify).
sources: catalog/action-catalog.json entries naloxone_bolus, glucagon, hydrocortisone_bolus, known_gaps

brief: Since v0.18a naloxone, glucagon and hydrocortisone need no IV line, since each has a non-IV route.
One button covers both routes, so high-dose IV glucagon for toxicity also needs no line.
MGCA's critical hydrocortisone can now be given before a line.
short.now: All three have route class unspecified and no access prerequisite.

opts.A: All three given without a line. IV-only glucagon uses also pass, though no case teaches them.
opts.B: Glucagon needs IV access again. Blocks IM glucagon for hypoglycemia without a line.
opts.C: Six route-specific buttons, and only IV ones need a line. Every case must tag each.

short.why: No current case turns on these routes, and the change removes a false block on MGCA's critical hydrocortisone. Against it, a future toxicology case would need C, or at least B, for glucagon.

questions.title: Do you sign off the new catalog defaults and diagnosis synonyms?
questions.question: v0.18a changed several catalog defaults and added two diagnosis synonyms. Do you sign off each one?
questions.context:
The changes are:
- Blood type and screen now defaults to O positive (it was O negative, which would have created an Rh immune globulin indication for any unauthored patient).
- The soft-tissue ultrasound default reads "No discrete fluid collection or abscess. No cobblestoning. No echogenic foreign body identified."
- The CSF cell count default gains a differential line ("Not performed (too few cells)"), and CSF glucose gains a range stated with a CSF-to-serum ratio.
- Serum hCG is now numeric ("< 5 mIU/mL").
- The diagnosis catalog gains the synonyms "high-risk PE" and "altitude sickness".

Blood type and pregnancy status are patient attributes, not normal values. A default states them for every patient a case does not author, including the two male patients, for whom the catalog's own note says hCG should arguably be unavailable. Both female patients (DIPH and MGCA) author their own hCG, and MGCA authors its blood type.
questions.current: catalog/action-catalog.json entries[id=blood_type_and_screen], [id=ultrasound_soft_tissue], [id=csf_cell_count], [id=csf_glucose], [id=serum_hcg_quantitative] default_result. Diagnosis synonyms are in the diagnosis catalog (not among the files read for this question).

quotes.text: Defaults: blood type O positive, an ultrasound foreign body described as echogenic, CSF differential and glucose range, a numeric serum beta-hCG. Diagnosis synonyms "high-risk PE" and "altitude sickness".
Every unauthored patient is now not pregnant, including male patients, for whom the study should arguably be unavailable.
Blood type is a patient attribute, not a normal value, and no case should depend on this default.

options.label: Sign off all as drafted
options.detail: Every listed default and synonym stands.
options.tradeoff: Closes the item. A male patient's hCG still returns "< 5 (non-pregnant)", which is odd but not clinically false.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off.

options.label: Sign off, but hCG is not applicable for male patients
options.detail: As drafted, except that serum and urine hCG return "Not applicable" when patient.sex is male.
options.tradeoff: Removes an odd result. It needs the engine to choose a default by sex, which the catalog cannot express today.
options.implementation: engine.js result resolution: when patient.sex is male and the study is serum_hcg_quantitative or urine_hcg_qualitative, return a not-applicable payload. Add an engine test.

options.label: Patient attributes must be authored by every case
options.detail: Blood type and hCG lose their defaults. The validator makes every case author them, so no case relies on a stated attribute it did not choose.
options.tradeoff: The most honest. It adds authoring to AFRVR and CHFE (and DIPH's blood type) and a validator rule.
options.implementation: catalog: replace the two defaults with a "not stated" payload. engine/validate_case.py errors when a case omits blood_type_and_screen or (for female patients) the hCG studies. Author them in AFRVR, CHFE and DIPH.

questions.reasoning: The drafted defaults are reasonable, and the one real hazard (O negative implying an Rh indication) was removed. The cases where pregnancy matters already author their own hCG. The strongest argument against A is principle: a default that states an attribute is an unreviewed clinical assertion about every future patient, which C prevents at a small authoring cost.
questions.evidence: O positive is the most common ABO/Rh type in the US population (from memory, verify).

brief: Blood type now defaults to O positive. O negative implied an Rh immune globulin indication for unauthored patients.
Serum hCG now reads < 5 mIU/mL for every unauthored patient, including the two male patients.
Also changed are CSF and soft-tissue ultrasound defaults, plus two diagnosis synonyms.
short.now: Blood type defaults to O positive, hCG to < 5 mIU/mL. DIPH and MGCA author their own hCG.

opts.A: Every listed default and synonym stands. Male patients still get a non-pregnant hCG.
opts.B: hCG returns not applicable for male patients. Needs the engine to choose defaults by sex.
opts.C: Blood type and hCG lose their defaults. The validator makes every case author them.

short.why: The defaults are reasonable, the one real hazard (O negative) was removed, and cases where pregnancy matters author hCG. Against it, a default attribute is an unreviewed clinical claim about every future patient.

questions.title: Should a study covered by another action return that action's result?
questions.question: Since v0.18a, ordering a study that a case has covered with another action (for example, a cardiac ultrasound that is part of a combined lung and cardiac POCUS) returns the covering action's authored result instead of a catalog normal. Do you sign off this rule?
questions.context:
A case can declare that one action covers another (also_covers). CHFE authors a combined lung and cardiac POCUS. Before v0.18a, a learner who ordered the separate catalog entry for a cardiac ultrasound got the catalog default: a normal ventricle, in a patient with an ejection fraction of 25 percent. The educator review rated unauthored studies contradicting the diagnosis as critical (C2).

The engine now returns the covering action's authored payload instead. The side effect is that a learner who ordered only the cardiac view may see the combined report, lung findings included.
questions.current: engine.js result resolution (v0.18a): for an action covered through also_covers, the covering action's authored result is served before the catalog default. The audit marks this Engine row "Sign-off: Yes".

quotes.text: A study covered by another action returns that action's authored result, not a catalog normal. CHFE's cardiac ultrasound read as a normal ventricle.
Unauthored studies returned normal results that contradicted the diagnosis (CHFE cardiac ultrasound, blood gases, CT chest)

options.label: Sign off as drafted
options.detail: A covered study returns the covering action's full result.
options.tradeoff: Removes the contradiction everywhere with no authoring. The learner may see more than the one view they ordered.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off.

options.label: Return only the relevant part
options.detail: Each case splits combined results so the cardiac view returns only cardiac findings and the lung view only lung findings.
options.tradeoff: The most faithful to the order. It needs authoring in every case with a combined study, and a missed split falls back to showing everything.
options.implementation: In CHFE-case.json content_keys.imaging, author separate ultrasound_cardiac and ultrasound_lung rules from the pocus_lung_cardiac text. Do the same in any other case with a coverage group over studies.

options.label: Return a pointer to the combined study
options.detail: A covered study returns a short line such as "Done as part of the bedside lung and cardiac ultrasound. See that result."
options.tradeoff: Honest and cheap. It adds a step for the learner and may read as the tool refusing the order.
options.implementation: engine.js: for a covered study, return a report payload naming the covering action, and show the covering action's result in the record if not yet ordered. Add an engine test.

questions.reasoning: The rule removes a class of silent, clinically wrong normals with no case authoring, which is the most important property. Showing a little extra information is a far smaller harm than a normal ventricle in a failing heart. The strongest argument against A is that it can reveal findings the learner did not order, which in a case built on discovering something could give it away. Watch for that in each case's review.
sources: audit-v018a.txt Educator C2 and Fixes made (Engine row 7)

brief: Before v0.18a, CHFE's separate cardiac ultrasound returned a normal ventricle in a patient with ejection fraction 25 percent.
Now a covered study returns the covering action's authored result, so the cardiac view may show lung findings too.
short.now: A covered study returns the covering action's full authored result, served before the catalog default.

opts.A: A covered study returns the full combined result. The learner may see more than they ordered.
opts.B: Each case splits combined results by view. Needs authoring, and a missed split shows everything.
opts.C: A covered study returns a line pointing to the combined study. May read as a refusal.

short.why: It removes silent, clinically wrong normals with no authoring, a far larger harm than extra information. Against it, extra findings could give away a case built on discovery, so each case review should watch for that.

questions.title: Should reports seen during a case carry findings only, with no impression?
questions.question: Lab comments that interpret a result are shown only in the debrief. Imaging and ECG reports shown during the case are meant to state findings, not conclusions, but CHFE's reports still interpret. What is the rule for all cases?
questions.context:
Since v0.9, a lab panel shows only numbers while the case runs. The authored comment that reads the result is printed once, in the debrief section "Your results, read". Imaging and ECG reports are shown during the case. The authoring rule says they carry findings, not conclusions, and AFRVR's reports were cut to findings on that argument.

The four cases are not consistent. CHFE's ECG report includes "consistent with an established anterior infarct", and its POCUS reports also use "consistent with" wording. A scan found no interpretive phrases in DIPH's reports. Real radiology reports carry an impression, and an ED physician reads it. A learner who performs a POCUS or reads their own ECG gets no impression in real life.

The choice is between making the learner interpret everything (the current written rule) and matching what real reports look like.
questions.current: Lab comment: debrief only (CHANGELOG v0.9, authoring section 11.4). Reports: shown live. The findings-only rule is applied in AFRVR (CHANGELOG "Reports state findings, not conclusions") but not throughout CHFE (for example CHFE-case.json content_keys.imaging.ecg_12_lead.rules[2].value.report).

quotes.text: The authored `comment` under a panel was the case reading the result for the resident. It is now printed once, in a new debrief section, "Your results, read", with the panel it belongs to.
Author findings, not conclusions, and keep them short.
Q waves in V1 to V4 with associated T wave inversion, consistent with an established anterior infarct.

options.label: Findings only everywhere, comments debrief-only
options.detail: Every report shown during a case states findings only, in all four cases. Interpretation lives in the debrief note and in lab comments.
options.tradeoff: Consistent, and it keeps the reasoning for the learner. Radiologist-read studies look less real, and interpreting CT text becomes a skill the case tests without meaning to.
options.implementation: Strip interpretive clauses from report payloads in CHFE-case.json and MGCA-case.json content_keys.imaging, and check cases/AFRVR and cases/DIPH generators. Move the removed reasoning into each study's debrief_note.

options.label: Formal reads get an impression, bedside studies do not
options.detail: Studies another clinician formally reads (radiology CT and plain films, a formal echo) may end with a one-line impression, as real reports do. Learner-performed studies (POCUS, the twelve-lead tracing) state findings only. Lab comments stay debrief-only.
options.tradeoff: Realistic, and it keeps interpretation where the learner would really do it. An impression can give away what the case wants discovered, so each case must check its impressions.
options.implementation: Write the rule into case-authoring-requirements.md section 11.4. Add impression lines to radiologist-read reports, and strip interpretation from POCUS and ECG reports in all four cases. Each case reviewer checks that no impression gives away the case.

options.label: Leave it to each case
options.detail: Each case decides, and the review packet records the choice.
options.tradeoff: No work now. The inconsistency across cases stays, and learners meet different conventions.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off per case.

questions.reasoning: B matches what a learner will meet at work: they read a radiologist's impression, and they interpret their own ultrasound and ECG. That keeps interpretation practice where it belongs without making CT text a hidden reading test. The strongest argument against B is that an impression can give away the diagnosis a case is built around, which is why the platform chose findings-only in the first place. A is the safer option if you think giveaways are the larger risk.
questions.evidence: Standard radiology reports include an impression section (for example, ACR practice parameters on communication, from memory, verify). No evidence compares these choices for simulation learning.
sources: CHANGELOG.md v0.9 and "Reports state findings, not conclusions"
scan of all four case JSON report payloads

brief: Lab comments show only in the debrief. Imaging and ECG reports show live and should state findings only.
CHFE's ECG and POCUS reports still say "consistent with". AFRVR's were cut to findings.
Real radiology reports carry an impression, but learner-performed POCUS and ECG do not.
short.now: Lab comments debrief only. Reports shown live. Findings-only applied in AFRVR, not throughout CHFE.

opts.A: Live reports state findings only. Radiologist reads look less real, and CT text becomes a test.
opts.B: Formally read studies may end with a one-line impression. POCUS and ECG state findings only.
opts.C: Each case decides and records it. Learners meet different conventions across cases.

short.why: B matches real work, where learners read a radiologist's impression but interpret their own ultrasound and ECG. Against it, an impression can give away the diagnosis, so A is safer if giveaways worry you more.

questions.title: How should tests that cannot return during the encounter behave?
questions.question: Cultures return "Cultures pending", and tests the catalog lacks (for example serum cortisol) cannot be ordered at all. Should a test that would not come back within a real ED encounter be orderable and return "sent, not back yet"?
questions.context:
Turnaround is compressed to 5 to 10 seconds. That is fine for a basic panel, but misleading for tests that take hours or days. The catalog handles cultures by returning "Cultures pending". It handles cortisol, ACTH and similar send-out tests by not having them.

MGCA's author wanted the learner to be able to send a cortisol. With no entry, a learner who reaches for the right test finds it does not exist, which reads as a gap in the tool rather than as the real point that treatment precedes confirmation. The same applies to any future case with a send-out test.
questions.current: catalog/action-catalog.json: blood_culture_x_2, csf_culture and urine_culture default to "Cultures pending.". No serum cortisol, ACTH or cosyntropin entry (MGCA-case.json catalog_change_requests[id=no_serum_cortisol]).

quotes.text: It is still a gap: a resident who orders the right test should be told it has been sent and will not return, not find that the test does not exist.
Blood cultures take 24-48 hours

options.label: Add them, returning "sent, not back during this visit"
options.detail: Add catalog entries for common send-out tests (serum cortisol, ACTH and others you name). Each returns a fixed line saying the sample was sent and will not result during the encounter. Cultures keep "pending".
options.tradeoff: Honest, and a case can still credit the order. Each new entry must be tagged by every case (usually neutral or recommended).
options.implementation: catalog: add serum_cortisol, acth and others with a report payload "Sent. Will not result during this encounter." and turnaround class lab. Tag them in MGCA (recommended alongside hydrocortisone). Update section 11.4 of the authoring guide.

options.label: Keep as is
options.detail: Cultures stay pending and absent tests stay absent.
options.tradeoff: No work. A learner who reaches for the right confirmatory test is told nothing useful.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off.

options.label: Add them, with the result shown in the debrief
options.detail: As A, but a case may author the eventual result, which the debrief prints as "Resulted after you handed off".
options.tradeoff: Teaches the full story (for example, a low cortisol confirming the crisis). It adds authoring and a debrief section, and the learner never uses the number during the case.
options.implementation: As A, plus a payload field eventual_result read by a new debrief section in engine/ui.js.

questions.reasoning: A learner who orders the correct confirmatory test should be told it was sent, not find it missing. A is the smallest change that says that truthfully. The strongest argument against A is catalog growth: every send-out test added is a button each future case must consider. C is the richer teaching choice if you want the debrief to close the loop.
questions.evidence: Treating suspected adrenal crisis before cortisol results return is standard guidance (from memory, verify).

brief: Turnaround is compressed to 5 to 10 seconds, misleading for tests that take hours or days.
Cultures return pending. Send-out tests such as serum cortisol cannot be ordered at all.
MGCA's author wanted the learner to be able to send a cortisol.
short.now: Blood, CSF and urine cultures return "Cultures pending." No serum cortisol, ACTH or cosyntropin entry.

opts.A: Send-out tests become orderable and return sent, not back this encounter. Every case must tag each.
opts.B: Cultures stay pending and absent tests stay absent. The learner is told nothing useful.
opts.C: Orderable as in A, and the debrief prints an authored eventual result. Adds authoring.

short.why: A learner who orders the right confirmatory test should hear it was sent, and A says that most simply. Against it, each added test is a button every future case must consider. C closes the loop more fully.

questions.title: Should the catalog offer IM midazolam and IM ketamine?
questions.question: Midazolam and ketamine exist only as IV entries that need a line. Should the catalog add IM versions, for a seizing or dangerously agitated patient without access?
questions.context:
midazolam_bolus and ketamine_bolus both require an IV, IO or central line. A learner who wants IM midazolam for a seizing patient, or IM ketamine for a violent, agitated one, has no button for it. The nurse refuses and asks for a line first.

DIPH has both an agitated arrival and a seizure phase. The catalog review listed IM routes for midazolam and ketamine among open catalog details.
questions.current: catalog/action-catalog.json entries[id=midazolam_bolus] and [id=ketamine_bolus]: default_prerequisites require iv_access, central_access or io_access. No IM entries.

quotes.source: audit-v018a.txt, Open items, Catalog details row
quotes.text: Magnesium push duplicate, fixed furosemide 40 mg, route classes, pads gate on shocks, IM routes for midazolam and ketamine, vasopressin placement, synonym cleanup

options.label: Add separate IM entries
options.detail: Add "Midazolam IM" and "Ketamine IM" with no line requirement. The IM midazolam entry sets the same flag as the IV benzodiazepines where a case needs it.
options.tradeoff: Teaches a real first-line option in seizure and agitation. Each case must tag the new entries, and DIPH's benzodiazepine coverage group must include IM midazolam.
options.implementation: catalog: add midazolam_im and ketamine_im (non_iv, no prerequisite, Meds - Sedation/Analgesia). In cases/DIPH/case_2_actions.py add midazolam_im to the benzodiazepine coverage group and set benzo_given. Tag both in all four cases, add voice aliases, rerun.

options.label: Remove the line requirement from the existing entries
options.detail: midazolam_bolus and ketamine_bolus become route unspecified, like naloxone.
options.tradeoff: No new ids. It hides a real distinction: induction doses for intubation need a line, and the button would no longer teach that.
options.implementation: catalog: clear default_prerequisites on the two entries and set route_class unspecified. Rerun.

options.label: Keep IV only
options.detail: The learner must get access first.
options.tradeoff: No change. It teaches that a seizing patient must wait for a line, which contradicts current practice.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off.

questions.reasoning: IM midazolam is a standard option for a seizing patient without access, and a teaching tool should not block it. Separate entries keep the IV induction use distinct. The strongest argument against A is the tag work in every case, and the risk that DIPH's seizure rules miss the new entry and deny credit for a correct act.
questions.evidence: The RAMPART trial found IM midazolam at least as effective as IV lorazepam for prehospital status epilepticus (Silbergleit and colleagues, 2012, from memory, verify). IM ketamine for severe agitation is supported mainly by observational data (from memory, verify).

brief: Midazolam and ketamine need an IV, IO or central line. The nurse refuses and asks for a line.
A seizing or violently agitated patient without access has no IM option.
DIPH has both an agitated arrival and a seizure phase.
short.now: Midazolam and ketamine exist only as IV entries requiring IV, central or IO access. No IM entries.

opts.A: New Midazolam IM and Ketamine IM buttons, no line needed. Every case must tag both.
opts.B: Existing entries drop the line requirement. Hides that induction doses need a line.
opts.C: The learner must get access first. Implies a seizing patient must wait for a line.

short.why: IM midazolam is likely a standard option for seizures without access, and separate entries keep IV induction distinct. Against it, every case needs tagging, and DIPH's seizure rules could miss the new entry and deny credit.

questions.title: Should the furosemide button stop naming a fixed 40 mg dose?
questions.question: The catalog's only loop diuretic is "Furosemide 40 mg IV", while the engine implements no doses and the debrief notes teach dose relative to home dose. Should the entry drop the number?
questions.context:
furosemide_40_mg_iv is the loop_diuretic equivalence group's only member. AFRVR tags it critical. CHFE binds its furosemide_iv to it, and CHFE's note now has to explain the fixed dose ("The 40 mg offered here is the floor of that range for a man taking 40 mg daily").

The two notes also teach the home-dose rule differently. CHFE says an IV dose of one to two and a half times the total daily oral dose. AFRVR says "the usual rule of two to two and a half times the home oral dose" does not apply to a diuretic-naive patient. Whichever wording you prefer should appear in both.

A learner who wants 80 mg can only press 40 mg, and the debrief then explains why 40 was acceptable.
questions.current: catalog/action-catalog.json entries[id=furosemide_40_mg_iv], display "Furosemide 40 mg IV". AFRVR tag critical. CHFE furosemide_iv bound to it (CHFE-binding-map.json).

quotes.text: The 40 mg offered here is the floor of that range for a man taking 40 mg daily
Catalog carries the dose in the display name, so the case no longer needs its own.

options.label: Keep "Furosemide 40 mg IV"
options.detail: No change. Notes continue to explain the dose.
options.tradeoff: No id change. The button states a dose the engine does not model, and it may be wrong for a future patient on a high home dose.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off, and align the home-dose wording in the CHFE and AFRVR notes.

options.label: Rename to "Furosemide IV" with no dose
options.detail: The button names the drug and route only. Each case's note gives the dose reasoning for its patient.
options.tradeoff: Honest about what the engine models, and it fits every future patient. It needs an id change in two cases, batched with the other renames.
options.implementation: catalog: rename furosemide_40_mg_iv to furosemide_iv through the id map, and update equivalence_groups.loop_diuretic. Rebind CHFE-binding-map.json and cases/AFRVR/case_2_actions.py. Align the home-dose wording in both notes. Rerun.

options.label: Two entries: standard and high dose
options.detail: "Furosemide IV (standard dose)" and "Furosemide IV (high dose)", both loop diuretics, tagged by case.
options.tradeoff: Lets a case teach the dose decision. Doses still do nothing physiologically, so the difference lives only in the tag and the note.
options.implementation: catalog: add two entries and put both in loop_diuretic. Tag both in AFRVR and CHFE, rerun.

questions.reasoning: A dose on a button that the engine ignores invites a learner to think the dose was assessed. Removing it keeps the dose teaching in the notes, where each case can fit its own patient. The strongest argument against B is that C would let CHFE actually test the home-dose rule it teaches. If that rule is a learning objective you want scored, choose C.
questions.evidence: The DOSE trial found no significant difference in its co-primary endpoints between high and low dose (Felker and colleagues, 2011, from memory, verify). Heart failure guidelines advise an initial IV dose at least equal to the home oral dose in patients already on a loop diuretic (from memory, verify).
sources: CHFE-case.json and AFRVR-case.json furosemide debrief notes

brief: The only loop diuretic button is Furosemide 40 mg IV, but the engine implements no doses.
CHFE's note must explain why 40 mg is acceptable. A learner wanting 80 mg can only press 40.
CHFE and AFRVR notes teach the home-dose rule differently.
short.now: Furosemide 40 mg IV is the only loop diuretic. Critical in AFRVR, bound to CHFE's furosemide.

opts.A: Keeps 40 mg, which may be wrong for a future patient on a high home dose.
opts.B: The button names drug and route only. Notes carry the dose. Id change in two cases.
opts.C: Standard and high-dose buttons. The dose lives only in tags and notes, not physiology.

short.why: A dose the engine ignores invites learners to think it was assessed, so the notes should carry dose teaching. Against it, C would let CHFE score the home-dose rule it teaches.

questions.title: Which catalog additions should be made before a case needs them?
questions.question: The catalog review listed twelve missing entries, and the cases have asked for others. Which do you want added now?
questions.context:
Every learner sees the whole catalog, so a missing entry is a treatment nobody can give. The voice-order parser already refuses "calcium gluconate" rather than substituting calcium chloride.

The audit's list: vitamin K, protamine, calcium gluconate, hydroxocobalamin, methylene blue, deferoxamine, antivenom, idarucizumab, desmopressin, a 3 percent saline bolus (see ALL-05), an arrest intubation (see ALL-09) and a magnesium maintenance infusion.

The cases add their own requests. MGCA asks for serum cortisol (see ALL-14), fibrinogen (now worked around as a fourth component of the coagulation panel) and dextrose 10 percent. DIPH asks for gastric lavage (which its teaching discusses) and a core or rectal temperature.

Each new entry needs a route class, prerequisites, a default result where it is a study, and a tag decision in every case (neutral if nothing else).
questions.current: None of the listed entries exist in catalog/action-catalog.json (300 entries). MGCA-case.json and DIPH-case.json catalog_change_requests list the case-level gaps.

quotes.source: audit-v018a.txt, Open items, Catalog additions row
quotes.text: Vitamin K, protamine, calcium gluconate, hydroxocobalamin, methylene blue, deferoxamine, antivenom, idarucizumab, desmopressin, a 3 percent bolus, an arrest intubation, a magnesium maintenance infusion
calcium gluconate is not swapped for calcium chloride
The catalog offers D50 and D5, with nothing between them.

options.label: Add the audit's twelve now
options.detail: All twelve are added before any case needs them. The case-requested gaps wait.
options.tradeoff: Fills the antidote gaps a future case would hit. It leaves the gaps current cases already asked for.
options.implementation: catalog: add twelve entries with route_class, prerequisites and placement. Neutral by default in all four cases, with voice aliases. Rerun the validator and suites.

options.label: Add only what current cases touch
options.detail: Add the entries the four cases' teaching reaches: magnesium maintenance, a 3 percent bolus, arrest intubation, calcium gluconate, serum cortisol, fibrinogen, D10, core temperature. Defer the antidotes until a case needs them.
options.tradeoff: Least review now. A future case author must remember to request them, which is how these gaps arose.
options.implementation: catalog: add the eight entries. Tag them where each case's teaching needs it (MGCA cortisol, fibrinogen, D10, AFRVR magnesium infusion, DIPH core temperature), neutral elsewhere. Rerun.

options.label: Add the audit's twelve and the case requests
options.detail: Everything on both lists, in one reviewed batch with the renames in ALL-35.
options.tradeoff: One review pass instead of several. It is the largest batch, and each entry is a small clinical claim (route, access, default) you must check.
options.implementation: As A plus the case-requested entries (serum cortisol, fibrinogen as its own study, D10, gastric lavage, core temperature). Remove MGCA's fibrinogen workaround once the study exists. Tag in all four cases, rerun.

questions.reasoning: The catalog is shared, and each missing entry has already cost one case a workaround or a gap. Reviewing one batch now is cheaper than piecemeal later, and it keeps a learner from finding a standard antidote missing. The strongest argument against C is review load: about seventeen entries, each needing a route class and access rule you are willing to sign. B is the leaner choice if physician time is short.

brief: Every learner sees the whole catalog, so a missing entry is a treatment nobody can give.
The audit lists twelve missing entries, such as vitamin K, protamine, calcium gluconate and idarucizumab.
MGCA and DIPH request others, such as serum cortisol, D10 and core temperature.
short.now: None of the listed entries exist among the catalog's 300. Voice orders refuse calcium gluconate.

opts.A: The audit's twelve are added now. Gaps current cases already asked for stay open.
opts.B: Eight entries current cases touch. Antidotes wait until a future case requests them.
opts.C: Both lists in one reviewed batch with the ALL-35 renames. The largest batch to check.

short.why: Each missing entry has already cost a case a workaround or gap, and one batch now is cheaper than piecemeal. Against it, about seventeen entries each need a route and access rule you will sign.

questions.title: Is a 10-second drug effect acceptable compression for the learner's own actions?
questions.question: Deteriorations must wait at least 30 seconds, but a delayed consequence of the learner's own action may act after 5. AFRVR's second rate-control dose and DIPH's bicarbonate change the phase 10 seconds after they are given. Is that floor right?
questions.context:
The validator applies a 30-second floor (with a warning below 60) to things that happen to the learner: a deterioration on inaction, or scheduled natural history. Since v0.9, a delayed consequence of the learner's own action (a positive guard measured from when it became true) has a 5-second floor instead. The reasoning is that there is nothing to prevent, so fairness is not at stake.

In the cases now: AFRVR moves to the rate-controlled phases 10 seconds after the second nodal-blocking dose, with a nurse alert that the drugs take time. DIPH moves to stabilizing 10 seconds after bicarbonate plus a benzodiazepine or propofol, and to seizing 10 seconds after bicarbonate alone in the wide-complex phase. MGCA's adrenal crisis after fluid without hydrocortisone waits 90 seconds, because its guard also names a missing drug.

Real onsets are minutes, not seconds. DIPH's own nurse alert on bicarbonate says "a minute or two", while the phase changes at 10 seconds, so the case currently says two different things. The question is how much compression still teaches the right expectation.
questions.current: engine/validate_case.py: 30 s floor for negative-guard and unguarded timed transitions, 5 s for guard_true rules whose guard negates no flag. AFRVR phases[id=presentation] and [id=breathing_supported] rate-control rules after_seconds 10. DIPH bicarbonate rules after_seconds 10 in presentation, post_ictal and wide_complex_tachycardia.

quotes.text: It can take a minute or two before you see the complexes change.

A delayed consequence of an action they took (`measured_from: "guard_true"` with a guard that negates no flag) has nothing to prevent and no reflex to test: it is the case saying how long a drug takes to work, and its floor is five seconds, below which the consequence is on the same click as the action and the drug is a button again.

options.label: Keep the 5-second floor, cases choose
options.detail: As now. Cases may set any delay of 5 seconds or more for their own drugs.
options.tradeoff: Keeps cases short. It lets a case show a drug working in seconds, which a learner may carry into practice as an expectation.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off.

options.label: Raise the floor to 30 seconds for all timed transitions
options.detail: Every timed transition, including the learner's own drug effects, waits at least 30 seconds.
options.tradeoff: A more believable onset. A 10-minute case with several drugs then spends much of its time waiting, and AFRVR and DIPH need retiming and rescheduled prompts.
options.implementation: engine/validate_case.py: apply the 30 s floor to guard_true rules. Retime AFRVR (cases/AFRVR/case_1_shell.py) and DIPH (cases/DIPH/case_1_shell.py) and rerun the scenarios.

options.label: Keep 5 seconds, but require the real onset to be stated
options.detail: Short delays stay, but each must state the real-world onset in its author_rationale, and pair it with a nurse_alert or debrief note that says the simulator compresses it.
options.tradeoff: Keeps the pace and stops the compression passing as physiology. It adds a validator check and some note text.
options.implementation: engine/validate_case.py: warn when a guard_true rule under 30 s has no author_rationale mentioning onset. Align the existing nurse_alert on DIPH's bicarbonate (cases/DIPH/case_2_actions.py) with the 10-second change, for example by saying the simulator shortens the wait. AFRVR's rate-control alert already says the drugs take time.

questions.reasoning: The compression is needed for a case that runs about ten minutes, but a learner should not leave thinking bicarbonate narrows the QRS in ten seconds. C keeps the pace and makes the compression explicit where the learner meets it. The strongest argument against C is that learners may not read a nurse alert, so B is the only option that makes the timing itself truthful.
questions.evidence: Onset of IV rate control and of bicarbonate on QRS width is minutes (from memory, verify). No evidence addresses time compression in screen-based simulation.

brief: Deteriorations wait at least 30 seconds, but the learner's own drug effects may act after 5.
AFRVR's second rate-control dose and DIPH's bicarbonate change the phase after 10 seconds.
DIPH's nurse says bicarbonate takes a minute or two. Real onsets are minutes.
short.now: AFRVR rate control and DIPH bicarbonate change phase after 10 seconds. MGCA's adrenal crisis waits 90.

opts.A: Delays of 5 seconds or more stay allowed. Learners may expect drugs to act in seconds.
opts.B: Every timed transition waits 30 seconds or more. Cases spend more time waiting and need retiming.
opts.C: Short delays stay, but each must state its real onset and say the simulator compresses it.

short.why: Compression is needed in a case of about ten minutes, but learners should not think bicarbonate narrows the QRS in ten seconds. Against it, learners may not read the nurse alert, so only B makes the timing truthful.

questions.title: Should the case clock keep running while the learner reads?
questions.question: The clock stops for the leave dialog, the three-minute pause and a hidden window, but it keeps running while a learner reads a consultant's answer or a result. Should reading stop the clock?
questions.context:
Deadlines are claims about how long a patient tolerates something. The clock is held while the leave dialog is open (v0.17m), during the three-minute reflection pause (v0.17n), and while the window is hidden or unfocused (the case pauses until the learner clicks to resume). It runs while the learner reads a consultant response, a report or an image, or composes orders.

The decision record deferred this as open decision 9 and said it should be settled against real learners rather than argued. The mitigations today are the 30-second floor and the mandatory prompt before a deterioration, which ALL-02 shows do not always hold in Normal mode.
questions.current: One running clock with holds for the leave dialog, the reflection pause and window blur or hide (CHANGELOG v0.17m, v0.17n, "The case waits for you"). No hold for reading.

quotes.text: A resident reading a long consultant response is on the same clock as one who has frozen, which is unfair in a way a prompt firing is not.
This should be revisited against a real learner rather than argued about.

options.label: Keep one running clock, measure in a pilot
options.detail: No change now. The first pilot records time spent reading consultant and result panels next to each deterioration, and you revisit with data.
options.tradeoff: Real time pressure is part of emergency care. Slow readers are penalized until the data exist, and the analytics currently send no panel-level timing.
options.implementation: No engine change. Add consented panel-open and panel-close timing events in engine/analytics.js for the pilot, and record the decision as provisional.

options.label: Hold the clock while long text is open
options.detail: Opening a consultant response, a report or an image holds the clock until it is closed.
options.tradeoff: Removes the reading penalty. It lets a learner stop time by opening panels, and it makes deadlines less realistic.
options.implementation: engine/ui.js: take the same clock hold the leave dialog uses while the consult, report or image panel is open. Log the holds and show them on the debrief timeline.

options.label: Add a visible pause the learner may use
options.detail: A pause control the learner can press at any time. Each pause is shown on the debrief timeline.
options.tradeoff: Gives control to the learner and shows how they used it. It weakens time pressure for anyone who pauses freely.
options.implementation: engine/ui.js: a pause button calling pauseSim(), logged as a timeline event. Debrief shows total paused time.

questions.reasoning: The decision record is right that this is an empirical question, and the fairness concern is partly handled by ALL-02. Holding the clock on reading changes what every deadline means, so it should rest on evidence from learners. The strongest argument against A is that the first cohort of learners carries the unfairness while the data are collected.
sources: CHANGELOG.md v0.17m, v0.17n and "The case waits for you"

brief: The clock stops for the leave dialog, the reflection pause and a hidden window, but not for reading.
A learner reading a consultant response runs on the same clock as one who froze.
The decision record deferred this to data from real learners.
short.now: One running clock, held for the leave dialog, the three-minute pause and a hidden window. No hold for reading.

opts.A: No change now. A pilot records reading time near each deterioration. Slow readers penalized meanwhile.
opts.B: The clock holds while a consult, report or image is open. Learners could stop time.
opts.C: A pause button the learner may press, shown on the debrief timeline. Weakens time pressure.

short.why: Holding the clock for reading changes what every deadline means, so it should rest on learner data, as the decision record says. Against it, the first cohort carries the unfairness while data are collected.

questions.title: What should the monitor show when a harmful action halts the case?
questions.question: Each case has one halted phase whatever the harmful action was. CHFE, DIPH and MGCA draw a slow, wide, P-less idioventricular rhythm there, and AFRVR now draws the patient's own atrial fibrillation. What should the policy be?
questions.context:
When a harmful action halts a case, the engine moves to that case's halted phase. It has one set of vitals and one ECG block, so every halt in a case looks the same whatever the mechanism. The monitor blocks for these phases are model output, not physician-authored.

Current state: CHFE halted is rate 34, 48/28, with a wide P-less rhythm (QRS 180). DIPH halted is 36, 58/32 (QRS 200). MGCA halted is 44, 52/30 (QRS 180), and MGCA's cardiac_arrest phase is 26, 44/24 (QRS 200). AFRVR changed in v0.18a. Its only halt is a crystalloid bolus causing respiratory failure, so its halted phase is rate 150, saturation 76, in atrial fibrillation with a narrow QRS.

A single picture can contradict a halt reason. CHFE's dobutamine halt says the drug "precipitated sustained ventricular tachycardia", while the halted monitor shows a slow idioventricular rhythm at 34. The review packets' addenda still describe AFRVR's halted block as the generic wide rhythm, so they are stale on that point.
questions.current: ecg blocks: CHFE-case.json phases[id=halted].ecg {p_waves false, qrs_ms 180}, DIPH-case.json phases[id=halted].ecg {p_waves false, qrs_ms 200}, MGCA-case.json phases[id=halted] and [id=cardiac_arrest]. AFRVR halted is set in cases/AFRVR/case_1_shell.py (p_waves false, qrs_ms 88).

quotes.text: If you would rather see asystole, or a converted sinus bradycardia with P waves, the block for that phase changes and nothing else does.
v0.18a. His own rhythm at the point of respiratory failure: atrial fibrillation with a narrow QRS.
the rise in myocardial oxygen demand and its arrhythmogenic effect precipitated sustained ventricular tachycardia with hemodynamic collapse.
One vitals block per terminal phase. Every halt shows the same numbers whatever the mechanism.

options.label: Keep the current blocks and check halt reasons against them
options.detail: CHFE, DIPH and MGCA keep the generic peri-arrest picture and AFRVR keeps its own rhythm. Each case reviewer rewrites any halt reason the picture contradicts (for example CHFE's dobutamine).
options.tradeoff: No engine change, and the generic picture fits most collapse mechanisms. Specific halt reasons have to be softened to match one picture.
options.implementation: No ECG change. Record sign-off of each block. Edit contradicting halt_reason text in the case files (CHFE dobutamine first). Update the stale addendum tables in the four review packets.

options.label: Asystole in every halted and arrest phase
options.detail: Every halt and arrest shows a flat line with no beats.
options.tradeoff: Unambiguous that the case is over. Asystole seconds after a drug is rarely the true mechanism, and it would contradict AFRVR's respiratory failure halt.
options.implementation: Set ecg.pattern to asystole in phases[id=halted] of all four cases and phases[id=cardiac_arrest] in MGCA. Change the AFRVR block in cases/AFRVR/case_1_shell.py and rerun.

options.label: Let each halt choose its picture
options.detail: An engine change: a harmful action may name its own terminal phase, so each halt shows its own mechanism (VT for dobutamine, bradycardic collapse for a beta blocker).
options.tradeoff: The most faithful. It needs an engine change, several new terminal phases per case, and more model-authored terminal content to review.
options.implementation: engine.js: allow case_actions[*].halt_phase naming a terminal phase, defaulting to halted. Author the phases in each case and extend the validator and matrix tooling.

questions.reasoning: The halted phase shows for only a few seconds before the debrief, and a generic peri-arrest picture is honest for most harms in these cases. What matters is that the words and the picture agree, which the halt reasons can be edited to achieve. The strongest argument against A is CHFE, where ten different harms share one picture, so a physician may reasonably want C before CHFE is released.
sources: the four review packets, Addendum: the monitor trace (v0.16)

brief: Each case has one halted phase, so every harmful halt looks the same whatever the mechanism.
CHFE's dobutamine halt cites sustained VT, but the monitor shows a slow idioventricular rhythm at 34.
These monitor blocks are model output, not physician-authored.
short.now: CHFE, DIPH and MGCA show a slow, wide, P-less rhythm. AFRVR shows atrial fibrillation, rate 150, saturation 76.

opts.A: The pictures stay. Reviewers rewrite halt reasons the picture contradicts, softening specific mechanisms.
opts.B: Every halt and arrest shows asystole. Rarely the true mechanism, and contradicts AFRVR's halt.
opts.C: Each harmful action names its own terminal phase and picture. Needs an engine change and review.

short.why: The halted phase shows only seconds before the debrief, and a generic peri-arrest picture fits most harms here, so editing words to match suffices. Against it, ten CHFE harms share one picture, which may justify C.

questions.title: Is the patient's "Do you mean X, or Y?" clarifying question acceptable?
questions.question: When the interview matcher cannot choose between two topics, the patient asks "Sorry, do you mean X, or Y?" instead of guessing. That turns an invisible wrong answer into a visible question, but it may hint at a topic the learner did not think of. Do you keep it?
questions.context:
The interview is free text matched to authored topics. A wrong match gives a confident wrong answer that the learner cannot detect, which the authoring guide calls the highest technical risk. Since v0.8, when two topics score within a hair of each other, the patient names both in lay words and answers neither.

On the held-out question sets there were eight clarifications: four had the right topic in the pair, two replaced a wrong answer, and two replaced a false match on an out-of-scope question. The design note that proposed this asked a physician educator to decide it, because naming both options tells the learner both are worth asking. The build put the question in the patient's mouth rather than the nurse's, as first proposed.
questions.current: engine interview composer: clarify_template from interviewDefaults ("Sorry, do you mean ... or ...?"), using each topic's echo phrase. It can be overridden per case under interview.clarify_template. It is live in all four cases.

quotes.text: "Do you mean whether he sleeps flat, or whether he wakes at night?" tells the resident that both are things worth asking. That is a hint they did not earn, delivered at the moment they were closest to missing something.
A physician educator should decide this, not me.
Of the eight clarifications on the held-out sets, four had the right topic in the pair, two replaced a wrong answer, two replaced an out-of-scope false accept.

options.label: Keep the patient's clarifying question
options.detail: As now. The patient asks which of two things you meant.
options.tradeoff: Prevents confident wrong answers and reads like a real patient. It sometimes names a topic the learner had not thought to ask.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off.

options.label: Answer the best match, visibly flagged
options.detail: No clarifying question. The patient answers the top topic, opening with its echo phrase ("About my tablets..."), so a wrong match is visible.
options.tradeoff: Never hints at a second topic. More wrong answers reach the learner, marked only by the echo phrase.
options.implementation: engine interview composer: disable the clarify branch and always use the marginal-match echo prefix for near ties. Rerun engine/matcher_eval.mjs and record the new wrong-topic counts.

options.label: Say nothing specific
options.detail: On a near tie the patient says they did not understand (the out-of-scope fallback), and the learner rephrases.
options.tradeoff: No hint and no wrong answer. It costs a turn and may read as the tool failing, especially for questions a clinician phrased correctly.
options.implementation: engine interview composer: route near ties to the case's out_of_scope_fallback. Rerun matcher_eval.mjs.

questions.reasoning: A wrong interview answer can teach a false history, while a clarifying question costs at most an unearned hint. The echo phrases are lay words, so the hint is about what the patient heard rather than a medical prompt. The strongest argument against A is the design note's own: the hint arrives exactly when the learner was about to miss something. If history-taking is what a case scores, C is the stricter choice.
questions.evidence: The measured counts are from held-out sets written by an AI assistant and a case author, not by residents (authoring section 10.6), so real-world rates are unknown.

brief: On a near tie between two topics, the patient asks which one the learner meant.
This turns an invisible wrong answer into a visible question, but may hint at an unasked topic.
Held-out sets gave eight clarifications, four with the right topic in the pair.
short.now: Live in all four cases. The patient asks "Sorry, do you mean ... or ...?" in lay words.

opts.A: The patient asks which of two things you meant. Sometimes names a topic not yet considered.
opts.B: The patient answers the top match, opening with its echo phrase. More wrong answers reach learners.
opts.C: The patient says they did not understand, and the learner rephrases. Costs a turn.

short.why: A wrong answer can teach a false history, while a clarifying question costs at most an unearned hint in lay words. Against it, the hint arrives just as the learner was about to miss something.

questions.title: Should a volunteered answer count as asked, including for critical actions?
questions.question: Since v0.18b, patients volunteer an adjacent topic, and that topic then counts as asked for the History score and for interview actions. In CHFE this can satisfy a critical action the learner never asked about. What credit should volunteered topics earn?
questions.context:
Real patients say more than they are asked. Since v0.18b a topic may name up to two adjacent topics. When it is first answered, a short volunteer line from each adjacent topic is added, and those topics count as asked. Safety screens in interview.must_ask are never volunteered.

In CHFE, medication adherence is a critical action (interview_topic_medication_adherence). It is listed as adjacent to urine output, current medications and dietary sodium. A learner who asks any of those hears "I ran out of the water tablet about five days ago" and is credited with the critical adherence question.

The must-ask lists are: AFRVR allergies, caffeine and stimulants, anticoagulant history, code status. CHFE allergies, stimulants, PDE5 inhibitor use. DIPH nine screens including self-harm, suicidal intent and what she took. MGCA allergies, pregnancy, sexual history, menstrual and tampon use, social history, code status. Please check these lists too.
questions.current: engine.js volunteersFor: an adjacent topic counts as asked for the History score and for any interview_topic_ action. CHFE-case.json interview.topics: urine_output, current_medications and dietary_sodium list medication_adherence as adjacent. CHFE case_actions interview_topic_medication_adherence is tagged critical.

quotes.text: When it is first asked, the `volunteer` line of each adjacent topic that has not been spoken about is added to the answer in the same voice, and the adjacent topic counts as asked, for the History score and for any `interview_topic_` action.
'I ran out of the water tablet about five days ago.'

options.label: Keep full credit
options.detail: A volunteered topic counts as asked everywhere, including critical interview actions.
options.tradeoff: Rewards the information the learner actually obtained. It can credit a critical question the learner never thought to ask.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off, including the must-ask lists.

options.label: History score credit only
options.detail: Volunteered topics count toward the History score. A critical or recommended interview action is satisfied only when the learner asks the topic itself.
options.tradeoff: Keeps the scored action tied to the learner's own reasoning. A learner who heard the answer and acted on it is still marked as missing the question.
options.implementation: engine.js: record volunteered topics as volunteered, not asked. interview_topic_ actions test asked only, and summaryScores History counts both. Update section 10.7 and rerun the CHFE suite and scenarios.

options.label: No credit, information only
options.detail: Volunteered content is heard but never counts as asked.
options.tradeoff: The strictest. It penalizes efficient interviewing and makes the volunteer feature invisible to scoring.
options.implementation: engine.js: volunteered topics excluded from both History and interview actions. Update section 10.7.

questions.reasoning: A critical action should measure something the learner did. Hearing the adherence story by chance while asking about urine output is not the same as asking why the patient decompensated, which is what CHFE's objective names. B keeps that distinction and still rewards an efficient interview in the History score. The strongest argument against B is that it penalizes a learner who got the information, which a real attending would not. If you see history-taking as information gathered, choose A.

brief: Since v0.18b, patients volunteer up to two adjacent topics, which then count as asked.
In CHFE, asking about urine output, medications or sodium credits the critical adherence question.
Must-ask safety screens are never volunteered. Please check those lists too.
short.now: Volunteered topics count for the History score and interview actions. CHFE adherence is tagged critical.

opts.A: Volunteered topics count everywhere. Can credit a critical question the learner never asked.
opts.B: Volunteered topics count for History only. Scored actions need the learner to ask directly.
opts.C: Volunteered content never counts as asked. Penalizes efficient interviewing.

short.why: A critical action should measure what the learner did, and hearing adherence by chance differs from asking why the patient decompensated. Against it, B marks down a learner who got the information, which a real attending would not.

questions.title: May a critical action depend only on the free-text interview matcher?
questions.question: CHFE's critical adherence question can be satisfied only through the interview, which a free-text matcher decides. Should any critical action rest on the matcher alone?
questions.context:
Interview topics can be bound to actions and tagged like any other. The matcher is measured, not perfect. On CHFE's held-out set it answered 39 of 46 in-scope questions correctly, with 4 wrong topics. A learner who asks about adherence in words the matcher misses is marked as missing a critical action.

The audit raised this for CHFE (Educator minor 8) and suggested accepting the precipitant named at handoff as a second route. The same question applies to any future case that makes an interview topic critical.
questions.current: Only CHFE tags an interview action critical (CHFE-case.json case_actions interview_topic_medication_adherence, tag critical). The matcher accuracy table is in case-authoring-requirements.md section 10.6.

quotes.source: audit-v018a.txt, Open items, CHFE adherence question row
quotes.text: A critical action depends on the free-text matcher

quotes.source: audit-v018a.txt, Open items, CHFE adherence question row, suggested default
quotes.text: Also accept the precipitant named at handoff

options.label: Allowed, but always with a second route
options.detail: An interview topic may be critical only if a second, non-matcher route also satisfies it, such as naming the precipitant at handoff or asking a consultant. This generalizes the audit's CHFE default.
options.tradeoff: Keeps history-taking scored while limiting matcher error. It needs a second route authored per case, and the handoff route credits the knowledge after the fact.
options.implementation: Write the rule into section 7.3 of the authoring guide. In CHFE-case.json, add a satisfied_when or coverage on interview_topic_medication_adherence for a handoff diagnosis or a precipitant field, and add a validator warning for critical interview actions without a second route.

options.label: Never critical, recommended at most
options.detail: Interview topics can be recommended but not critical. The debrief still teaches why the question matters.
options.tradeoff: Removes matcher error from pass or fail. It downgrades history-taking in the one case that makes it a core objective.
options.implementation: Retag interview_topic_medication_adherence recommended in CHFE-case.json. Add a validator error for critical interview actions.

options.label: Keep as is
options.detail: The matcher decides, and the measured error rate is accepted.
options.tradeoff: No work. Some learners who asked correctly will be told they missed a critical action.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off.

questions.reasoning: Asking why the patient decompensated is a real objective and should stay scorable, but a critical verdict should not rest on a matcher with a measured wrong-topic rate. A second route caps the damage from a mismatch. The strongest argument against A is that a handoff route rewards naming the precipitant after the fact rather than seeking it during the resuscitation. B is cleaner if you think that difference matters more.
questions.evidence: Matcher figures are from held-out sets not written by residents (authoring section 10.6).
sources: audit-v018a.txt Educator minor 8 and Open items

brief: CHFE's critical adherence question can be satisfied only through the free-text interview matcher.
On CHFE's held-out set the matcher got 39 of 46 in-scope questions right, with 4 wrong topics.
The audit suggested also accepting the precipitant named at handoff.
short.now: Only CHFE tags an interview action critical (medication adherence), decided by the matcher alone.

opts.A: Critical interview topics need a second route, such as naming the precipitant at handoff.
opts.B: Interview topics can be recommended but not critical. Downgrades CHFE's core history objective.
opts.C: The matcher decides. Some learners who asked correctly are marked as missing it.

short.why: Asking why the patient decompensated should stay scorable, but not rest on a matcher with a measured wrong-topic rate. Against it, a handoff route rewards naming the precipitant after the fact.

questions.title: Who should write the held-out question sets that measure the interview matcher?
questions.question: The matcher's accuracy figures come from held-out questions written by an AI assistant and a case author, not by the residents who will use it. Who should write the sets that the figures are quoted from?
questions.context:
Each case has a held-out question file used to quote matcher accuracy, and a tuning file used to set thresholds. The held-out sets were written by an AI assistant and a case author. The phrasing library they test was written the same way. If the same people write the bank and the test, the test measures the register they already wrote in.

The site's analytics currently send no questions (v0.18f), so there is no pool of real learner questions to draw from. Collecting one would need consent and a change to what is logged.
questions.current: Held-out sets: <PREFIX>-matcher-eval-questions.json per case, written by an AI assistant and a case author (authoring section 10.6). No resident-written or logged questions exist.

quotes.text: Nothing here was collected from residents. The held-out sets were written by an AI assistant and a case author, and the tuning sets are the library's own withheld phrasings, so they measure the matcher against the registers the library anticipated.
If it is written after the variants by the same person, the measurement is close to worthless.

options.label: Independent clinicians write them now
options.detail: Two or three residents or attendings who did not author the case each write questions for it in their own typing style, at least 30 in scope and 30 out of scope, before any further tuning. Claude does not see them until the harness runs.
options.tradeoff: A real measurement soon. It takes clinician time, and their register may still differ from learners under time pressure.
options.implementation: Create <PREFIX>-matcher-eval-questions.json from the submitted questions with a provenance field naming the writers. Freeze the old sets as tuning-only. Rerun engine/matcher_eval.mjs and update the table in section 10.6.

options.label: Use real learner questions from a consented pilot
options.detail: Log typed interview questions (with consent) during a pilot and use a held-back sample as the held-out set.
options.tradeoff: The most valid source. It needs consent wording, a logging change and a pilot, so there are no numbers until then.
options.implementation: engine/analytics.js: an opt-in event carrying the question text and the matched topic. Consent text on sign-up. A script to sample and label a held-out set. Physicians label the expected topics.

options.label: Keep the current sets
options.detail: The AI and author sets remain the reference.
options.tradeoff: No work. The quoted accuracy likely overstates real performance.
options.implementation: No change. Record the limitation in each review packet.

questions.reasoning: An independent set is the quickest way to learn whether the quoted accuracy holds, and it is a prerequisite for trusting ALL-21 to ALL-23. B is the better long-term source and can follow in a pilot. The strongest argument against A is that clinicians writing questions at a desk still do not type like a resident in a timed case.

brief: Matcher accuracy comes from held-out questions written by an AI assistant and a case author.
The same people wrote the phrasing library, so the test measures their own register.
Analytics send no questions, so no pool of real learner questions exists.
short.now: Each case's held-out set was written by an AI assistant and a case author. No resident-written questions exist.

opts.A: Two or three outside clinicians each write at least 30 in-scope and 30 out-of-scope questions.
opts.B: A consented pilot logs real learner questions. No numbers until the pilot runs.
opts.C: The current sets stay. Quoted accuracy likely overstates real performance.

short.why: An independent set is the quickest check that quoted accuracy holds, and ALL-21 to ALL-23 depend on it. Against it, clinicians at a desk still do not type like residents in a timed case.

questions.title: Should the debrief print seven percentage scores at all?
questions.question: The debrief summary prints seven percentages (History, Physical, Stabilization, Interventions, Investigations, Consults, Handoff) with their arithmetic. Should it keep percentages, or show counts and named lists?
questions.context:
The formulas: History is key topics asked over key topics listed. Physical is regions examined over the exams tagged critical or recommended, or the case's key_exams list. Each ordering tab scores critical at two points and recommended at one, minus one per discouraged action. Handoff is level of care (40), primary diagnosis (40, or 60 with no additional diagnoses), and additional diagnoses (20, pro rata). A defensible answer earns half, and each unsupported diagnosis costs five.

The weights were set by the design, not by an educator. The audit found the tab percentages low even on a textbook run (ALL-01). The authoring guide says the scores are not a claim about ranking residents. A learner will still read 45 percent as failing.
questions.current: engine.js summaryScores, described in case-authoring-requirements.md section 13.0. Arrest and harmful-halt runs are not scored (v0.18a).

quotes.text: Nothing here is a claim about how residents should be ranked

options.label: Keep seven percentages
options.detail: As now, after the tagging fix in ALL-01.
options.tradeoff: A number learners can track. The weights are arbitrary, and a percentage invites ordering more to raise it.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off of the weights in section 13.0.

options.label: Counts and named lists, no percentages
options.detail: Each area shows what was done and what was missed by name, with counts ("7 of 9 critical actions", "3 discouraged actions taken"). No overall percentage.
options.tradeoff: Keeps attention on what to change next time. Learners and programs lose a single number to compare runs.
options.implementation: engine/ui.js debrief summary: replace percentage cells with counts and lists from the same summaryScores data. Rewrite section 13.0.

options.label: Percentages for ordering tabs only
options.detail: The four ordering tabs keep a percentage (after ALL-01). History, Physical and Handoff show named items only.
options.tradeoff: Keeps a number where the tagging policy makes it meaningful. Mixed presentation may confuse.
options.implementation: engine/ui.js: percentages for the four tabs, lists for the other three. Rewrite section 13.0.

questions.reasoning: This is a formative tool, and a named list tells the learner what to do differently, which a percentage does not. The weights behind the percentages have no educational basis a physician has signed. The strongest argument against B is that learners and program directors often want a number to track progress, and removing it may reduce engagement.
questions.evidence: Feedback that names specific behaviors is generally more useful for learning than a grade alone (feedback literature, for example Hattie and Timperley 2007, from memory, verify).

brief: The debrief prints seven percentages with their arithmetic, using weights set by the design, not an educator.
Tab percentages run low even on a textbook run.
The guide says scores do not rank residents, but a learner will read 45 percent as failing.
short.now: Seven percentages (History, Physical, Stabilization, Interventions, Investigations, Consults, Handoff). Arrest and harmful-halt runs unscored.

opts.A: Seven percentages stay, after ALL-01. Arbitrary weights may invite ordering more to score higher.
opts.B: Each area names what was done and missed, with counts. No overall percentage.
opts.C: Ordering tabs keep percentages. History, Physical and Handoff show named items. Mixed presentation.

short.why: In a formative tool a named list tells learners what to change, and no physician has signed the weights. Against it, learners and program directors often want a number to track progress.

questions.title: Should learning objectives be rewritten as behaviors the case can observe?
questions.question: Several objectives ask the learner to "state why" or "justify", which the case cannot observe. Should every objective be rewritten as a behavior the simulator can see?
questions.context:
Each case lists learning objectives in metadata. Some describe observable acts ("Give sodium bicarbonate for QRS widening"). Others ask the learner to state or justify something, which no action or handoff field records. The educator review found this in several cases and suggested rewriting them as behaviors. The DIPH-specific gap (no objective for involving toxicology and critical care) is in the DIPH bank.

Examples: AFRVR's objective 4, CHFE objectives 1 and 2, DIPH objectives 3 and 5, MGCA objective 4.
questions.current: metadata.learning_objectives in each <CASE>-case.json (AFRVR in cases/AFRVR/case_1_shell.py).

quotes.text: DIPH has none for toxicology and critical care, and several "state why" objectives cannot be observed

quotes.source: audit-v018a.txt, Open items, Objectives row, suggested default
quotes.text: Add DIPH objective 7 and rewrite as behaviours
Select a rate-control strategy that accounts for reduced systolic function, and state why a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker is the wrong agent once the ejection fraction is known.

options.label: Keep as written
options.detail: Objectives stay as they are. The debrief notes carry the "why".
options.tradeoff: No work. Some objectives cannot be assessed, and the debrief cannot say whether they were met.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off.

options.label: Rewrite as observable behaviors
options.detail: Each objective names an act the case records, for example "Avoids diltiazem once the ultrasound shows reduced function". The "why" moves into the debrief notes.
options.tradeoff: Every objective becomes checkable against the run. Some reasoning goals lose their place in the objective list.
options.implementation: Rewrite metadata.learning_objectives in CHFE-case.json and MGCA-case.json and in cases/AFRVR and cases/DIPH case_1_shell.py. Link each to the action ids that evidence it in a new objectives_map field for the debrief.

options.tradeoff: Keeps reasoning goals and invites the learner to articulate them. Nothing checks the answer.

opts.B: Each objective names an act the case records. The why moves into debrief notes.
opts.C: State-why objectives stay, with an unscored reflection question in the debrief. Nothing checks answers.

questions.title: Should case categories describe the presentation rather than the diagnosis?
questions.question: The case list filters by category, and DIPH's "Toxicology" tells the learner the answer before they start. Should categories name presentations instead?
questions.context:
Categories now: AFRVR "Cardiovascular", CHFE "Cardiovascular", DIPH "Toxicology", MGCA "Infectious disease". The list also shows each case's short complaint ("Confusion and fever" for DIPH). DIPH's teaching frame depends on the learner finding the toxidrome, and a Toxicology label removes that step. "Infectious disease" does less harm for MGCA, but still frames the case.

The same list now appears on the public welcome page (v0.19).

questions.title: How should the model-drafted action and diagnosis catalogs be reviewed?
