questions.title: Do you confirm how the drawn patient looks across all cases?
questions.question: The figure in the room (faces, alertness, seizure, breathing, devices, build and age) was drawn and ruled by a model. Please check the global depictions that every case shares.
questions.context:
The figure is a cartoon patient between the panels. Its global conventions apply in every case: a standard man or woman chosen by patient.sex, brown skin, dark hair. Distress sets the brows and mouth. Alertness sets the eyes: level 1 is drowsy with a nodding head, level 2 is closed eyes opening to a sliver every five to ten seconds with a slack jaw. A seizure is drawn with the eyes open and the jaw clenched at any alertness level. An intubated patient is always drawn with eyes closed, which assumes sedation. Everyone sits on a stretcher at about 45 degrees. Defibrillation pads bare the chest, a central line is drawn in the right internal jugular (no case names a site), the bag-valve mask shows a C-E grip, and obese and older builds add fuller or lined faces.

The case-specific rules (which phase shows what) are in each case's own bank. This item is the shared drawing and behavior.

**How to check:** open build/patient-lab.html. Step through the four alertness levels, the seizure, the three work-of-breathing levels, each device, and the obese and older builds. Or ask Claude for a one-page contact sheet of every state. Note anything a clinician would read as wrong or that you would not show learners (for example a sitting posture for a patient the text says is supine).

questions.title: Should cardioversion and defibrillation require pads to be placed first?

A gate teaches setup before a planned shock. In an arrest, a gate adds a step to the most time-critical act, although in practice pads go on first there too.

questions.title: Should pulseless phases show a respiratory rate of zero?
questions.question: Arrest and halted phases author a respiratory rate of 4 to 6 while their descriptions say there is no effort, so the drawn patient's shoulders still rise and the monitor shows a rate. What should they show?
questions.context:
The drawn patient breathes at the monitor's rate, and only a rate of zero stops the chest. Current terminal phases: CHFE halted 6. DIPH pulseless_vt 4 (pressure 0/0, saturation 52) and halted 5. MGCA cardiac_arrest 4 (26, 44/24, saturation 58) and halted 6. AFRVR halted now shows respiratory failure at 40.

Agonal gasps are real early in arrest and worth teaching. But a steady rate of 4 on the monitor and a slow, regular rise of the shoulders do not look like gasping. A pulseless patient with a displayed saturation of 52 is also not what a pulse oximeter would show. Whether MGCA's arrest phase is pulseless at all is a question in the MGCA bank.

options.tradeoff: Teaches that agonal breathing is not breathing. The figure still shows regular slow breaths rather than gasps.

options.tradeoff: The figure and monitor agree with "no pulse, no breathing". The saturation shown in a pulseless phase stays a separate oddity.

questions.title: Does the heartbeat sound right: irregularity in AF and pitch with saturation?
questions.question: The monitor's beep follows the heart rate, varies beat to beat in an irregularly irregular rhythm, and falls in pitch as saturation falls. Every parameter is a teaching choice, none is measured. Please listen and confirm.
questions.context:
The irregular rhythm draws each R-R interval from a shifted exponential that keeps the average rate equal to the number on the monitor. There is a floor of 240 ms between beats, enforced by narrowing the spread rather than clipping. Beat loudness varies a little. The pitch falls one semitone per percent of saturation, anchored so that 88 percent sounds at 880 Hz. The parameters are global, so every irregular case sounds the same.

**How to check:** open AFRVR, attach the monitor and listen for 30 seconds at 160 (presentation). Give two rate-control doses and listen at about 108. Then open CHFE (regular, 118) and compare. For pitch, listen to CHFE at arrival (85 percent) and at completion (94 percent). Ask yourself whether AF at 160 sounds like AF to you, and whether the pitch change is noticeable without being tiring.

questions.title: Is a 50 mm/s monitor sweep right, and does the stylized trace look acceptable?
questions.question: The monitor draws lead II at 50 mm/s, twice the usual display speed, so a wide QRS is visible. Wide complexes use a stylized shape that is not fitted to data. Do you keep this?
questions.context:
The trace was first built at 25 mm/s. At that speed DIPH's 132 ms QRS did not look wide, so the sweep became 50 mm/s and the wide-complex blend was steepened (it begins at 90 ms and saturates at 170). The cost is about three seconds on screen, which is five to eight beats. A learner used to 25 mm/s may misjudge the rate or the width from the screen. Nothing on the monitor says which speed it is.

The wide complex is one stylized shape (a short initial r, a broad terminal S, a discordant T). The decision record calls it the weakest claim in the change.

**How to look:** open DIPH and compare arrival (132 ms), seizing (148 ms), wide-complex tachycardia (180 ms) and stabilizing (104 ms). Then open AFRVR to see the P-less irregular trace.
questions.current: engine/monitor.js sweep 50 mm/s (CHANGELOG v0.16b). The shapes are in SHARED.monitor.ecg with a provenance note. Per-phase ecg blocks are in each case.

quotes.text: It is one shape of wide complex among several a real patient might show, and `t_mv` and `st_mv` are the author's way to move it. This is the weakest claim in the change and the provenance note says so.
The cost is half the seconds on screen, about three on a 600 px trace.

options.detail: Keep the speed and the shapes, and print "50 mm/s" on the trace as a real monitor would.
options.tradeoff: Widths stay legible and the label prevents misreading. It still differs from the default display most learners know.
options.implementation: engine/monitor.js: draw a "50 mm/s" label in the trace corner. Record sign-off of the shapes.

options.label: Return to 25 mm/s
options.detail: Standard display speed, with the steeper blend kept so borderline widths still slur.
options.tradeoff: Familiar to learners. DIPH's early widening is harder to see, which is the reason the speed changed.
options.implementation: engine/monitor.js sweep back to 25 mm/s. Check DIPH phases visually and record the result.

options.detail: Default 25 mm/s. The learner can switch to 50 mm/s, as on a real monitor.
options.tradeoff: Realistic, and it teaches a real control. It adds interface, and a learner who never toggles may miss DIPH's widening.
options.implementation: engine/ui.js and engine/monitor.js: a speed control on the monitor, logged as a timeline event.

The strongest argument against A is realism: learners should practice at the speed they will meet, and C would teach choosing the speed to look at a QRS, which is the real skill.

questions.title: Should the catalog's naming and placement problems be fixed in one pass?
questions.question: The catalog review found several names and placements that could mislead: a duplicated magnesium entry, vasopressin under resuscitation drugs, "TDaP", an unnamed amphotericin formulation, and penicillin G without a formulation. Ids come from names, so each rename touches every case that uses it. How do you want these handled?
questions.context:
The items:
- Magnesium: magnesium_sulfate (four placements) and magnesium_sulfate_bolus both exist. No maintenance infusion exists (see ALL-17).
- Vasopressin bolus sits in Meds - Resuscitation, although vasopressin was removed from the adult arrest algorithm.
- "TDaP" is the only tetanus entry, with no Td or tetanus immune globulin.
- "Amphotericin" does not say deoxycholate or liposomal, whose doses differ several-fold.
- "Penicillin G" does not say aqueous (IV) or benzathine (IM only).
- Several entries have route class "unspecified", and synonyms need cleanup.

Two of these are known causes of real medication errors: amphotericin formulation confusion and benzathine penicillin given IV. The epinephrine split (ALL-04), the hypertonic rename (ALL-05) and furosemide (ALL-16) belong in the same pass.
questions.current: catalog/action-catalog.json entries: magnesium_sulfate, magnesium_sulfate_bolus, vasopressin_bolus (Meds - Resuscitation), tdap ("TDaP"), amphotericin, penicillin_g, and entries with route_class "unspecified".

options.label: One pass with an id map
options.detail: Fix all names, placements and duplicates at once, together with ALL-04, ALL-05 and ALL-16. Old ids map to new ones, and every case is retagged and retested.
options.tradeoff: One review and one retest. A large change set, so errors in the map would affect every case at once.
options.implementation: catalog: apply the renames with an id_map in catalog/build_catalog.py. Rename to Tdap and add Td and tetanus immune globulin. Split amphotericin into deoxycholate and liposomal. Rename to penicillin G aqueous (IV). Merge the magnesium duplicate. Move vasopressin_bolus out of Resuscitation. Update the bindings in all four cases and the voice aliases, then rerun everything.

options.label: Safety-relevant renames only
options.detail: Fix amphotericin, penicillin G, epinephrine and hypertonic saline now. Leave cosmetic items.
options.tradeoff: Smaller change focused on error-prone drugs. The duplicates and placements stay confusing.
options.implementation: As A for the four named items only.

options.label: Defer until a case needs them
options.detail: Leave the catalog as is until a case binds these entries.
options.tradeoff: No work now. The misleading names remain visible to every learner, because the whole catalog is on every menu.
options.implementation: No change. Keep the items in known_gaps.

questions.reasoning: Every learner sees every entry, so a misleading name matters even when no case uses it. One id-mapped pass is safer than several partial ones. The strongest argument against A is blast radius: a mistake in the map breaks bindings in every case at once, so the full suites and scenarios must pass before release.
questions.evidence: Fatal errors from confusing amphotericin B formulations, and from giving benzathine penicillin IV, are described in medication safety alerts (ISMP and FDA, from memory, verify). Vasopressin was removed from the AHA adult arrest algorithm in 2015 (from memory, verify).

brief: Misleading entries include duplicate magnesium, vasopressin under resuscitation drugs, TDaP, and amphotericin and penicillin G without formulation.
Amphotericin confusion and IV benzathine penicillin are known causes of real medication errors.
Ids come from names, so each rename touches every case using it.
short.now: Vasopressin bolus sits under resuscitation drugs. TDaP is the only tetanus entry. Some routes are unspecified.

opts.A: All names, placements and duplicates fixed with ALL-04, ALL-05 and ALL-16. Map errors hit every case.
opts.B: Amphotericin, penicillin G, epinephrine and hypertonic saline fixed now. Duplicates and placements stay confusing.
opts.C: Catalog unchanged until a case binds these. Every learner still sees misleading names.

short.why: Every learner sees every entry, so misleading names matter even unused, and one mapped pass is safer than several. Against it, a map mistake breaks bindings in every case, so all suites must pass before release.

questions.title: Is the three-minute reflection pause right for every case?
questions.question: At three minutes of case time every case stops for a pause that the learner cannot dismiss: "consider your differential diagnosis." The note now appears in the debrief beside the diagnosis. Keep it as is?
questions.context:
The pause fires once per case at 3:00, whatever is happening. It holds the clock and cannot be dismissed without pressing Continue. It is global by design, so no case can switch it off.

Since v0.18a, the learner's note is printed in the debrief beside the case's diagnosis (v0.17n had said it would not be shown). In all four cases the first timed change is at 240 seconds (DIPH's seizure, and the first deterioration in AFRVR, CHFE and MGCA), so the pause lands about a minute before it. That may be a good moment to think, or it may feel like a warning.
questions.current: SHARED.reflect in engine/build_simulator.py: one pause at 180 s case time. The note is shown in the debrief since v0.18a.

quotes.text: Pause: consider your differential diagnosis. Consider the implications of each. What do you need to check or give?

options.label: Keep a fixed pause at 3:00 in every case
options.detail: As now.
options.tradeoff: Predictable and simple. Its timing relative to each case's clock differs, and in some cases it may read as a hint that something is coming.
options.implementation: No change. Record sign-off.

options.label: Case-authored moment, 3:00 by default
options.detail: Each case may set when the pause fires (for example after the first results return), and the default stays at 3:00.
options.tradeoff: Lets the pause land where thinking pays off in that case. It adds an authored field to review, and the design deliberately kept this out of case control.
options.implementation: Add metadata.reflect_after_seconds, read by engine/ui.js, with the validator range 60 to 300. Set it per case.

options.label: Optional pause
options.detail: The learner can dismiss the pause without writing.
options.tradeoff: Respects learner autonomy. It turns the pause into something many will skip.
options.implementation: engine/ui.js: add a Skip button to the reflection modal and log skips.

questions.reasoning: A fixed, universal pause is easy to explain and cannot be misused by a case to hint at timing. The strongest argument against A is that landing a minute before every case's first timed change may teach learners to expect trouble after the pause, which a case-set moment (B) would avoid.
questions.evidence: Structured pauses for reflection ("diagnostic time-outs") are proposed to reduce premature closure, with limited outcome evidence (from memory, verify).
sources: AFRVR, CHFE and DIPH phases timed transitions

brief: Every case stops at 3:00 for a pause the learner cannot dismiss, asking them to consider their differential.
In all four cases the first timed change is at 240 seconds, about a minute later.
That may be a good moment to think, or feel like a warning.
short.now: One global pause at 180 seconds that holds the clock. Since v0.18a the note shows in the debrief.

opts.A: A fixed pause at 3:00 everywhere. May read as a hint that something is coming.
opts.B: Each case may set the pause time, default 3:00. Adds an authored field to review.
opts.C: The learner can dismiss the pause without writing. Many will skip it.

short.why: A fixed, universal pause is easy to explain and cannot be misused by a case to hint at timing. Against it, landing a minute before every first timed change may teach learners to expect trouble.

questions.title: Do you confirm the roughly 30 notes reworded to remove reviewer wording?
questions.question: In v0.18a, about 30 debrief notes across the four cases were reworded to remove author, reviewer and engine language, and reviewer markers are now stripped at display. Please confirm the rewording kept each note's clinical meaning.
questions.context:
Learners had been seeing text such as "[UNVERIFIED, confirm before release]", "AUTHOR NOTE" and references to the catalog and the engine. The fix strips markers at display and rewrote about 30 notes. Rewording a clinical sentence can change its meaning, and the audit marks this row as needing sign-off.

**How to check:** ask Claude for a before-and-after list of every reworded note (from the v0.18a diff), grouped by case. Read each pair and mark any where the teaching changed.

questions.title: Do you confirm the shared phrasing library, lexicon and voice vocabulary?
questions.question: Several shared language resources decide which question or order the learner meant: the interview phrasing library, the clinical abbreviation lexicon, the out-of-scope bank, the volunteer adjacencies and the voice-order vocabulary. A wrong mapping gives a confident wrong answer in every case. Please confirm them.
questions.context:
The resources, all model-drafted:
- catalog/interview_phrasings.py: about sixty concepts, with lay, clinical and shorthand phrasings.
- The abbreviation lexicon in ui.js: about 120 entries (pnd, nkda, lmp and others), rewritten into lay words.
- catalog/interview_out_of_scope.py: questions each case treats as having no answer.
- catalog/author_interview_volunteers.py: which topics volunteer which (see ALL-22).
- The voice-order vocabulary: about 5,000 phrases, 2,200 of them added in v0.17n.

The authoring guide itself says the phrasing library is clinical content and belongs on the review list.

**How to check:** a full read is long. Ask Claude for a sample focused on management-changing concepts and pertinent negatives: each phrase with the topic or order it maps to, plus every abbreviation. Mark wrong mappings.
questions.current: catalog/interview_phrasings.py, catalog/interview_out_of_scope.py, catalog/author_interview_volunteers.py, the lexicon in engine/ui.js and the voice vocabulary in engine/voice.js. None is physician-reviewed.

quotes.text: The library is clinical content and belongs on the review list. A phrasing that maps a question to the wrong concept produces a confident wrong answer for every case that uses the concept.

questions.title: Do you confirm the welcome-page demo and the red arrival-vital thresholds?
questions.question: The public welcome page has a 30-second pulmonary edema demo whose numbers are illustrative, and each case card shows arrival vitals in red outside set adult ranges. Both are clinical content that every visitor sees. Please confirm them.
questions.context:
The demo: a 65-year-old man in pulmonary edema on a live monitor. Three buttons (sit him upright, non-rebreather, BiPAP) move the numbers toward better targets. Untreated, he drifts toward exhaustion. It ends on "Better. Not fixed." or "He's tiring." Its numbers are independent of the CHFE case.

The case card thresholds: heart rate under 60 or over 100, systolic under 90 or 140 and over, diastolic 90 and over, SpO2 under 94, respiratory rate under 12 or over 20, temperature under 36.0 or 38.0 and over.

**How to check:** open the signed-out site and play the demo three ways (each button alone, all three, none). Check that the direction and size of each change is believable and that nothing teaches a wrong priority. Then look at the four case cards.
questions.current: engine/landing.js (demo) and the case card thresholds in engine/ui.js (CHANGELOG v0.19 and v0.18g).

quotes.text: Its numbers are illustrative and independent of the CHFE case pack, which the page never loads.
